Initially created: 2025-12-06T13:40:56.259+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
奉命编辑
后 学 天 台
齐宣德太后诏令萧衍从建安郡公进爵为梁公，
这是萧衍的意愿。
不久进爵为王，
不久接受齐的禅让，
国家因此定国号为梁。
高祖武皇帝
名衍，
字叔达，
小名练儿，
南兰陵中都里人，
姓萧。
与齐皇室同出自淮阴县令萧整，
传三世至萧顺之，
萧顺之是齐高帝的族弟，
皇帝，
是萧顺之的儿子。
按《通鉴》武皇帝纪共十八卷，
以一二为序，
此卷
“武皇帝”
之下应有
字。
天监元年（壬午年，502年）
从本年三月以前，
仍是齐和帝中兴二年。
1 春季，
正月，
齐和帝派遣兼侍中席阐文等人慰劳建康。
2 大司马萧衍下令：
“凡是东昏侯时期的不必要开支，
除非是用于演习礼乐的仪容，
修缮铠甲兵器的储备，
其余一律禁止。”
3 戊戌日，
迎接宣德太后入宫，
临朝听政，行使皇帝权力；
萧衍解除承制职权。
萧衍承制之事见上卷上年。
暂时解除以观察人心。
朝，
音直遥反。
4 己亥日，
任命宁朔将军萧昺监管南兖州各项军事。
萧昺，
是萧衍的堂弟。
5 壬寅日，
晋升大司马萧衍为都督中外诸军事，
允许佩剑穿鞋上殿，
朝拜时赞礼官不直呼其名。
6 己酉日，
任命大司马长史王亮为中书监、尚书令。
7 当初，
大司马与黄门侍郎范云、南清河太守沈约、司徒右长史任昉同在竟陵王西邸，
事见一百三十六卷齐武帝永明二年。
守，
音式又反。
任，
音壬。
昉，
音分两反。
敦，
意为厚。
好，
音呼到反。

萧衍录尚书事，
其录府事务让范云掌管。
任命沈约为骠骑大将军府司马。
骠，
音匹妙反。
骑，
音奇寄反。
参与谋划商议。
前吴兴太守谢朏、国子祭酒何胤先前都已弃官家居，
齐明帝建武初年，
谢朏、何胤都弃官离去。
朏，
音敷尾反。
先，
音悉荐反。
谢朏、何胤都未到任。
大司马内心有接受禅让的志向，
沈约略微试探其意图，
大司马没有回应；
他日，
又进言说：
“今时与古代不同，
不能用淳朴的风气来期望世人。
淳风，
指淳朴古风。
都期望能建立尺寸之功。
如今连孩童牧童都知道齐的国运已尽，
明公应当承继其运数，
天文谶记又都明白显著；
天意不可违背，
人心不可失去。
如果天命所在，
即使想谦让，
也不可能了。”
《易经》说：谦逊而能光大。
“我正在考虑此事。”
沈约说：
“公当初在樊、沔建立军府时，
此时就应该考虑；
如今王业已成，
还有什么可考虑的！
如果不早日确定大业，
倘若有一人提出异议，

况且人非金石，
时事难以保证，

不再有异心，
君主在上英明，
臣子在下尽忠，

大司马认为他说得对。
沈约出来后，
大司马召来范云告诉他，

大司马说：
“智者竟然如此暗合。
你明早带休文再来！”
将，

挟带，
带领。
休文，

范云告诉沈约，

“你一定要等我！”
范云答应，
但沈约提前进入。
大司马命他起草相关事宜，

到殿门，
不能进入，

咄，

范云问道：
“（给我）安排了什么职位？”

意思是安排他担任尚书左仆射。
处，
音昌吕反。
“没有违背期望。”
过了一会儿，

several Imperial Guards pronounced the decree and summoned him,

Zhēn Chēn and Wáng Xiǎn supervised his punishment,
preparing five strong individuals for interrogation,
who alternately whipped him,
with the intention to ensure his death.
Xiū, normally robust,
could endure severe torture,
but secretly endured over three hundred lashes and did not die.
He was then mounted on a post horse,
hastened on his journey,
and as he left the city, unable to support himself,
he was lifted and set upon the saddle.
Lifted,
means carried.
Xiū was extremely weakened, unable to ride,
and needed two people to lift him onto the horse,
tying him to the saddle.
After traveling eight miles,
he died.
Upon hearing this,
the emperor rebuked Yuán Shào for not promptly reporting,
Shào said:
"Xiū's deceitful favor
was a major corruption to the state,
if I hadn't seized the opportunity to eliminate him,
opportunity,
means rift.
Opportunity,
is pronounced 'xù'.
The emperor accepted this reasoning,
and did not punish him.
When Shào left,
Guǎngpíng King Huái bowed to him and said:
"You are more upright than Jí Àn."
Shào replied:
"I only regret executing him too late,
which is my only shame."
Shào,
was Sù's grandson.
Chángshān King Sù is in Volume 122, Year Yuanjia 11 of Emperor Wén of Sòng.
Guǎngpíng King Huái,
was Emperor Xiaowen's son,
and due to familial seniority,
addressed Shào as 'Elder'.
Zhēn Chēn and Li Píng were implicated in Xiū's faction and were dismissed from office,
while over twenty of his associates suffered execution or dismissal.
Regular Cavalry Attendant Gāo Cōng, having been close to Xiū,
but also ingratiatingly served Gāo Zhào as a clansman,
uniquely avoided punishment.
In the spring,
on the day Gēngxū,
General Zhào Zuǒyuè battled the Wèi Jiangzhou Inspector Chén Bózhī at Dōngguān,
resulting in Zuǒyuè's defeat.
On the day Guǐchǒu,
Minister Shàngshū Righthand Servant Wáng Yíng was appointed Left Servant,
and Crown Prince Chamberlain Liǔ Tán became Right Servant.
On the day Bǐngchén,
Wèi Eastern Jingzhou Inspector Yáng Dàyǎn attacked the rebellious tribes of Fán Jì'ān and others,
achieving a major victory.
Jì'ān,
was the younger brother of Sù Ān.
5. Xiāo Bǎoyín advanced to Rǔyīn,
but Dōngchéng had already been captured by Liáng,
so he stationed his troops at Qīxián Temple in Shòuyáng.
In February,
on the day Wùzǐ,
General Jiāng Qìngzhēn took advantage of the fact that Rènchéng Wáng Yuán Chéng was away from the city—
last year, Wèi had sent Chéng to invade,
and his army was encamped outside—
and seized the outer walls.
The Chief Clerk Wéi Zuǎn was caught off guard and lost his composure;
the Princess of Rènchéng, Mèng shì, rallied troops to mount the parapets,
first securing the strategic points,
which the enemy would inevitably attack,
and which we must defend—these are called “strategic points.”
As for “advantageous positions,”
they refer to terrain that is favorable and can be held,
places that are convenient for controlling the enemy.
Parapet,
pronounced pí, with the tone mián.
She reassured both the new and old troops,
the “new” referring to
the soldiers and civilians of Shòuyáng;
the “old” referring to
the generals and soldiers who had come from the north.
Some say: the “new” are
those newly attached;
the “old” are
the original inhabitants.
The soldiers all felt inspired.
The princess personally inspected the city’s defenses,
not avoiding arrows and stones.
Xiāo Bǎoyín led his troops to arrive,
and together with the provincial army, they attacked,
fighting from the fourth watch until late afternoon,
before the sun had set,
which is called “late afternoon.”
Wéi Zuǎn was dismissed from his post.
Rènchéng Wáng Chéng attacked Zhōnglí,
and the Emperor sent Champion General Zhāng Huìshào and others with five thousand troops to deliver provisions to Zhōnglí.
Chéng sent General of Pacifying Distances Liú Sīzǔ and others to intercept them.
On the day Dīngyǒu,
they fought at Shàoyáng;
this is Shàoyáng Prefecture.
They captured Huìshào and ten other generals,
killing or capturing nearly all the soldiers.
Sīzǔ
was the nephew of Liú Fāng.
Liú Fāng was esteemed for his Confucian scholarship during the Tàihé era.
Defeated,
pronounced bù, tone mài.
General,
pronounced jiàng, tone jí liàng.
Nephew,
pronounced cóng, tone cái yòng.
He should have been enfeoffed as a marquis with a thousand households;
but the Palace Attendant and Commander of the Right Guard Yuán Huī requested two maidservants from Sīzǔ,
and when he did not get them,
the matter was dropped.
This shows that Wèi’s rewards and punishments were inappropriate.
He was the grandson of Sù.
The Emperor sent General of Pacifying the West Cáo Jǐngzōng and General of the Rear Army Wáng Sēngbǐng and others with thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to rescue Yìyáng.
“Rear Army” refers to
the General of the Rear Army.
Command,
pronounced shuài, meaning “to lead.”
Záoxiàn is south of the pass.
Now, thirty-five li south of Xìnyáng Garrison is Cáodiàn,
which is where Jǐngzōng stationed his troops and built at the mouth of Záoxiàn.
Xiàn,
pronounced hù diǎn.
Yuán Yīng sent Champion General Yuán Chěng and others to hold Fánchéng to resist them.
In March,
on the day Rénshēn,
they heavily defeated Sēngbǐng at Fánchéng,
capturing and killing over four thousand people.
Sēngbǐng was defeated at Fánchéng,
and never reached Záoxiàn.
Otherwise, this is not the Fánchéng of Xiāngyáng,
but a different place altogether.
Wèi issued an edict to Rènchéng Wáng Chéng,
saying
“In April, the Huái River will swell,
and boats will have no obstacles,
giving the southern army an advantage.
Do not be blinded by immediate gains and later regret it.”
Just then, heavy rain fell,
and the Huái River suddenly rose,
so Chéng led his troops back to Shòuyáng.
The Wèi army’s retreat was disorderly,
with over four thousand casualties.
The Secretariat Gentleman Jiǎ Sībó of Qí Commandery served as Chéng’s army supervisor,
staying behind to cover the retreat,
and Chéng, thinking him a mere scholar,
assumed he would surely die.
But when he arrived,
Chéng was overjoyed and said:
“ ‘The benevolent are sure to be courageous,’
as Confucius said in the Analects.
Sībó excused himself by saying he had lost his way,
and did not boast of his merit.
The responsible officials recommended stripping Chéng of his title of Kāifǔ,
and demoting him three ranks.
The Emperor offered to exchange the captured Wèi generals and soldiers for Zhāng Huìshào,
and the Wèi returned him.
Commentary: Huìshào’s biography does not mention his capture and return.
Here, we follow the Wèi Shū.
6. The Grand Tutor, concurrently Minister over the Masses, and Director of the Imperial Secretariat of Wèi, Běihǎi Wáng Yuán Xiáng,
was arrogant, extravagant, fond of music and women,
greedy and insatiable,
extensively building mansions,
seizing others’ residences,
favoring his close attendants,
accepting requests everywhere,
causing resentment both inside and outside the court.
The Wèi Emperor, because of his seniority and kinship,
did not diminish his favor and courtesy,
and consulted him on all major military and state affairs,
approving whatever he requested.
When the Wèi Emperor first took personal control of the government,
he summoned his uncles with troops,
as seen in the first year of the Zhōnghéng era of the Qí Hé Emperor, in the previous volume.
The guards were strict and tight.
The Grand Empress Dowager Gāo was greatly frightened,
following in a carriage and weeping.
After they were spared,
she said to Xiáng:
“From now on, I do not desire wealth and honor,
only that mother and son remain safe,
and I will sweep the market with you to make a living.”
When Xiáng again held power,
in the first year of the Zhōnghéng era of the Qí Hé Emperor, in the first month,
the Wèi Emperor took personal control of the government,
and in the eleventh month,
Xiáng became Minister over the Masses.
She exclusively helped Xiáng in his greed and cruelty.
Champion General Rú Hào,
clever and ingenious, was favored by the Emperor,
often staying by his side,
transmitting imperial approvals for memorials from the Chancellery,
abusing power and accepting bribes,
feared by the court and the public,
and Xiáng also attached himself to him.
Hào married the cousin of the Imperial Secretary Lìng Gāo Zhǎo;
Hào’s wife’s elder sister was the wife of Xiáng’s uncle Āndìng Wáng Yuán Xiè;
Xiáng had an illicit relationship with Xiè’s wife,
and because of this, he became even closer with Hào.
General of the Direct Guard Liú Zhòu,
originally recommended by Xiáng,
Palace General Cháng Jìxián, skilled in horse breeding,
and Chén Sǎojìng, in charge of grooming,
all gained the Emperor’s favor,
and together with Hào, they collaborated,
selling their influence.
Gāo Zhǎo originally came from Gāolì,
and was looked down upon by the prominent families of the time.
After the Emperor dismissed the six regents,
when the Wèi Gāozǔ died,
he had six people receive the testament to assist the young ruler,
as seen in the first year of the Yǒngyuán era of the Qí Dōng Hūn Hóu, in volume 142.
As seen in the first year of the Zhōnghéng era of the Qí Hé Emperor, in the previous volume.
Zhǎo, because he had few relatives in the court,
sought to form cliques and alliances,
promoting those who attached themselves to him within a month,
and framing those who did not with serious crimes.
He particularly feared the imperial princes,
and because Xiáng was above him in rank,
he wanted to remove him,
to monopolize the court’s administration,
so he slandered him to the Emperor,
saying
“Xiáng conspired with Hào, Zhòu, Jìxián, and Sǎojìng to rebel.”
In summer,
in April,
the Emperor summoned the Palace Aide to the Censor-in-Chief Cuī Liàng into the palace at night,
ordering him to impeach Xiáng for greed, debauchery, extravagance, and license,
and Hào and the other four for abusing power and greed,
arresting Hào and others and imprisoning them in the Southern Terrace,
and sending a hundred Tiger Guards to surround Xiáng’s mansion.
Fearing that Xiáng might panic and flee,
he sent his attendant Guō Yì to ride out through the Jīnyōng Gate to convey the imperial decree,
showing him the impeachment document from the Palace Aide.
Xiáng said:
“If it is truly as the Palace Aide has accused,
what is there to worry about!
I only fear that greater crimes may be unjustly imposed.
If people gave me things,
I indeed accepted them.”
The next morning,
the responsible officials recommended sentencing Hào and others,
and all were ordered to commit suicide.
The Emperor summoned the Prince of Gāoyáng, Yuán Yōng, and four other princes to deliberate on Yuán Xiáng’s crimes.
Xiáng was placed under guard in a single carriage
and sent to Huálín Garden.
His mother and wife followed him inside.
A few young male and female servants were provided,
the enclosure was heavily guarded,
and no communication with the outside was allowed.
In the fifth month,
on the first day, Dīngwèi,
an edict was issued pardoning Xiáng from death,
reducing him to a commoner.
Shortly after,
Xiáng was moved to the Tàifǔ Temple,
where the confinement became even stricter.
His mother and wife were both returned to the southern residence,
permitted to visit him only once every five days.
Initially,
Xiáng had married the daughter of Liú Chǎng, the Prince of Sòng,
but treated her coldly and neglectfully.
After Xiáng was imprisoned,
the Grand Empress Dowager Gāo learned about the affair with Āndìng Gāo.
Furious, she said:
"You have so many wives and concubines,
why did you need that Gāolì slave girl,
to bring such guilt upon yourself!"
She had him beaten over a hundred strokes.
His wounds festered with pus,
and it took more than ten days before he could stand again.
She also had Lady Liú beaten several dozen strokes,
saying:
"All women are jealous,
why are you alone not jealous!"
Lady Liú smiled and accepted the punishment,
and in the end said nothing.
Several of Xiáng’s household slaves secretly formed a gang,
intending to rescue Xiáng by force.
They wrote down their names in secret,
and entrusted a maidservant to deliver the list to Xiáng.
Xiáng had just taken hold of it to read
when the officer in charge of the gate guard saw it from a distance,
rushed in, and snatched it from Xiáng’s hand.
He reported it,
and Xiáng wept bitterly several times,
then suddenly died.
An edict ordered the relevant officials to bury him with proper rites.
The officer in charge of the gate guard
commanded the gate guard troops responsible for guarding Xiáng.
Prior to this,
the clerk Shǐ Yuánxiàn presented a chick
with four wings and four feet.
A clerk
is similar to today’s Zhǔshì in the Six Ministries of the Shàngshū,
a clerical position.
In Jiāngnán, the Bureau of Control had clerks.
Prior,
all recommended Fān.
Guāng submitted a memorial stating:
"During the Chūyuán era of Hàn Yuándì,
a hen belonging to a clerk of the Chancellor’s office hatched chicks
that gradually transformed into roosters.
Yán Shīgǔ said:
'At first it still hatched chicks,
but later gradually transformed into a rooster.
Hatch,
pronounced fáng fù fān.
Yán Shīgǔ said: The spur,
is the bone attached to a chicken’s foot,
used to stab in fights.
Lead,
means to command its flock.
There was a presentation of a rooster growing horns.
Liú Xiàng believed that 'the chicken is a small domestic animal,
responsible for marking the times and rousing people,
an omen of petty officials handling affairs and administering governance.
The event is recorded in the Treatise on the Five Elements of the History of the Western Hàn.
Shí Xiǎn met his deserved end,
this was its effect.'
In the first year of the Guānghé era of Emperor Líng of Hàn,
a hen at the Nángōng Temple was about to transform into a rooster,
but only its comb had not yet changed.
An edict inquired of the Court Gentleman for Consultation, Cài Yōng,
who replied: 'The head represents the sovereign,
the symbol of the ruler.
Now the chicken’s body has already transformed,
but not yet reached the head,
and Your Majesty knows of it.
This is an omen that an affair will arise but not reach completion.
If the response is not precise,
and governance shows no reform,
should the comb fully form,
the calamity would grow greater.'
The event is recorded in the Biography of Cài Yōng in the History of the Later Hàn.
The empire subsequently fell into great chaos.
Although the present chicken’s form differs from that of the Hàn,
its portent is quite similar,
truly fearsome.
I infer from the words of Xiàng and Yōng that
the numerous wings and feet
also symbolize subordinates inciting and assisting each other;
a chick not yet grown,
with feet and feathers still rather small,
also indicates the situation is still minor,
easy to control.
I have heard that the appearance of calamities and anomalies
all serve to reveal good or ill fortune.
An enlightened ruler sees them and fears,
thus able to attract blessing;
a benighted ruler sees them and is negligent,
thus bringing about disaster.
Perhaps now too there are those rising from lowly to noble status,
meddling in government affairs,
like Shí Xiǎn of former times!
I wish Your Majesty would promote the worthy and dismiss the sycophants,
then the ominous would cease and felicity gather."
Several days later,
Rú Hào and others were executed,
and the Emperor held Guāng in even greater esteem.
The Wèi sovereign considered Rú Hào’s execution as validation of Guāng’s words.
Was not Gāo Zhào alone one who rose from lowly to noble status,
meddling in government affairs?
Gāo Zhào persuaded the Emperor
to have the commanders of the palace guard units lead the Yǔlín and Hǔbēn guards to guard the residences of the various princes,
nearly equivalent to house arrest.
Prince Péngchéng, Yuán Xié, vehemently remonstrated,
but he was not heeded.
Xié’s aspirations were lofty and transcendent;
he took no pleasure in glory and power.
He avoided affairs and stayed at home,
yet when he went out, he had no delight in mountains and waters,
and at home, no companionship of intimate friends.
Alone facing his wife and children,
he was often depressed and unhappy.
7 The Wèi besieged Yìyáng.
The city’s troops numbered less than five thousand,
and provisions could last only half a year.
The Wèi army attacked,
ceaselessly day and night.
The Regional Inspector, Cài Dàogōng, resisted and defended as circumstances allowed,
each time repelling them handily.
The stalemate lasted over a hundred days,
with countless beheadings and captures on both sides.
The Wèi had besieged Yìyáng since the tenth month of last year;
Cài Dàogōng died in the fifth month of this year.
The above
refers to before Dàogōng’s illness became severe.
Shèng,
pronounced shēng.
They were about to retreat.
Then Dàogōng fell critically ill.
He summoned his cousin, the General of Agile Cavalry, Cài Líng’ēn,
his elder brother’s son, the Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat, Cài Sēngxié, and the various commanders and aides,
and said to them:
"I have received the state’s deep favor,
yet cannot repel and exterminate the bandit invaders.
Now my suffering grows critical,
and I cannot endure much longer.
You must hold fast to your integrity unto death,
and not let me die with regret!"
All wept.
After Dàogōng died,
Líng’ēn acted as administrator of the province,
taking his place in defending the city.
8 In the sixth month,
on Guǐwèi,
a general amnesty was declared.
9 There was a great drought in Wèi.
the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and concurrent Shàngshū, Xíng Luán, submitted a memorial stating:
"The enlightened kings of old valued grain and cloth,
and disdained gold and jade.
Why?
Because grain and cloth nourish the people and bring peace to the state,
while gold and jade are useless and corrupt virtue.
The late Emperor deeply understood extravagance,
and strove to promote frugality,
even using paper and silk for curtains and screens,
copper and iron for bridles and bits.
The gold in the treasury
was only sufficient for needs,
not further accumulated to waste state resources.
By the beginning of the Jǐngmíng era,
inheriting a time of peace and prosperity,
the four borders were tranquil,
and distant and near all came in harmony.
Then tribute baskets arrived in succession.
The phrases ‘tribute baskets’ originate from the Tribute of Yǔ,
meaning precious fine goods
presented in baskets as tribute.
All the offerings
far exceeded the usual,
gold and jade were constantly in surplus,
yet state expenditures were constantly insufficient.
If we do not impose limits on this,
I fear the annual accounts will not be balanced.
From now on, I request that all non-essential items be refused."
The Wèi sovereign accepted this.
In the autumn of the tenth year,
in the seventh month,
on the day Guǐchǒu,
the garrison commander of Jiǎochéng, Chái Qìngzōng, surrendered the city to Wei.
Yuán Jiàn, the Wei Inspector of Xúzhōu, dispatched Wú Qínshēng, the Grand Administrator of Huáiyáng, leading over a thousand men to reinforce him.
The relief forces from Huáiyīn cut off their route,
but Qínshēng fought repeatedly,
defeated them,
and thus captured Jiǎochéng.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
the Emperor’s son Zōng was enfeoffed as Prince of Yùzhāng.
Lǐ Chóng of Wei defeated the rebelling Man tribes of Dōngjīng,
capturing Fán Sù’ān alive,
then advanced to attack the various Man tribes of Xījīng,
all of whom surrendered.
Xījīng
precisely refers to Jīngzhōu.
During the Tàihé era of Wei,
the seat of Jīngzhōu was moved to Rǎngchéng,
administering the commanderies of Nányáng, Shùnyáng, Xīnyě, Dōnghénóng, Hànguǎng, Xiāngchéng, Běiqīng, Hénóng, and others.
Its territory lay directly west of Dōngjīngzhōu.
The Wei forces, hearing of Cài Dàogōng’s death,
attacked Yìyáng with increasing urgency,
engaging in close combat daily.
Cáo Jǐngzōng encamped at Záoxiàn and did not advance,
merely parading his troops and engaging in hunting excursions.
The Emperor again dispatched the General of Nìngshuò, Mǎ Xiānpín, to relieve Yìyáng.
Xiānpín fought his way forward,
his military momentum extremely fierce.
Yuán Yīng established fortifications at Shàngyǎ Mountain.
“Shàngyǎ Mountain”
should be
“Shìyǎ Mountain.”
[Chapter note: In the twelve-line edition,
“Shàng”
is correctly written as
“Shì”;
the eleven-line edition is the same;
the Kǒng edition is the same,
except
“Yǎ”
is written as

] According to the Shuǐjīng Zhù,
east of Yìyáng is Dàmù Mountain,
which is where Zǔ Tì of Jin moved his family to take refuge.
Tì’s courtesy name was Shìyǎ,
and later generations thus named the mountain after him.
Dù Yòu said: In Tángzhōu’s Tóngbǎi County is Dàmù Mountain,
where Zǔ Tì, as Inspector of Yùzhōu during Jin,
concealed his family within this mountain.
[Yuán Yīng] feigned weakness.
Xiānpín, riding the momentum of victory, advanced directly to the long siege lines,
launching a surprise attack on Yīng’s camp.
Yīng pretended to flee north to lure him,
and when they reached level ground,
unleashed his troops to attack.
The Army Commander Fù Yǒng, clad in armor and grasping a lance,
charged in alone on horseback,
with only the Army Commandant Cài Sānhǔ assisting him,
breaking through the enemy formation horizontally.
Liáng troops shot at Yǒng,
piercing his left thigh,
but Yǒng pulled out the arrow and charged in again.
Xiānpín was severely defeated,
with one of his sons dying in battle,
and Xiānpín retreated.
Yīng said to Yǒng:
“You are wounded,
you should return to camp.”
Yǒng said:
“In the past, Hàn Gāozǔ touched his foot, not wishing others to know [he was wounded].
The event is recorded in the tenth scroll, fourth year of Hàn Gāozǔ.
As a general of the state,
how can I let the enemy have the reputation of wounding a general!”
He then pursued with the various armies,
returning only at daybreak;
he was over seventy years old at the time,
and none in the army did not admire his valor.
Xiānpín again led over ten thousand men to attack Yīng,
but Yīng defeated him once more,
killing General Chén Xiùzhī.
Knowing Yìyáng was in critical danger,
Xiānpín committed all his elite forces for a decisive battle,
engaging three times in a single day,
but each time was greatly defeated and returned.
Had Mǎ Xiānpín fought strenuously,
and had Cáo Jǐngzōng followed up with the main army,
Wei would certainly have been defeated and retreated,
and Yìyáng would have been preserved.
In the eighth month,
on the day Yǐyǒu,
[Yìyáng] surrendered to Wei.
The garrison commanders of the Three Passes, hearing of this,
on the day Xīnyǒu,
also abandoned their cities and fled.
Yǐyǒu is thirty-six days from Xīnyǒu,
which is too far apart;
perhaps it should be Xīnmǎo!
Yīng had his Marshal Lù Xīdào draft a victory dispatch,
but finding it insufficiently refined,
ordered Fù Yǒng to revise it.
Yǒng did not add literary embellishment,
but simply laid out the military arrangements and strategic essentials.
Yīng deeply appreciated it,
saying:
“Seeing this strategic calculation,
even if one had a metal-walled city and a moat of boiling water,
it could not be defended.”
The historian states that Yīng boasted of his achievements,
hence he deeply appreciated Fù Yǒng’s ability to lay them out.
The Prince Huì of Nán’ān, due to his involvement in Mù Tài’s plot,
had his noble title and fief posthumously revoked.
The affair of Mù Tài is recorded in scroll 140, third year of the Jiànwǔ era of Qímíngdì.
Thus, Yīng was re-established as Prince of Zhōngshān.
The Palace Aide to the Censor-in-Chief, Rén Fǎng, submitted a memorial impeaching Cáo Jǐngzōng.
The Emperor, considering him a meritorious minister,
suppressed it and did not prosecute.
The Commandant of the Guards, Zhèng Shàoshū, was loyal in serving his sovereign.
Whatever he heard or learned externally,
not the slightest detail was concealed.
Whenever he reported matters to the Emperor,
if they were good, he attributed the merit to the Emperor;
if they were not good, he took the blame upon himself.
The Emperor thus held him dear.
An edict established Sīzhōu at Nányìyáng,
moving the garrison south of the pass,
and appointing Shàoshū as its Inspector.
Nányìyáng administered Lùchéng Pass.
In Suí, it became Mùlán County of Huángzhōu.
In Táng, Mùlán was merged into Huánggāng County.
[Shàoshū] repaired weapons and equipment,
expanded fields and accumulated grain,
gathered scattered refugees,
and the people lived in peace.
Wei established Yìngzhōu at Yìyáng,
appointing Sīmǎ Yuè as its Inspector.
According to Wèi Shōu’s Treatise on Geography,
Yìngzhōu administered the commanderies of Ānyáng, Chéngyáng, and Rǔnán.
Máyáng corresponds to the territory of present-day Mǎchéng County in Huángzhōu.
Textual analysis notes: The biography of Sīmǎ Yuè records
“Inspector of Yùzhōu, Mǎ Xiānpín.”
However, Xiānpín had not yet been appointed Inspector of Yùzhōu at that time.
[Yuè] captured it.
In the ninth month,
on the day Rénzǐ,
Fúliánchóu, King of Tǔyùhún, was appointed Inspector of Xīqín and Hézhōu, and Prince of Hénán.
Tǔ
is pronounced as tù, entering tone.
Yù
is pronounced as yù.
16 The Róurán invaded Wòyě and Huáishuò Town of Wèi.
The Hàn Dynasty's Wòyě County belonged to Shuòfāng Commandery.
In the later Wèi Dynasty, it became a town.
According to Wèi Shōu's records,

25. Yuán Huái, the Duke of Huì of Féngyì and General of the Cavalry and Grand General of Wèi, passed away.
Huái was by nature broad-minded and straightforward,
disliking trivial details.
He often said:
"A person of high status should grasp the main principles;
why must every single matter be examined in detail?
For example, when building a house,
as long as it looks tall and imposing from the outside,
its pillars and beams are straight and even,
and its foundation and walls are solid and secure,
that is enough.
If the axe marks are not smooth
or the carving and cutting are not fine,
these are not flaws of the house."

the seventh month,

Some generals suggested hiding troops in mountain paths,

Chūn said:

The reason the bandits have fled deep into hiding

Now, if we restrain the various armies

Wait until they are unprepared,

Chūn again used horses and livestock as bait,

General Xiāo Jí stationed at Gùchéng,

pronounced mǒu bǔ fān.

night,

The Wèi emperor ordered Zhōngshān Wáng Yīng to take advantage of the victory to pacify the southeast.

Since Mǎtóu had fallen,

In winter,
in the tenth month,
Yuán Yīng advanced and besieged Zhōnglí.
The Wei emperor ordered Xíng Luán to lead troops to join him.
Xíng Luán submitted a memorial,
stating that
"Although our southern army is no match for the enemy in field battles,

Now, if we exhaust our elite forces attacking Zhōnglí,

Moreover, it is situated beyond the Huái River;

we would still fear lacking provisions to hold it,

Furthermore,
the soldiers of the southern campaign have been engaged in warfare for two seasons,
meaning the fighting has been continuous,
from summer through autumn.
This is obvious without asking.
Although we have the advantage of momentum from victory,

In my humble opinion,
it would be better to repair and restore the old garrisons,
pacify and govern the various provinces,

As for troubles in Jiāngdōng,
we need not worry about their absence."

Hesitate,

Zhōnglí is a natural fortress,
known to all the court nobles,
meaning the noble ministers at court are all aware of it.
Court,
pronounced directly as yáo.

if they are aware,

2. The Wèi Prince of Zhōngshān, Yuán Yīng, and the General Who Pacifies the East, Yáng Dàyǎn, among others, led hundreds of thousands of troops to attack Zhōnglí.
The city of Zhōnglí was blocked to the north by the Huái River.
The Wèi people built bridges and erected barricades spanning several hundred paces on both banks of the Shàoyáng Islet,
creating a passage across the Huái.
Yīng occupied the southern bank to attack the city,
while Dàyǎn occupied the northern bank to establish a camp,
ensuring the transport of provisions.
The city defenders numbered only three thousand.
Chāng Yìzhī commanded the officers and soldiers,
resisting flexibly according to the situation.
The Wèi people used carts to carry soil to fill the moat,
with their troops carrying soil behind them.
Cavalry pressed closely from the rear,
and anyone who failed to retreat in time
was buried by the soil.
Soon, the moat was filled.
Where battering rams struck,
the city walls crumbled.
Yìzhī used mud to repair them,
so even when the battering rams breached the walls, they could not cause significant damage.
The Wèi people attacked relentlessly day and night,
taking turns in shifts.
They fell and climbed again,
with no one retreating.
Dozens of battles were fought in a single day,
resulting in tens of thousands of casualties on both sides.
The bodies of the Wèi dead piled as high as the city walls.
In the second month,
the Wèi Emperor summoned Yīng to return,
but Yīng submitted a memorial stating:
"Your subject is determined to annihilate the fleeing enemy.
Since the beginning of the month,
(note: 'yǐ' and 'yǐ' are interchangeable.)

The Wèi Emperor replied with an edict:

"Fù" means

Dù Yòu's Tōngdiǎn says: When building a city wall,
the bottom width is double the height,
and the top width is half the bottom width.
If the wall is five zhàng high,
the bottom width is two zhàng and five chǐ,
and the top width is one zhàng, two chǐ, and five cùn.
The height, bottom width, and top width should follow this standard.
Calculating labor: Add the top width and bottom width to get three zhàng, seven chǐ, and five cùn,
halve it to get one zhàng, eight chǐ, seven cùn, and five fēn.
Multiply by the height of five zhàng,
and the volume of one chǐ of wall is ninety-three zhàng, seven chǐ, and five cùn.
For each laborer,
two chǐ of earth can be built per day,
requiring about forty-seven laborers.
For a wall five chǐ long, two hundred thirty-five laborers are needed,
for one hundred paces, twenty-three thousand five hundred laborers.
Following this, one lǐ can be extrapolated to ten lǐ.
The labor for carrying earth and baskets is included in the total labor.
The moat's surface width is two zhàng,
depth one zhàng,
bottom width one zhàng.
Add the surface width and bottom width, take two-thirds,
to get one zhàng and five chǐ.
Multiply by the depth of one zhàng,
and the volume of one chǐ of moat is fifteen zhàng.
Each laborer can excavate three zhàng per day,
requiring five laborers.
For five chǐ, twenty-five laborers are needed,
for ten paces, two hundred fifty laborers.
For one lǐ, seventy thousand five hundred laborers are needed.
Using this as a basis,
one hundred lǐ can be extrapolated.
"Bǐ"

first month,

3 An edict ordered the Minister of Personnel Xú Miǎn to establish the nine ranks of all officials into eighteen grades,
with higher grades indicating greater prestige.
In the second month,
on the day Yǐchǒu,
additional military positions from General of the Garrison and General of the Guard and below were set into ten ranks,
totaling twenty-four grades;
those not reaching the ten ranks
were separately assigned eight grades.
Additionally, twenty-four grades of generals for foreign affairs were established,
totaling one hundred and nine titles.
The Chancellor, Grand Steward, Grand Mentor, Grand Guardian, Grand Marshal, Grand General, Grand Commandant, Minister over the Masses, and Minister of Works were placed in the eighteenth grade.

Generals with the authority to establish their own offices and equal in status to the Three Excellencies, as well as Left and Right Ministers of the Palace with the authority to establish their own offices and equal in status to the Three Excellencies, were placed in the seventeenth grade.
The Director of the Imperial Secretariat, the Grand Mentor of the Heir Apparent, and Left and Right Ministers of the Palace were placed in the sixteenth grade.

The Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat on the Left, the Junior Mentor of the Heir Apparent, the Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, the Vice Director on the Right, the Director of the Central Secretariat, the Special Counselor, and the Generals of the Central and Palace Guards were placed in the fifteenth grade.

The Central and Palace Guards, the Minister of Personnel, the Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent, the Minister of the Palace with the Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon, and the Minister of Ceremonies were placed in the fourteenth grade.

The Director of the Central Secretariat, the Ministers of the Various Departments, the Chancellor of the National University, the Ministers of the Imperial Clan and the Imperial Treasury, and the Minister of the Palace were placed in the thirteenth grade.

The Palace Attendant, the Regular Attendant of the Scattered Cavalry, the Generals of the Left and Right Guards, the Senior Administrator of the Minister over the Masses on the Left, and the Minister of the Guards were placed in the twelfth grade.

The Palace Aide to the Censor-in-Chief, the Gentleman of Personnel in the Imperial Secretariat, the Director of the Palace Library, the Acting Regular Attendant of the Scattered Cavalry, the Commanders of the Left and Right Guards of the Heir Apparent, the Generals of the Left and Right Rapid as Cavalry and Roaming Cavalry, the Grand Palace Grandee, the Tutors of Imperial Younger Brothers and Imperial Sons, the Ministers of Agriculture, the Lesser Treasury, and the Judiciary, the Palace Attendant of the Heir Apparent, and the Minister of the Imperial Clan were placed in the eleventh grade.

Another edict stated that
"the names of generals
are confused in terms of high and low status,
and should be further rectified."
Thereupon, the responsible officials memorialized to establish one hundred and twenty-five titles of generals.
Generals of the Garrison, Guard, Agile Cavalry, and Chariot and Cavalry were placed in the twenty-fourth grade,
used both internally and externally;
Generals Who Pacify the East,
West, South, and North were used externally,
while Generals of the Central Army, Central Guard, Central Pacification, and Central Protection were used internally,
placed in the twenty-third grade;
Generals Who Garrison the East, West, South, and North were used externally,
while Generals Who Garrison the Left, Right, Front, and Rear were used internally,
placed in the twenty-second grade;
Generals Who Secure the East, West, South, and North were used externally,
while Generals Who Secure the Left, Right, Front, and Rear were used internally,
placed in the twenty-first grade;
Generals Who Pacify the East, West, South, and North were used externally,
while Generals Who Assist the Left, Right, Front, and Rear were used internally,
placed in the twentieth grade: these were the prestigious general titles.
Generals of Loyalty and Martiality and Military Strategists were placed in the nineteenth grade;
Generals of Martial Officials, Claws and Teeth, Dragon Cavalry, and Cloud Banners were placed in the eighteenth grade,
replacing the old Front, Rear, Left, and Right Generals;
Generals of Garrison Troops, Assisting Commanders, Spreading Favor, and Spreading Resolution were placed in the seventeenth grade,
replacing the old Four Colonels: ten titles constituted one rank.
Generals of Wisdom and Might, Benevolence and Might, Courage and Might, Trust and Might, and Severity and Might were placed in the sixteenth grade,
replacing the old General Who Conquers the Caitiffs;
Generals of Wisdom and Martiality, Benevolence and Martiality, Courage and Martiality, Trust and Martiality, and Severity and Martiality were placed in the fifteenth grade,
replacing the old Champion General: ten titles constituted one rank,
these were the so-called Generals of the Five Virtues.
Generals of Light Chariots, Distant Conquest, Garrisoning the North, Martial Journeys, and Chaste Resolution were placed in the fourteenth grade,
replacing the old General Who Assists the State.
For generals receiving additional honors,
they could only reach the level of Chaste Resolution,
advancing one step,
with the outstanding ones then being comparable to those following the Dukes.
Generals of Pacifying Distant Lands, Illustrious Might, Shaking Distant Lands, Lightning Radiance, and Awe-inspiring Radiance were placed in the thirteenth grade, [
8. On the Guǐmǎo day,
Ānchéng Wáng Xiù was appointed as the Governor of Jīngzhōu.
Prior to this,
the Mǎyíng Mán barbarians of Bālíng had been raiding along the river,
and the provincial and commandery authorities were unable to suppress them.
Xiù dispatched his guard officer Wén Chì to lead troops in burning down their forests.
Under the Liáng system,
the imperial palace and the Eastern Palace established direct guard officers,
while princes and dukes established guard officers.
Wén
is a surname.
Shuài
is read as "lead."
The province was thus free from banditry.
The Mán barbarians, having lost their cover and strongholds,
dared not engage in raiding.
9. In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Jiǎwǔ day,
Wèi established Noble Consort Gāo as Empress.
The Minister of Works, Gāo Zhào, gained even greater power and influence.
Zhào frequently altered the old systems of previous reigns,
reduced ranks and emoluments,
and suppressed and demoted meritorious officials,
causing widespread resentment.
Court officials and imperial clansmen all treated him with deference,
except for the Minister of Revenue, Yuán Kuāng, who stood up to Zhào.
Kuāng first had a coffin made and placed in his office,
intending to carry it to the palace gate to accuse Zhào of his crimes,
and to commit suicide as a desperate remonstrance.
Zhào heard of this and despised him.
It happened that Kuāng and the Minister of Ceremonies, Liú Fāng, were discussing matters of weights and measures.
Wèi, while deliberating on music,
also discussed and standardized weights and measures.
Liàng
is pronounced with the falling tone.
Kuāng then engaged in a heated dispute with Zhào,
jìng
meaning "to contend."
He compared Zhào to Zhào Gāo.
The authorities sentenced Kuāng to death;
an imperial edict pardoned him from death,
demoting him to the post of Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments.
10. In the eighth month,
on the Guǐchǒu day,
Jìnglíng Zhuàng Gōng Cáo Jǐngzōng passed away.
11. Earlier,
the Wèi Emperor had arranged for Jīngzhào Wáng Yú to marry the younger sister of Empress Yú,
but Yú did not love her,
instead favoring his concubine Lǐ Shì,
who bore him a son named Bǎoyuè.
Empress Yú summoned Lǐ Shì into the palace
and had her beaten.
Yú was arrogant, extravagant, greedy, and unrestrained,
and many of his actions were unlawful.
The Emperor summoned Yú into the palace for interrogation,
caned him fifty times,
and sent him out to serve as the Governor of Jìzhōu.
Yú felt that, being older,
his power and status were inferior to those of his two younger brothers.
The two younger brothers
were Qīnghé Wáng Yì
and Guǎngpíng Wáng Huái.
Moreover,
he and his concubine had repeatedly suffered humiliation.
Gāo Zhào frequently slandered Yú and his brothers,
and Yú could no longer contain his anger.
On the Guǐhài day,
he killed his Chief Clerk Yáng Língyǐn and Military Administrator Lǐ Zūn,
falsely claiming to have received a secret memorial from Qīnghé Wáng Yì,
stating
"Gāo Zhào has committed regicide and rebellion."
He then set up an altar south of Xìndū,
the seat of the Wèi Governor of Jìzhōu was Xìndū.
declared a general amnesty,
changed the era name to Jiànpíng,
and established Lǐ Shì as Empress.
The Legal Consultant Cuī Bójì refused to comply,
and Yú killed him.
The northern provincial garrisons suspected that the Wèi court was in turmoil,
referring to the garrisons north of Jìzhōu.
Cháo
is pronounced with the rising tone.
The provincial garrisons then calmed down.
On the Yǐchǒu day,
Wèi appointed Minister Lǐ Píng as Commander of the Northern Expeditionary Forces and Acting Governor of Jìzhōu to suppress Yú.
Píng
was a younger cousin of Lǐ Chóng.
12. On the Dīngmǎo day,
Wèi declared a general amnesty,
and changed the era name to Yǒngpíng.
13. Wèi's Jīngzhào Wáng Yú sent an envoy to persuade the Administrator of Píngyuán, Fáng Liàng of Qīnghé,
but Liàng beheaded the envoy.
Yú dispatched his general Zhāng Línghé to attack him,
but was defeated by Liàng.
Lǐ Píng's army reached Jīngxiàn,
Jīngxiàn
belonged to Ānpíng Commandery during the Hàn and Jìn dynasties,
and according to Wèi Shōu's records, it was part of Jùlù Commandery.
At night,
several thousand Mán soldiers attacked Píng's camp,
with arrows reaching Píng's tent.
Píng remained steadfast and unmoving,
and the situation soon stabilized on its own.
The Mán soldiers were likely also under Lǐ Píng's command,
intending to cause internal turmoil,
but as Píng remained unmoved,
they settled down on their own.
On the first day of the month, Xīnsì,
Yú engaged in battle south of the city at Cǎogiáo,
and Píng launched a fierce attack,
routing him completely.
Yú fled into the city,
and Píng advanced to besiege it.
On the Rénchén day,
Ānlè Wáng Quán defeated Yú's troops north of the city.
14. On the Guǐsì day,
the imperial son Jī was enfeoffed as Nánkāng Wáng.
In the establishment of the Wei Empress Dowager Gao,
Péngchéng Wǔxuān Wáng Xié firmly remonstrated,
but the ruler of Wei did not listen.
As a result, Gāo Zhào resented him
and frequently slandered Xié to the ruler of Wei,
but the ruler did not believe it.
Xié recommended his maternal uncle Pān Sēnggù to be the Prefect of Chánglè.
When Jīngzhào Wáng Yú rebelled,
he coerced Sēnggù into joining him.
Jìzhōu and Chánglè Commandery were both governed from Xìndū,
so Sēnggù was coerced by Yú.
Lè,
pronounced as Luò.
He sought to ally with the southern barbarians.
South of Yīquē,
reaching Huái, Rǔ, Jiāng, and Miǎn,
all had barbarians on their left.
Formerly, Gāozǔ Zhēn had once been a guard for Xié;
by this time, he had left his position,
thus called the former guard.
The plan was brought to fruition.
Zhào had Shìzhōng Yuán Huī report it,
but Huī did not comply,
so he then had Zuǒwèi Yuán Zhēn speak of it.
The emperor questioned Huī,
and Huī clarified that Xié was not involved;
he also questioned Zhào,
who cited Wèi Yǎn and Gāozǔ Zhēn as witnesses.
The emperor then believed it.
On Wùxū,
he summoned Xié and Gāoyáng Wáng Yōng, Guǎngyáng Wáng Jiā, Qīnghé Wáng Yì, Guǎngpíng Wáng Huái, and Gāo Zhào to a banquet.
Xié's wife, Lady Lǐ, was in labor,
so he firmly declined to attend.
The palace sent messengers one after another to summon him,
and he reluctantly
bid farewell and got into the carriage,
entering the East Gate,
crossing a small bridge,
but the ox refused to move.
After striking it for a long time,
a long time,
somewhat long,
or said to be very long.
They then removed the ox,
and people pulled the carriage onward.
At the banquet in the palace,
it was night,
and all were drunk,
each retreating to a separate place to rest.
They were instructed to retire to a convenient place,
to expel the intoxication and recover their energy.
Xié said:
"I am innocent;
I wish to see the Emperor once,
then I would die without regret!"
Yuán Zhēn said:
"How can you see the Emperor again!"
Xié said:
"The Emperor is wise and enlightened;
he should not kill me without cause;
I ask to confront my accuser to determine the truth!"
The guards struck him with the hilt of their knives;
Xié loudly said:
"Injustice,
O Heaven!
Being loyal and yet killed."
The guards again struck him,
and Xié drank poisoned wine,
then the guards killed him.
Approaching dawn,
they wrapped his body in a mat and returned it to his residence,
saying the prince died of intoxication.
Lady Lǐ cried out mournfully, saying:
"Gāo Zhào has unjustly killed him;
if there is justice in Heaven,
how can you die a good death!"
The ruler of Wei mourned in the Eastern Hall,
granting posthumous honors and a lavish funeral.
At court, high and low,
all were dejected,
and travelers wept, saying:
"Gāo the head minister unjustly killed a virtuous prince."
Zhào was the Director of the Secretariat,
thus referred to as the head minister.
This laid the groundwork for the execution of Gāo Zhào.
Evil,
pronounced in the manner of Willow.
Jīngzhào Wáng Yú could not hold Xìndū;
Guǐmǎo day,
he burned the gates,
taking Lady Lǐ and his four sons with over a hundred riders and fled.
Lǐ Píng entered Xìndū,
executed Wéi Chāo and others placed by Yú as Governors of Jìzhōu,
sent Tǒngjūn Shūsūn Tóu to pursue and capture Yú,
imprisoning him in Xìndū,
reporting it.
Officials requested to execute Yú,
but the ruler of Wei did not permit it,
ordering him to be escorted to Luòyáng,
admonishing him as family.
Yú,
being the ruler's brother,
thus sought to instruct and admonish him.
Gāo Zhào secretly sent someone to kill him.
Regarding discrepancies, it is noted: Both the Book of Wei and the Northern History's account of Yú say:
"Whenever Yú lodged at inns,
he always held Lady Lǐ's hand,
confiding total intimacy,
even while shackled,
drinking and feasting as usual,
showing no sign of shame or fear.
Upon reaching Yèwáng,
Yú told someone: 'Though the sovereign's kindness is profound,
and cannot bear to kill me,
how can I face the Emperor!'
He then wept and stopped breathing.
Some say Gāo Zhào had someone kill him."
Indeed, once Yú was defeated and captured,
he still showed no shame or fear,
how could he suddenly feel ashamed to see the ruler of Wei,
be passionately moved and die!
It must be that Zhào secretly had Yú killed,
using these words to deceive the ruler of Wei.
However, the ruler of Wei pardoned everyone.
The ruler of Wei intended to execute Lady Lǐ and her family,
but Central Secretariat Excellency Cuī Guāng remonstrated:
"Lady Lǐ is pregnant,
executing with fetal extraction
was the practice of Jié and Zhòu.
Wǔ Wáng enumerated Zhòu's crimes, saying: 'He gouged out the wombs of pregnant women.'
Please wait until childbirth
before carrying out the sentence."
This was followed.
Lǐ Píng arrested more than a thousand remaining followers of Yú,
intending to execute them all,
but Clerk Gāo Hàoshēng said:
"These were coerced into following;
they were previously promised pardon,
it should be petitioned."
Píng followed this advice,
and all were spared from death.
Hào,
was Yòu's grandson.
Gāo Yòu,
cousin to Yǔn's father,
served Wèi Xiàowén in literary matters.
Jǐzhōu's Inspector Gāo Zhí led state troops against Gāo Yú,
having merit to be enfeoffed,
but Zhí declined,
saying:
"Our family has long been graced with heavy favors,
serving the state is a duty,
selling one's body for this cause, dying in its service is fulfilling duty.
Graced,
pronounced as 'under obligation.'
How dare I seek reward!"
Zhí,
was Zhào's son.
Added the title of Dispersed Cavalry Attendant to Lǐ Píng.
Gāo Zhào and Zhongwèi Wáng Xiǎn consistently disliked Píng,
Xiǎn accused Píng of concealing officials in Jìzhōu,
meaning male and female rebels were to be confiscated for the state.
Disliked,
pronounced in the manner of Willow.
Accused,
pronounced as "accusing in such manner."
His name was removed,
denying him access to prohibited gates.
初，
显祖之世，
柔然万余口
降魏，
置之高平、薄骨律二镇，
魏世祖太延二年置高平镇，
是后肃宗正光五年改置原州。
又太延二年置薄骨律镇，
肃宗孝昌中改置灵州。
宋白曰：太和十年改薄骨律镇为沃野镇。
降，
户江翻。
叛走略尽，
唯千余户在。
太中大夫王通请徙置淮北以绝其叛，
诏太仆卿杨椿持节往徙之，
椿上言：
「先朝处之边徼，
所以招附殊俗，
且别异华、戎也。
今新附之户甚众，
若旧者见徙，
新者必不自安，
是驱之使叛也。
且此属衣毛食肉，
乐冬便寒，
南土湿热，
往必歼尽。
进失归附之心，
退无藩卫之益，
置之中夏，
或生后患，
非良策也。」
不从，
遂徙于济州，
缘河处之。
及京兆王愉之乱，
皆浮河赴愉，
所在抄掠，
如椿之言。
16庚子，
魏郢州司马彭珍等叛魏，
潜引梁兵趋义阳，
三关戍主侯登等以城来降。
郢州刺史娄悦婴城自守，
魏以中山王英都督南征诸军事，
将步骑三万出汝南以救之。
十月，
魏悬瓠军主白早生杀豫州刺史司马悦，
自号平北将军，
求救于司州
马仙琕。
时荆州刺史安成王秀为都督，
秀以荆州刺史督诸州，
司州其所统也。
签前叙求应赴之事，
注见一百二十卷宋文帝元嘉元年。
谓宜奏上天台而待报。
江左率谓朝廷为台，
亦谓之天台。
「彼待我以自存，
彼，
谓白早生。
待敕虽旧，
谓旧制须待台敕。
即遣兵赴之。
上亦诏仙琕救早生。
仙琕进顿楚王城，
楚王城即楚王戍。
以兵二千助守悬瓠。
诏以早生为司州刺史。
考异曰：梁帝纪，
十月丙子，
「魏阳关主许敬珍以城内附，
诏大举北伐，
以始兴王憺帅众入清，
王茂帅众向宿豫。
丁丑，
白早生与豫州刺史胡逊以城内属，
以早生为司州、胡逊为豫州刺史。
明年正月壬辰，
魏镇东参军成景隽斩宿豫城主严仲宝，
以城内属。
二月丁卯，
魏楚王城主李国兴以城内附。」
姓名年月事迹既与魏书参差，
又遍检诸列传皆无其事。
今并从魏书。
18丙寅，
以吴兴太守张稷为尚书左仆射。
19魏以尚书邢峦行豫州事，
将兵击白早生。
魏主问之曰：
「卿言，
早生走也，
守也？
何时可平？」
对曰：
「早生非有深谋大智，
正以司马悦暴虐，
乘众怒而作乱，
民迫于凶威，
不得已而从之。
纵使梁兵入城，
水路不通，
粮运不继，
亦成禽耳。
早生得梁之援，
溺于利欲，
必守而不走。
若临以王师，
士民必翻然归顺，
不出今年，
当传首京师。」
魏主悦，
命峦先发，
使中山王英继之。
峦帅骑八百，
倍道兼行，
五日至鲍口。
丙子，
早生遣其大将胡孝智将兵七千，
离城二百里逆战，
峦奋击，
大破之，
乘胜长驱至悬瓠。
早生出城逆战，
又破之，
因渡汝水，
围其城。
诏加峦都督南讨诸军事。
丁丑，
魏镇东参军成景隽杀宿豫戍主严仲贤，
以城来降。
时魏郢、豫二州，
自悬瓠以南至于安陆诸城皆没，
唯义阳一城为魏坚守。
蛮帅田益宗帅㣥蛮以附魏，
魏以为东豫州刺史，
魏东豫州治新息广陵城，
领汝南、东新蔡、新蔡、弋阳、长陵郡。
益宗不从。
十一月，
庚寅，
魏遣安东将军杨椿将兵四万攻宿豫。
魏主闻邢峦屡捷，
命中山王英趣义阳，
英以众少，
累表请兵，
弗许。
英至悬瓠，
辄与峦共攻之。
十二月，
己未，
齐苟儿等开门出降，
斩白早生及其党数十人。
英乃引兵前趋义阳。
宁朔将军张道凝先屯楚王城，
癸亥，
弃城走，
英追击，
斩之。
魏义阳太守狄道辛祥与娄悦共守义阳，
将军胡武城、陶平虏攻之，
祥夜出袭其营，
擒平虏，
斩武城，
由是州境获全。
论功当赏，
娄悦耻功出其下，
间之于执政，
赏遂不行。
20壬申，
魏东荆州表
「桓晖之弟叔兴前后招抚太阳蛮，
归附者万余户，
请置郡十六，
县五十，」
自是之后，
蛮左郡县不可胜纪矣。
道元，
范之子也。
郦范见一百三十二卷宋明帝泰始三年。
21是岁，
柔然佗汗可汗复遣纥奚勿六跋献貂裘于魏，
魏主弗受，
报之如前。
前事见上卷五年。
In the beginning,
the Gaoche Marquis Bèi Qióngqí was killed by the Yèdā.
The Yèdā state,
a branch of the Great Yuèzhī,
is also called a separate tribe of the Gaoche.
Their origins lie north of the Great Wall,
from the Jīnshān Mountains southward,
located west of Yútián,
ten thousand and one hundred lǐ from Cháng'ān;
their king's capital is Bádǐ City,
which is likely the same as the ancient city of Rājagṛha.
Yè,
is pronounced with the rhyme of yì and shè.
Dā,
is pronounced with the rhyme of dāng and gē,
also tuó and gé,
and also zhái and yà.
Their people scattered,
some fleeing to Wèi,
some fleeing to Róurán.
The Wèi emperor sent the Yǔlín Supervisor, Mèng Wēi of Hénán, to pacify and accept the surrendering households,
settling them at Gāopíng Garrison.
The Gaoche king Āfú Zhìluó was cruel and tyrannical,
and his people killed him,
establishing his clansman Bálìyán in his place.
The Yèdā supported Mí'étū to attack Gaoche,
and the people killed Bálìyán,
welcoming Mí'étū and establishing him as king.
Mí'étū fought Tuóhàn Kèhán at Púlèi Lake,
but was defeated,
fleeing over three hundred lǐ westward.
Tuóhàn stationed his army at the northern mountains of Yīwú.
At that time, the King of Gāochāng, Qū Jiā, requested to move inward to Wèi,
and Mèng Wēi was then the Lóngxiāng General.
The Wèi emperor sent Wēi to dispatch three thousand soldiers from Liángzhōu to welcome him,
arriving at Yīwú.
When Tuóhàn saw Wēi's army,
he became frightened and fled.
Mí'étū, hearing of his disarray and panic,
pursued and attacked,
crushing him utterly,
killing Tuóhàn north of Púlèi Lake,
cutting off his hair and sending it to Wēi,
and also sent an envoy to present tribute to Wèi.
The Wèi emperor sent Yú Liàng of Dōngchéngzi to respond,
bestowing generous gifts.
The King of Gāochāng, Jiā, failed to arrive at the appointed time,
and Wēi led his troops back.
Tuóhàn Kèhán's son Chǒunú succeeded him,
with the title Dòuluófúbádòufá Kèhán,
Wèi Shōu said: In Wèi language,
it means
"Manifesting Order."
22 According to the old rituals of Sòng and Qí,
when sacrificing to Heaven, one wore the gǔn miǎn crown and robe.
The concurrent Zhùzuò Láng, Xǔ Mào of Gāoyáng, requested the creation of a dà qiú robe,
and this was approved.
The Zhōulǐ, Tiānguān section states: The Sīqiú is in charge of making the dà qiú for the king's robe when sacrificing to Heaven.
Zhèng Zhòng's commentary says: The dà qiú,
is a black lambskin robe,
worn when sacrificing to Heaven,
to show simplicity.
At that time, the officials sought the regulations for the dà qiú,
but only Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the Sīfú states: The dà qiú,
is a lambskin robe.
Since there was no source for this,
it could not be taken as authoritative.
According to the six miǎn robes, the upper garment is black and the lower is reddish-yellow.
Now it should be made of black silk,
its style like a fur robe,
the lower garment in reddish-yellow,
both without patterned embroidery;
the miǎn crown should have no hanging beads.
The decree said: Approved.
23 The emperor was about to perform ceremonies at the Tàimiào temple,
and issued an edict stating:
"On fasting days, there shall be no music. From now on, when the imperial carriage first departs,
the drummers and musicians shall follow but not play.
Upon returning to the palace,
the usual protocol shall be followed."
Upon returning to the palace, the drummers and musicians shall then play vigorously.
Chuī,
is pronounced with the rhyme of chāng and ruì.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the Xīnsì day,
the Emperor performed sacrifices at the southern suburb,
and granted a general amnesty.
At that time, there were those who requested to perform the Fēng ceremony at Kuàijī and the Shàn ceremony at Guóshān.
Guóshān is located in Guóshān County of Yìxīng.
The Suí dynasty abolished Yìxīng Commandery and made it Yìxīng County,
merging Guóshān into it.
In the first year of the Tàipíng Xīngguó era of our dynasty,
due to the taboo of Tàizōng's princely residence,
Yìxīng was changed to Yíxīng.
Kuài,
pronounced as Guài.
They wished to carry it out.
Xǔ Mào submitted a proposal,
believing that
"When Shùn burned firewood at Dàizōng,
it was for the royal inspection tour.
Yet Zhèng quotes the 'Chūnqiū Wéi·Xiàojīng Gōumìngjué' saying:
'Performing Fēng at Tàishān,
examining achievements and burning offerings;
performing Shàn at Liángfǔ,
engraving stone to record the title,'
this is a distorted interpretation from apocryphal texts,
not the general meaning of the orthodox classics.
Shùn conducted a royal inspection tour every five years,
traveling to the four sacred mountains in spring, summer, autumn, and winter.
The 'Shū·Shùn Diǎn' states:
In the second month of the year,
he toured east to Dàizōng,
burning firewood and making offerings to the mountains and rivers in order.
In the fifth month,
he toured south to the Southern Sacred Mountain.
In the eighth month,
he toured west to the Western Sacred Mountain.
In the eleventh month,
he toured north to the Northern Sacred Mountain.
Zǎi,
pronounced as Zǎi.
How frequent were these!
Furthermore, as Guǎn Yíwú spoke of seventy-two rulers,
before Suìrén's time,
the world was simple and the people pure;
how could there be sealing with clay and examining with jade!
They governed by knotting ropes;
how could there be engraving texts to announce completion!
Yíwú also said:
'Only rulers who received the Mandate could then perform Fēng and Shàn.'
King Chéng of Zhōu was not a ruler who received the Mandate;
how could he perform Fēng at Tàishān and Shàn at Shèshǒu!
Shénnóng is the same as Yándì,
yet Yíwú separated them into two persons;
his falsehood is extreme.
If a sage ruler,
there is no need for Fēng and Shàn;
if an ordinary ruler,
he should not perform Fēng and Shàn.
It was because Duke Huán of Qí wished to carry out this matter,
and Yíwú knew it was not permissible,
therefore he raised strange things to dissuade him.
The 'Hànshū·Treatise' says: After Duke Huán of Qí achieved hegemony,
he assembled the feudal lords at Kuíqiū,
and wished to perform Fēng and Shàn.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
'In ancient times, those who performed Fēng at Tàishān and Shàn at Liángfǔ numbered seventy-two families,
of which Yíwú remembers twelve.
In the past, Wúhuáishì performed Fēng at Tàishān,
and Shàn at Yúnyún;
Fúxī performed Fēng at Tàishān,
and Shàn at Yúnyún;
Shénnóngshì performed Fēng at Tàishān,
and Shàn at Yúnyún;
Yándì performed Fēng at Tàishān,
and Shàn at Yúnyún;
Huángdì performed Fēng at Tàishān,
and Shàn at Tíngtíng;
Zhuānxū performed Fēng at Tàishān,
and Shàn at Yúnyún;
Dìkù performed Fēng at Tàishān,
and Shàn at Yúnyún;
Yáo performed Fēng at Tàishān,
and Shàn at Yúnyún;
Shùn performed Fēng at Tàishān,
and Shàn at Yúnyún;
Yǔ performed Fēng at Tàishān,
and Shàn at Kuàijī;
Tāng performed Fēng at Tàishān,
and Shàn at Yúnyún;
King Chéng performed Fēng at Tàishān,
and Shàn at Shèshǒu: all received the Mandate before they could perform Fēng and Shàn.'
Duke Huán said:
'I have assembled the feudal lords nine times,
and rectified the world once;
how is this different from the Three Dynasties receiving the Mandate!'
Guǎn Zhòng saw that Duke Huán could not be persuaded by words,
therefore he set forth matters, saying:
'In ancient Fēng and Shàn ceremonies,
millet from Hàoshàng,
and grain from Běilǐ,
were used for the offerings;
from the Jiāng and Huái rivers, three-ridged thatch,
was used for the mats;
the Eastern Sea sent flatfish,
the Western Sea sent birds that share wings,
and then there were fifteen kinds of creatures that came without being summoned.
Now, phoenixes and qílín do not come,
auspicious grain does not grow,
yet weeds and thorns flourish,
owls and hawks gather and soar,
and you wish to perform Fēng and Shàn—
is it not inappropriate!'
Duke Huán then stopped.
Sūn Hào once sent the concurrent Minister of Works Dǒng Cháo to Yángxiàn to perform Fēng and Shàn at Guóshān.
The 'Wǔdài Zhì' says: Yìxīng,
formerly called Yángxiàn.
This is not worth emulating.
Thus, the rituals of Fēng and Shàn
are all hearsay,
losing their original text,
because the ruler above seeks fame,
and the ministers below flatter his wishes.
In ancient times, sacrificing to Heaven and Earth,
the rituals had constant norms;
the way of sincere reverence
was fully expressed therein and complete.
As for Fēng and Shàn,
I dare not hear of it.'
The Emperor praised and accepted his advice,
and accordingly elaborated Xǔ Mào's argument,
issuing an imperial decree to reply to the petitioners,
and thus the matter was halted.
2 The Wèi general Zhōngshān Prince Yuán Yīng arrived at Yìyáng,
intending to capture the Three Passes.
He first strategized, saying:
'The Three Passes rely on each other like left and right hands;
if we capture one pass,
the other two will fall without attack;
attacking the difficult is not as good as attacking the easy;
we should first attack the Eastern Pass.'
The Eastern Pass is Wǔyáng Pass.
Yì,
pronounced as Yì;
the following 'shì yì' is the same.
He then sent Chief Clerk Lǐ Huá to lead five armies toward the Western Pass.
Five armies,
meaning the troops of five commanding armies.
The Western Pass is Píngjìng Pass.
Shuài,
read as Shuài.
He personally commanded the various armies toward the Eastern Pass.
Previously,
Mǎ Xiānpín had sent Cloud Cavalry General Mǎ Guǎng to garrison at Chángbó,
and Army Commander Hú Wénchāo to garrison at Sōngxiàn.
On the Bǐngshēn day,
Yuán Yīng arrived at Chángbó.
On the Wùxū day,
Chángbó collapsed,
Mǎ Guǎng fled into Wǔyáng,
and Yuán Yīng advanced to besiege it.
The Emperor sent Champion General Péng Wèngshēng and Swift Cavalry General Xú Yuánjì to lead troops to aid Wǔyáng.
Yuán Yīng intentionally let them enter the city,
saying:
'I observe the terrain of this city is easy to capture.'
After Wèngshēng and others entered,
Yuán Yīng urged his troops to attack,
and captured it in six days,
taking three generals and over seven thousand soldiers captive.
He then attacked Guǎngxiàn.
Guǎngxiàn,
likely refers to Huángxiàn Pass.
He also attacked the Western Pass,
and Mǎ Xiānpín also abandoned the city and fled.
The Emperor sent Nánjùn Grand Administrator Wéi Ruì to lead troops to rescue Xiānpín.
After the victory at Shàoyáng,
Ruì was promoted to Left Guard General,
and soon became Chief Clerk of Ānxī and Grand Administrator of Nánjùn.
He increased the city walls by over two zhàng,
further dug a large moat,
and erected tall towers.
Many ridiculed him for showing cowardice,
but Ruì said:
'Not so;
a general should have moments of caution,
and cannot be solely brave.'
Zhōngshān Prince Yuán Yīng urgently pursued Mǎ Xiānpín,
intending to avenge the shame of Shàoyáng.
Hearing that Ruì had arrived,
he then withdrew.
初，
魏主遣中書舍人鮦陽董紹慰勞叛城，
鮦陽縣，
漢屬汝南郡，
晉屬汝陰郡，
魏屬新蔡郡。
孟康曰：鮦，
音紂紅翻。
隋廢新蔡郡為縣，
屬豫州。
鮦陽之地當在新蔡縣界。
勞，
力到翻。
送於建康。
魏主既克懸瓠，
命於齊苟兒等四將之中分遣二人，
敕揚州為移，
魏揚州治壽陽。
移，
移文也。
考異曰：紹傳云
「歸苟兒等十人」 ，
今從司馬悅傳。
領軍將軍呂僧珍與紹言，
愛其文義，
言於上，
上遣主書霍靈超謂紹曰：
「今聽卿還，
令卿通兩家之好，
彼此息民，
豈不善也！ 」
因召見，
賜衣物，
令舍人周捨慰勞之，
舍人，
中書通事舍人。
勞，
力到翻。
「戰爭多年，
民物塗炭，
吾是以不恥先言與魏朝通好，
比亦有書全無報者，
卿宜備申此意。
今遣傳詔霍
靈秀送卿至國，
遲有嘉問。 」
又謂紹曰：
「卿知所以得不死不？
今者獲卿，
乃天意也。
夫立君以為民也，
凡在民上，
豈可以不思此乎！
若欲通好，
今以宿豫還彼，
彼當以漢中見歸。 」
紹還魏言之，
魏主不從。
3 三月，
魏荊州刺史元志將兵七萬寇潺溝，
潺溝在漢北，
據梁書吳平侯昺傳，
「破志於潺溝，
流尸蓋漢水， 」
則潺溝之水南注于漢。
潺，
仕山翻。
㣥蠻悉渡漢水來降，
雍州刺史吳平侯昺納之。
綱紀皆以蠻累為邊患，
不如因此除之，
州郡上佐，
謂之綱紀，
言其綱紀州郡之事也。
「窮來歸，
我誅之不祥。
且魏人來侵，
吾得蠻以為屏蔽，
不亦善乎！ 」
乃開樊城受其降，
命司馬朱思遠等擊志於潺溝，
大破之，
斬首萬餘級。
志，
齊之孫也。
拓跋齊見一百二十卷宋文帝元嘉四年。
四月，
戊申 ，
以臨川王宏為司空，
加車騎將軍王茂開府儀同三司。
5 丁卯 ，
魏楚王城主李國興以城降。
七月，
癸巳 ，
巴陵王蕭寶義卒。
7 九月，
辛巳 ，
魏封故北海王詳子顥為北海王。
詳得罪死事見一百四十五卷天監元年。
8 魏公孫崇造樂尺，
以十二黍為寸；
劉芳非之，
更以十黍為寸。
尚書令高肇等奏：
「崇所造八音之器及度量皆與經傳不同，
詰其所以然，
云『必依經文，
聲則不協。 』
請更令芳依周禮造樂器，
俟成集議並呈，
從其善者。 」
詔從之。
夫作樂者先定律，
律起於黃鍾，
黃鍾之長以黍審其度，
黃鍾之龠以黍審其容。
周禮典同雖曰掌六律六同之和，
以辯天地四方陰陽之聲，
以為樂器，
然度之長短，
容之多少，
未嘗詳言之也。
冬官考工既出於漢，
而鳧氏為鍾但言其廣長圓徑深厚，
而絫黍之法無聞焉。
肇請令芳依周禮造樂器，
未知其何所依也。
魏收曰：太和中，
詔中書監高閭脩正音律，
久未能定。
閭表太樂祭酒公孫崇參知律呂鐘磬之事。
景明四年，
幷州獲古銅權，
詔付崇以為鍾律之準。
永平中，
崇更造新尺，
以一黍之長絫為寸法。
尋太常卿劉芳受詔脩樂，
以秬黍中者一黍之廣即為一分，
而中尉元匡以一黍之廣度黍二縫以取一分，
三家紛競，
久不能決。
太和十九年，
高祖詔以一黍之廣用成分體，
九十黍之長以定銅尺。
有司奏從前詔，
而芳尺同高祖所制，
故遂典脩金石。
更，
工衡翻。
傳，
直戀翻。
詰，
去吉翻。
十月，
癸丑 ，
魏以司空廣陽王嘉為司徒。
10十一月，
己丑 ，
魏主於式乾殿為諸僧及朝臣講維摩詰經。
時魏主專尚釋氏，
不事經籍，
中書侍郎河東裴延雋上疏，
以為
「漢光武、魏武帝，
雖在戎馬之間，
未嘗廢書，
先帝遷都行師，
手不釋卷，
良以學問多益，
不可暫輟故也。
陛下升法座，
親講大覺，
凡在瞻聽，
塵蔽俱開。
然五經治世之模楷，
應務之所先，
伏願經書互覽，
