則內外俱周，
真俗斯暢矣。 」
時佛教盛於洛陽，
沙
門之外，
自西域來者三千餘人，
魏主別為之立永明寺千餘間以處之。
處士南陽馮亮有巧思，
魏主使與河南尹甄琛、沙門統僧暹擇嵩山形勝之地立閒居寺，
極巖壑土木之美。
由是遠近承風，
無不事佛，
比及延昌，
州郡共有一萬三千餘寺。
In the eleventh year,
Yuán Shù, the Minister of Ancestral Rites of Wèi, defected.
He was granted the title of Prince of Yè.
Shù,
was the younger brother of Yì.
At that time, Yì was serving as the Inspector of the two provinces of Qīng and Jì,
stationed at Yùzhōu.
In the "Commentary on the Water Classic,"
it is noted that there is a large island in the northeast sea of Qú Mountain,
called Yùzhōu.
Yì plotted to bring his province to submit to Wèi,
but the plan leaked, leading to his death.
Yuán Yì's defection to Wèi is recorded in the fifth year of the previous scroll.
The term "defection"
is metaphorically referred to as "crossing the river."
1 In spring,
during the first month,
on the day Yǐhài,
Shěn Yuē was appointed as the Minister of the Left, and
Wáng Yíng as the Minister of Documents.
Yuē was highly esteemed for his literary talents at that time,
but he was greedy for honor and profit.
For more than a decade in office,
regarding the successes and failures of governance,
he simply nodded and complied.
He considered that he had long held the top government position,
aspiring to a high office.
Some believed he deserved it,
but the emperor never used him;
and when he sought an assignment outside,
it was not granted.
Xú Miǎn requested for him the ceremony of "Three Excellencies,"
according to Liáng's official system, which had a ceremony for opening the office equivalent to the Three Excellencies,
ranking below the opening ceremony equivalent to the Three Excellencies.
The term "for"
is used metaphorically as "in a fake manner."
2 On the day Gēngyín,
new embankments along the Huái River were constructed,
with the north bank starting from Shítóu to Dōngyě,
and the south bank from the rear Zhǔlí Gate to the Sānqiáo.
3 In the third month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
a prince of Wèi, Xǔ, was born.
Xǔ's mother was Hú Chōnghuà,
from Línjīng.
"Chōnghuà,"
refers to a system created by Jìn Wǔdì.
In the time of Sòng Míngdì, the titles Jiéyú and Chōnghuà were among the five positions subordinate to the Nine Consorts,
and during the Xiāo Qí dynasty,
they were listed among the Nine Consorts.
Línjīng County,
since Hàn times, belonged to Andìng Commandery.
The name "Xǔ"
is voiced as "narrate as if flying."
According to the "Sui Records,"
Jīnchéng Commandery, Dídào County,
later under Wèi became Wǔshǐ Commandery.
Colleagues, following custom, congratulated her,
saying, "May you bear princes and princesses,
and not the crown prince."
Chōnghuà replied,
"My aspirations differ from those of others.
How can I, out of fear of my own death, cause the state to have no heir?"
When she became pregnant,
her colleagues advised her to terminate it,
but Chōnghuà refused.
She privately vowed,
"If fortunate enough to bear a son,
he should be next in line to the throne.
If the son is born and I die,
I will have no regrets."
Subsequently, she gave birth to Xǔ.
Prior to this,
the Wèi ruler had frequently lost princes.
As the ruler aged,
he took extreme precautions,
selecting wet nurses from good families capable of nurturing children,
with wet nurses and nursemaids.
Both the empress and Chōnghuà were not permitted to come near.
4 On the day Jǐchǒu,
the emperor visited the National Academy,
personally attending lectures and practices.
On the day Yǐwèi,
an edict was issued for the crown prince and the sons of nobles eligible for apprenticeship to all enter the academy.
5 According to former regulations: all clerks of the five sections of the Shàngshū were recruited from common backgrounds.
In summer,
during the fourth month,
on the day Dīngsì,
an edict stated:
"The five sections of the Shàngshū,
holding positions crucial to governance,
not only oversee various departments,
but also align in rank with the two assistants;
'Align in rank'
referring to proceeding together.
'Two assistants,'
referring to the left and right assistants.
Thus was this set down with respect."
The clerks were thus allowed to attend court requests in the morning,
and Liú Nà, a Tàixué academician, was appointed concurrently to the inner palace section,
with Liú Xiǎn, military law officer in Sīkōng, concurrently to the personnel section,
Kǒng Qiánsūn, a Tàixué academician, concurrently to the metal section,
Xiāo Guǐ, military law officer in Sīkōng, concurrently to both left and right household sections,
Wáng Yǒng, concurrently to the central military section,
military law officer in the military office of the Xuānyì General.
The word "Yǒng,"
pronounced "as happenstance with fish."
He was the first to receive such a selection.
6 In June,
Wu Chéngbó, a clerk from Xuānchéng Commandery, used sorcery to gather a crowd,
and on the day Guǐchǒu,
attacked the commandery, killing the Administrator Zhū Sēngyǒng,
and went on to massacre neighboring counties.
During the intercalary month,
on the day Jǐchǒu,
Chéngbó crossed over the mountains,
suddenly reaching Wu Xīng.
The people of the eastern land were normally not accustomed to war,
and both officials and civilians were fearful and scattered.
Some advised the Administrator Cài Zǔn to avoid him,
but Zǔn refused,
seeking brave volunteers to lock the gates and defend.
Chéngbó launched a full assault,
but Zǔn led his forces out to battle,
inflicting a great defeat upon them,
and confronting the enemy,
beheaded Chéngbó.
Zǔn,
is the son of Xīngzōng.
Cài Xīngzōng served between the Sòng dynasty's Dàmíng and Tàishǐ periods,
being straight and righteous himself.
He attacked and captured several counties such as Yī and Shè,
Administrator Xiè Lǎn sent troops to oppose him,
but was defeated,
fleeing to Kuàijī.
The central army suppressed the rebels,
and quelled them.
Lǎn,
is the son of Yuè.
Xiè Yuè served between the Sòng and Qí dynasties,
holding critical and close positions,
and was held in high regard for his integrity.
"Huì,"
metaphorically used as "mastering the outside."
7 In winter,
during the tenth month,
Yīng, the Wèi Prince of Xiànwǔ of Zhōngshān, passed away.
8 In the third year of the emperor's reign,
an edict was issued to establish a new calendar,
Zǔ Zhòu, an unattached gentleman, proposed using his father Chōngzhī's research on ancient methods as the standard,
stating that the calendar could not be altered.
By the eighth year,
the Grand Astrologer was commanded to compare the old and new calendars,
with the new calendar being denser,
and the old one sparser.
In that year,
Chōngzhī's Dàmíng Calendar began to be implemented.
The old calendar,
was by Hé Chéngtiān.
The new calendar,
was by Zǔ Chōngzhī.
Chōngzhī's calendar can be found in scroll 129 under Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng, year Dàmíng 6.
9 Wèi's Liú Fāng reported
that "the newly created musical instruments and the instructional dances 'Wén' and 'Wǔ,' with newly composed ceremonious songs and orchestra ensemble pieces" were completed,
requesting, as previously decreed, to gather high officials and learned scholars to discuss and determine them,
to be presented alongside the old music.
If the creations match the ancient rhythmic harmony,
he requested its use at the New Year feast the following year."
The decree responded:
"The dance can use the new,
but the rest shall remain old."
1 In spring,
during the first month,
on the day Xīnchǒu,
there was a worship in the Southern Suburbs,
followed by a general amnesty.
The Senior Grand Master of the Left of the Department of State, Zhāng Jì,
claimed his merits were great yet his rewards were meager,
as Zhāng Jì considered it a merit to have killed Qí's Eastern-Confused Duke.
When intoxicated,
his resentment showed in his words and demeanor.
The emperor said:
"Your brother killed the governor,
and Jì's brother Jiāng Huái killed Liú Xiá,
as reported in Volume 134 of the Records, during the reign of the Emperor Shùn of Sòng in the first year of Shēngmíng.
Governor,
this should be reversed.
What acclaim can there be!"
Zhāng Jì said:
"I indeed have no acclaim,
but as for Your Majesty,
one cannot speak of no merits.
The Eastern-Confused was tyrannical;
righteous forces also came to punish him.
How could it only be attributed to me!"
The emperor stroked his beard,
saying:
"Zhāng Gōng is indeed a formidable man!"
Zhāng Jì, both fearful and resentful,
therefore requested to be transferred outside.
In the year of Guǐmǎo,
Jì was appointed governor of the two provinces of Chīng and Jì.
Wáng Zhēnguó also harbored resentment,
as Wáng Zhēnguó had joined Zhāng Jì in killing the Eastern-Confused Duke,
and their resentment was the same.
After drinking, he mournfully lamented, saying:
"When I recently ascended Mount Liáng, I began to weep."
The emperor was greatly surprised and said:
"If you weep for the Eastern-Confused,
it is too late.
If you weep for me,
I am not yet dead!"
Zhēnguó rose, bowed, and thanked,
but did not reply,
and the session dissolved,
leading to his gradual withdrawal.
Later,
he was made Minister of the Department of Veteran Affairs.
In the year of Dīngsì,
Liú Lóngjū, a mountainous barbarian from Wèi's Fénzhōu, gathered his followers to rebel,
invading Xiàzhōu,
and an edict was issued instructing Xuē Hé, Gentleman Consultant, to mobilize the people of Eastern Qín, Fén, Huá, and Xià prefectures to suppress it.
In the eleventh year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Wèi,
Qínzhōu was divided and Huàzhōu was established,
administered at Huáyīn,
overseeing Huáshān, Dēngchéng, and Báishuǐ regions.
Xiàzhōu was also established at Tǒngwàn,
managing Huàzhèng, Chǎnxī, Jīnmíng, and Dàimíng counties.
Xià,
pronounced 'hù yǎ'.
Huá,
pronounced 'hù huà'.
In the year of Xīnyǒu,
an imperial sacrifice was offered at the Bright Hall.
In March,
Wáng Wànshòu from Lángyé killed the governors of Eastern Guǎng and Lángyé's two counties, Liú Zhé,
and took control of Mount Qú,
summoning the Wèi army.
In the year of Rénxū,
Jiā, the Illustrious and Fierce Prince of Guǎngyáng of Wèi, passed away.
Wèi's Xuzhou Governor Lú Chǎng sent Zhāng Tiānhuì, deputy of Tānjūn garrison,
where Qín originally established Tānjūn,
and Hàn later renamed it Dōnghǎi prefecture;
Wèi reestablished Tānjūn,
administratively part of Eastern Xuzhou.
Tānjūn,
pronounced 'tán'.
Zhāng Jì, governor of the two provinces of Chīng and Jì, sent troops to oppose,
but was not victorious.
Liáng's Chīng and Jì prefectures governed Yùzhōu.
In April,
Wénjì and others occupied Mount Qú,
and a decree was issued to General Mǎ Xiānpíng to attack.
Wèi also sent acting Annan General Xiāo Bǎoyín and acting Pingdong General Zhào Xiá of Tiānshuǐ with troops to occupy Mount Qú,
under Lú Chǎng's command.
In the year of Jiǎxū,
Xuē Hé of Wèi defeated Liú Lóngjū,
completely pacifying his faction,
and proposed the establishment of Eastern Xiàzhōu.
Eastern Xiàzhōu managed Piānchéng, Shuòfāng, Dìngyáng, and Shàng county.
Táng's Yánzhōu
was Wèi's Eastern Xiàzhōu.
Xià,
pronounced 'hù yǎ'.
In May,
on the day of Bǐngchén,
Wèi prohibited astronomical studies.
The Dean of the State University, Zhāng Chōng, was appointed Senior Grand Master of the Left of the Department of State.
Chōng,
was the son of Xù.
Zhāng Xù,
was the nephew of Dài,
renowned for his eloquence and logic.
Mǎ Xiānpíng besieged Mount Qú,
while Zhāng Jì temporarily positioned himself six li away to supervise supply transport,
and dispatched troops frequently to assist him.
In the autumn,
Lú Chǎng of Wèi submitted a report requesting an additional six thousand troops,
and one hundred thousand shí of rice;
the Wèi ruler supplied four thousand soldiers.
In the winter,
in November,
on the day of Jǐhài,
the Wèi ruler ordered Yángzhōu Governor Lǐ Chōng and others to prepare troops at Shòuyáng
to draw away forces from Mount Qú.
Lú Chǎng, originally a Confucian scholar,
was inexperienced in military affairs.
Within the city of Mount Qú, both food and firewood ran out,
leading Fù Wénjì to surrender the city;
in December,
on the day of Gēngchén,
Chǎng led his troops and fled first,
with the other forces following in collapse,
coinciding with a heavy snowfall,
resulting in two-thirds of the soldiers freezing to death or losing limbs.
Xiānpíng pursued and attacked,
achieving a great victory.
Within two hundred lǐ,
corpses lay connected,
only one or two out of ten soldiers survived.
The captured grain, livestock, and equipment
were beyond count.
Chǎng fled alone on horseback,
abandoning his credentials and ceremonial guards completely;
reaching Tánchéng,
borrowed Zhào Xiá's credentials for military authority.
The Wèi ruler ordered Yellow Gate Attendant Liú Chēn to gallop swiftly,
investigating Chǎng's defeat,
leading to the dismissal of Zhào Xiá and others.
Only Xiāo Bǎoyín returned with his forces intact.
During Lú Chǎng's stay at Mount Qú,
Censor-in-Chief Yóu Zhào spoke to the Wèi ruler, saying:
"Mount Qú is insignificant,
isolated by the seaside,
low and damp, difficult to inhabit,
not urgent for us,
but advantageous for the enemies.
Because it is advantageous,
they will fight desperately for it;
not urgent for us,
hence we are compelled to fight;
with reluctant forces against desperate foes,
I fear protracted conflict,
incurring great costs.
If we gain Mount Qú,
it will only lead to contention,
always hard to fully safeguard,
as it is a worthless territory.
In the Chronicles of Zǔozhuàn, when Wú intended to attack Qí,
Zǐxū advised:
"Achieving success in Qí,
is like gaining a stony field,
it is useless."
If such is necessary,
taking this worthless land,
to regain previous territory,
and temporarily ease military labor,
that would be greatly beneficial."
The Wèi ruler intended to follow this,
but coincided with Chǎng’s defeat,
promoting Zhào to Palace Attendant.
Zhào,
was the son of Mínggēn.
Yóu Mínggēn served Wèi’s Emperor Tàiwǔ and Xiàowén,
and was esteemed as a respected elder.
Mǎ Xiānpíng as a general,
shared joy and hardships with the soldiers,
dressed only in cloth,
lived without curtains and screens,
ate and drank the same as the lowest rank.
While at the borders,
he often ventured alone into enemy territories,
inspecting defenses and strategic hamlets,
leading many successful campaigns,
and the soldiers gladly served under him.
12. The state of Wei appointed Zhēn Chēn as Governor of Hénán.
Chēn submitted a memorial stating:
"When the state resided in Dài,
it suffered from rampant theft and robbery.
Emperor Shìzǔ, in his indignation, extensively established supervisors and village chiefs,
selecting only those from among the lower-ranking county magistrates and fifth-rank honorary nobles who possessed strategic ability to serve in these roles.
He also appointed many clerks and soldiers as their assistants,
elevating and valuing them,
and only then was he able to suppress the crimes.
Now, since the capital was moved,
the realm has expanded,
people from the four distant regions gather here,
affairs surpass those of the former capital Dài,
people from all directions mingle in confusion,
bandits and robbers act openly,
yet the village chiefs' positions are lowly and their duties fragmented,
most are men of inferior talent,
who harbor a careless attitude,
and are incapable of supervision and investigation.
I request that we select military officers of the eighth rank and below, down to those of capability, integrity, and effectiveness,
'integrity and effectiveness'
means firm in integrity and capable of accomplishing tasks.
The higher-ranking ones should lead the Six District Captains,
the middling ones lead the Main Road Captains,
and the lower ones lead the village chiefs.
The Wei official system provides both a salary,
and an allowance for supporting relatives,
hence it is called 'salary and support allowance'.
Wei divided the city of Luòyáng into six districts,
establishing Six District Captains.
Based on Zhāng Héng's "Eastern Capital Rhapsody" line
"The main roads are nine tracks wide",
they established Main Road Captains.
'Main roads'
refers to the major thoroughfares within the city.
In all other areas, village chiefs were established.
I request that we slightly raise the rank of the village captains,
selecting from among those in the lower ranks who are due for promotion and advancing them to these positions,
so that supervision and accountability have a proper place,
and the imperial capital can be cleansed."
Since the Hàn dynasty,
the capital has been called 'beneath the imperial carriage'.
"Village chiefs can be promoted up to the Meritorious Service rank,
'Meritorious Service rank',
is the initial rank for meritorious officials.
The Six District Captains are Regular Ninth Rank.
The Luòyáng Six District Captains were all established during the Eastern Hàn period;
Cáo Cāo served as the Northern District Captain of Luòyáng,
this is evidence of it.
'Cóng',
pronunciation according to Cáiyòng's transcription.
They need not necessarily be military men."
Chēn also memorialized to use the Yǔlín guards as patrol troops,
to investigate and apprehend thieves and robbers in the various wards and alleys.
Thereupon, the city of Luòyáng became peaceful and orderly,
and the practice was often followed thereafter.
13. This year,
within Liáng's borders there were twenty-three provinces,
this is according to the "Treatise on Geography" of the History of the Five Dynasties.
According to Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's "Records of Qí",
Qí had twenty-three provinces: Yáng, Nánxú, Yù, Yǎn, Nányǎn, Běixú, Qīng, Jì, Jiāng, Guǎng, Jiāo, Yuè, Jīng, Bā, Yǐng, Sī, Yōng, Liáng, Qín, Yì, Níng, Xiāng, and Nányù.
By this time, the province of Bā had already been abolished,
so it should be supplemented by the province of Wǎn established by Wáng Mào.
There were one thousand and twenty-two counties.
Thereafter, the names of provinces gradually increased,
with abolitions, establishments, divisions, and mergers,
too numerous to record.
The Wei court was also like this.
14. The Emperor [of Liáng] promoted harmony among the nine clans,
and treated court officials leniently and favorably.
If any committed crimes,
he would bend the law to pardon them.
But if common people committed crimes,
then he would judge them strictly according to the law.
In cases of collective punishment, even the old and young were not spared;
if one person fled,
the entire family was seized for forced labor.
The people, thus driven to poverty and desperation,
increasingly turned to treachery and crime.
Once, during a suburban sacrifice,
an old man from Mòlíng
In the Jiāngnán region, Jiànkāng and Mòlíng were considered 'red' (capital) counties;
Suí abolished Mòlíng and Jiànkāng, merging them into Jiāngníng County.
'Jiǒng'
pronunciation according to Qúyǔn's transcription.
'Guǐ',
pronunciation 'guǐ'.
said:
"Your Majesty's enforcement of the law
is harsh towards the common people,
but lenient towards the powerful and noble.
This is not the way to long-lasting rule.
If you could truly reverse this,
it would be the great fortune of the realm."
The Emperor then considered how to implement some leniency.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the Rénchén day,
an edict was issued:
"From now on, for families of fugitives and those whose crimes warrant seizure for forced labor,
if there are elderly or young among them,
they may be exempted from being sent away."
This was the extent of
the so-called leniency towards the common people.
But his inability to restrain the powerful and noble by law
led gentlemen to foresee the disorder of Liáng's governance.
2. Línchuān Prince Hóng was appointed Grand Commandant,
and General of Agile Cavalry Wáng Mào was appointed Minister of Works and President of the Imperial Secretariat.
3. On the Bǐngchén day,
Wei appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry, President of the Imperial Secretariat Gāo Zhào as Minister over the Masses,
and Prince of Qīnghé Yì as Minister of Works.
Prince of Guǎngpíng Huái was promoted to the title General of Agile Cavalry,
and granted the additional honor of 'Bearer of the Three Commissions'.
Although Zhào had risen to the Three Ducal Ministers,
he still felt he had been removed from a key post,
and his resentment showed in his words and expression.
'Key post'
refers to the Presidency of the Imperial Secretariat.
'Yàng',
pronunciation according to Yúliǎng's transcription.
The Vice Director of the Right of the Imperial Secretariat Gāo Chuò, and Erudite of the National University Fēng Guǐ,
had always taken uprightness and integrity as their guiding principle.
'Yè'
means 'to take as one's task'.
Taking uprightness and integrity as their task
is what is called forcing oneself to do it;
persisting in it without cease,
one becomes a gentleman.
Chuò went to greet and see off [Zhào] during his comings and goings,
but Guǐ ultimately did not visit Zhào.
Chuò, looking back and not seeing Guǐ,
hurriedly returned home,
and sighed:
"All my life I have considered myself not to have strayed from proper conduct,
but today's actions
fall far short of Master Fēng's."
Chuò was
the grandson of Gāo Yǔn;
Guǐ was
a clansman's grandson of Fēng Yì.
Gāo Yǔn served under four Wei emperors from Shìzǔ onward.
Fēng Yì left Yān and submitted to Wei,
but was dismissed for his aloofness and negligence.
Prince of Qīnghé Yì was talented, learned, and renowned.
Mindful of the disaster that befell Péngchéng,
referring to Prince of Péngchéng Xié being killed despite being innocent.
'Wén',
pronunciation 'wèn'.
He said to Zhào:
"How many brothers does the Son of Heaven have,
that they are being cut down almost completely!"
Referring also to the killing of Prince of Jīngzhào Yú.
'Jǐ',
pronunciation according to Jūyī's transcription.
Relying on the support of his maternal uncle,
he eventually usurped the Hàn throne.
The event is recorded in the Hàn annals.
I fear this may ultimately become a step towards disorder."
There was a great drought at the time,
and Zhào personally reviewed the cases of prisoners,
wishing to win popular support.
Yì said to the Wei Emperor:
"In the past, the Jì family made offerings to Mount Tài,
and Confucius condemned it.
Zhū Yuánhuì said: 'Lǚ'
is a name for a sacrifice.
According to ritual,
feudal lords sacrifice to the mountains and rivers within their domains.
For the Jì family to sacrifice to them
was an usurpation.
One should guard against the subtle and block the gradual,
and must not allow such profanations.
Reducing one's meals and reviewing prisoners' cases
are matters for the Emperor;
now the Minister over the Masses performs them,
is this the proper duty of a subject!
If a wise ruler neglects this above,
and treacherous ministers seize upon it below,
the foundation for calamity and disorder
lies herein."
The Emperor smiled but did not respond.
4. In summer,
the fourth month,
Wei issued an edict ordering the Imperial Secretariat and the judicial authorities to try and adjudicate legal cases,
and commanding famine-stricken people to go to Yān and Héng provinces and the six garrison towns to obtain grain.
5. On the Yǐyǒu day,
Wei declared a general amnesty,
6 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the Yǐhài day,
the state of Wèi established the imperial son Xǔ as crown prince,
and for the first time did not kill his mother.
This laid the groundwork for the later chaos caused by Empress Hú in Wèi.
Zuò once accompanied the Wèi sovereign on a visit to the Eastern Palace,
carrying a yellow gourd to present to the crown prince;
at that time, the attendant Zhào Táogōng, who responded to imperial summons, was deeply trusted by the emperor,
and Zuò privately served him,
so people of the time called him
"Táogōng's Minister of Works"
"Yellow Gourd Junior Mentor."
7 In the eleventh month,
on the Yǐwèi day,
Yuán Áng, the Grand Administrator of Wú Commandery, was appointed concurrently as Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs.
8 Earlier,
Fú Mànróng, Commandant of Infantry of the Crown Prince of Qí, submitted a memorial requesting the establishment of rituals and music for a generation,
and Emperor Shìzǔ issued an edict selecting ten academicians to revise the Five Rites,
the Five Rites being: auspicious, inauspicious, military, guest, and ceremonial.
After Jiǎn died,
the matter was entrusted to the Director of the Imperial Academy Hé Yìn.
Hé Yìn returned to Dōngshān,
Hé Yìn retired to Dōngshān in Kuàijī.
After Xiàosì was executed,
most of the materials were scattered and lost,
and an edict appointed General of Agile Cavalry Hé Tóngzhī to oversee it.
After the warfare at the end of Qí,
only a small portion remained.
When the emperor ascended the throne,
Hé Tóngzhī submitted a proposal to review what should be retained or abolished,
submitting it to the emperor,
reviewing what should be abolished or retained in the ritual bureau.
He ordered external officials to deliberate and report.
Máo Cháng said: Quányú,
means beginning.
This refers to the founding of the royal enterprise.
He wished to abolish the ritual bureau for the time being,
and merge it back into the Bureau of Ceremonial of the Department of State Affairs.
The edict stated:
"Rituals are corrupted and music is deficient,
it is indeed appropriate to revise and establish them in a timely manner.
But recently, the revision and compilation have not been entrusted to suitable people,
so over the years it has not been completed,
having a name but no substance.
Since this is of foremost importance for governing the state,
it should be compiled immediately."
The Zuǒzhuàn says: Rituals,
govern the state,
stabilize the altars of soil and grain,
order the people,
and benefit future generations.
Compile,

Fǎsēng

27. Yuán Mì, the Inspector of Qí Prefecture of Wei and Prince of Zhào,
was the son of Yuán Gàn.
Yuán Gàn, Prince of Zhào Commandery, appears in the 140th scroll, in the second year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Míng of Qí.
Here,
before
"Prince Mì"
the character

One day,

The historian states that in Wei, the Empress Dowager monopolized court affairs,

Posthaste,

Nephew,

The Empress Dowager, considering the Wei Emperor still young,

28. Huán Shūxīng, the Inspector of Nán Jīng Prefecture of Wei, submitted a request not to be subordinate to Dōng Jīng Prefecture,

Nán Jīng being subordinate to Dōng Jīng is mentioned in the eleventh year of the previous scroll.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the first day, the Wù-Chén day,
Wei proclaimed a general amnesty and changed the era name to Xīpíng.
2. Wèi's Cuī Liàng attacked Xiáshí but had not yet captured it.
He had agreed with Lǐ Chóng to advance together by water and land,
but Lǐ Chóng repeatedly failed to arrive at the appointed time.

Therefore, the Minister of Personnel Lǐ Píng was appointed as Envoy with Imperial Credentials, General Who Guards the Army, and concurrently Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs.

If there were any violations or disobedience,

Xiāo Bǎoyín sent the General of Light Chariots Liú Zhìwén and others across the Huái River,
attacking and breaking through three fortifications.
In the second month,
on the yǐsì day,
they further defeated Generals Yuán Mèngsūn and others north of the Huái.
When Lǐ Píng reached Xiáshí,
he supervised Lǐ Chóng, Cuī Liàng, and others in launching attacks by water
and land.
No one dared to disobey or act contrary.
(Disobey means
to differ or oppose.
Contrary means
to err or deviate.)
The Emperor sent the General of the Left Guard Chāng Yìzhī to lead troops to rescue Fúshān.
Before he arrived,
Kāng Xuàn had already attacked the Wèi forces
and repelled them.
The Emperor then ordered Chāng Yìzhī and Zhígé Wáng Shénniàn to sail up the Huái River to rescue Xiáshí.
Cuī Liàng sent General Bólíng's Cuī Yánbó to guard Xiàcài.
(Xiàcài County
belonged to the Pèi Commandery in the Hàn dynasty.

The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Huái River flows north from Xiáshí past the east of the old city of Xiàcài,

Wú's Jì Zhá first had his fief at Yánlíng,

In the Spring and Autumn Annals,
in the second year of Duke Xiāng,
Cài's Duke Chéng moved from Xīncài to Zhōulái,

On the eastern bank of the Huái, there is another city,

(Note: There were three Càis: Càizhōu's Shàngcài County,

and Xiàcài County,
where Duke Chéng of Cài moved.)
Cuī Yánbó took cart wheels, removed the rims,
sharpened the spokes,
paired them two by two,
twisted bamboo into ropes,
strung them together continuously,
making over ten such lines.
He laid them across the water as a bridge,
installing large windlasses at both ends.
(Windlasses are
revolving wooden devices.
Strung,
pronounced zhǔ,

It could not be burned or chopped.
This both cut off Zhào Zǔyuè's escape route
and blocked the passage of warships. Chāng Yìzhī and Wáng Shénniàn were stationed at Liángchéng and could not advance.
Lǐ Píng deployed forces for water and land attacks on Xiáshí,
capturing its outer wall.
On the yǐchǒu day,
Zhào Zǔyuè came out and surrendered.
He was beheaded,
and all his followers were captured.
Empress Dowager Hú sent a letter to Cuī Liàng,

Cuī Liàng disobeyed Lǐ Píng's command,

Although he achieved minor victories,

The Wèi army then withdrew.
3. Wèi's Palace Aide to the Censor-in-Chief Yuán Kuāng submitted an impeachment against Yú Zhōng:

Péi and Guō suffered injustice." (Referring to Péi Zhí and Guō Zuò.)
(Impeach,
pronounced tán.
Court,
pronounced cháo.)
"He caused Gāoyáng Wáng Yuán Yōng to be dismissed,

(Yú Zhōng) concurrently held the position of Commandant of the Chóngxùn Guard.
Considering his intent,

Since these events occurred after the amnesty,

"Regarding previous cases where procedures were bypassed,

The Empress Dowager ordered:

Yuán Kuāng also impeached the Palace Attendant Hóu Gāng for beating a member of the Yǔlín Guards to death.

Because he had done favors for the Empress Dowager (events seen the previous year),

The Vice Minister of Justice, Yuán Fān of Chénjùn, said:

(By chance,
pronounced xiè.
Chance,
pronounced hòu.)
Now this Yǔlín guard,

4. In the third month,
on the first day, wùxū,

Sāi (to block)
is pronounced xīzé fān.
[AS-FBEC]
Then the flowing waves will be broad and gentle,

dug a mountain channel five zhàng deep,

houses and graves

the dam was built within the territory of Xúzhōu,

[Liáng] established Xúzhōu at Zhōnglí.

8. Empress Dowager Hú of Wèi, recalling Yú Zhōng's merits,
said:
"How can we discard all his other achievements because of one fault!"
Empress Dowager Hú considered Yú Zhōng's support as meritorious;

his faults were certainly not just one.

9. Yuán Fǎsēng of Wèi sent his son Jǐnglóng to lead troops against Zhāng Qí.
Qí fought him at Jiāméng,
defeated him heavily,
slaughtered over ten cities,
and then besieged Wǔxīng.

appointing him as Governor of Yìzhōu and Commander of the Western Expedition,
to lead three thousand infantry and cavalry to the rescue.
Once Shùyǎn entered the region,
he fought continuously for three days,
advancing over two hundred lǐ,
and was victorious in all nine engagements.
In the fifth month,
Shùyǎn attacked and killed Liángzhōu Governor Rèn Tàihóng.
When the common people and the Lǎo tribesmen heard Shùyǎn had arrived,
they were delighted,
and those welcoming and bowing to him along the road followed one after another.
The people and Lǎo hated Fǎsēng but cherished Shùyǎn,
hence those welcoming him filled the roads.
Rèn
is pronounced rén.
Lǎo
is pronounced lǔ hào fān.
Shùyǎn entered the provincial capital,
entering Wǔxīng.
Wèi's Zǐtóng Administrator Gǒu Jīnlóng was also the commander of the Guānchéng garrison.
When Liáng troops arrived,
Jīnlóng was ill,
and unable to manage affairs.
His wife, Lady Liú, roused and led the city's inhabitants,
mounting the walls to resist the attack.
This lasted over a hundred days,
with more than half the soldiers dead or wounded.
The deputy garrison commander, Gāo Jǐng, plotted to rebel.
Lady Liú beheaded Jǐng and his several thousand accomplices.
Several thousand
should be several tens.
She shared clothes and reduced rations,
sharing toil and rest equally,
so all feared and cherished her.
The well was outside the city,
and was occupied by Liáng troops.
It happened to rain heavily,
so Lady Liú ordered public and private cloth, silk, and clothing to be hung out,
wringing them to collect water,
and storing all miscellaneous items in the city.
Miscellaneous items
refers to things like bottles, jars, pots, and basins.
The Liáng troops then withdrew.
The Wèi enfeoffed her son as Viscount of Píngchāng County.
10. In the sixth month,
on the Gēngzǐ day,
[Liáng] appointed Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Yíng as Left Guānglù Dàfū and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
Shàngshū Right Púshè Yuán Áng as Left Púshè,
and Lìbù Shàngshū Wáng Jiǎn as Right Púshè.
Jiǎn
was the son of [Wáng] Jiǎn.
11. Zhāng Qí repeatedly advanced from Báishuǐ,
invading Wèi's Jiāméng.
Fù Shùyǎn sent Hǔwēi General Qiáng Qiú to attack Xìnyì General Yáng Xīngqǐ,
killed him,
and recaptured Báishuǐ.
Níngshuò General Wáng Guāngzhāo was also defeated at Yīnpíng.
Zhāng Qí personally led over twenty thousand elite troops to battle Fù Shùyǎn.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Qí's army was heavily defeated,
and he fled back.
The garrisons at Xiǎojiàn, Dàjiàn, and others all abandoned their cities and fled.
Now, in Jiànzhōu's Jiànmén County, there is Dàjiàn Mountain,
and also Xiǎojiàn Mountain thirty lǐ to its northwest.
There is also the old Xiǎojiàn city fifty lǐ southwest of Yìchāng County.
Although Dàjiàn is reputed to be a natural barrier,
with narrow passes that can be defended,
between its high walls,
the paths are rather level.
Xiǎojiàn, however, has roads carved from rock and plankways built on frames,
so narrow that one cannot pass.
It is what Lǐ Bái described as
"One man guards the pass,
ten thousand cannot get through."
12. In the eighth month,
on the Yǐsì day,
Wèi appointed Hú Guózhēn as Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Governor of Yōngzhōu.
Guózhēn was old,
and the Empress Dowager actually did not want him to leave,
merely wishing to show him the honor of a regional appointment;
he ultimately did not go.
13. After Kāng Xuàn returned,
Zhāng Bàozi no longer maintained the Huái River dam.
In the ninth month,
on the Dīngchǒu day,
the Huái River water suddenly rose violently,
the dam collapsed,
with a sound like thunder,
heard for three hundred lǐ.
Over a hundred thousand people from the cities, garrisons, and villages along the Huái were swept into the sea.
Initially,
the people of Wèi were troubled by the Huái dam,
and appointed Rènchéng Prince Chéng as Dàjiāngjūn, Grand Commander of the Southern Expedition Forces,
mustering a host of one hundred thousand,
intending to advance from Xúzhōu to attack the dam.
Shàngshū Right Púshè Lǐ Píng believed
"Without using military force,
it will eventually collapse on its own."
Upon hearing it was destroyed,
the Empress Dowager was greatly pleased,
rewarded Píng richly,
and Chéng consequently did not set out.
14. On the Rénchén day,
a great amnesty was declared.
In the 15th year of Wèi, Empress Dowager Hú frequently visited the homes of imperial relatives and meritorious nobles.
Shìzhōng Cuī Guāng submitted a memorial to remonstrate, saying:
"According to ritual,
when feudal lords enter the homes of ministers without being concerned about their illnesses or deaths,
it is considered a jest between ruler and minister.

it is mockery.

This clearly shows the principle of not visiting a minister's home.
The lady,
while her parents are alive, returns to visit them,
and after their passing, sends an official to pay respects.
In the 27th winter of Zhuāng of Zuǒ Zhuàn,
Bó Jī visited
to pay respects.
Dù Yù's commentary says: paying respects,
is to inquire about the parents' well-being.
In the 12th year of Xiāng,
Chǔ Sīmǎ Zǐ Gēng was sent on a diplomatic mission to Qín
to pay respects for his wife,
which is the ritual.
The commentary states that for the wives of feudal lords,
once the parents have passed,

Huò Guāng,
the maternal grandfather,
personally served as chief minister,

Now, the imperial clan is flourishing,
the meritorious nobles are increasing in rank,
the respectful invitations are frequent,
and will become an established norm.
Flourishing,

Increasing in rank,

Respectful,
means reverence.
It refers to the homes of imperial relatives and meritorious nobles,
whenever there are celebrations,
they invite the Empress Dowager to visit.
In this way, the entire land benefits,
and all living beings look up in delight."
The Prince of Rénchéng, Chéng, noticed that the selection of military commanders for the northern frontier had become lax,
fearing that bandits and raiders would spy on the border,
threatening the mountains and tombs,
since the time of Wèi's Xiǎnzǔ and earlier,

He advocated strict maintenance of defenses,
and the Emperor issued an edict for ministers to discuss the matter.
The Deputy Minister of Justice, Yuán Fān, proposed,
since Qin and Han, the nine ministers each had one minister,
during Wèi Tàihé's fifteenth year, each of the nine ministers established deputy ministers,
emulating the remaining system of the six ministers from Zhōu, who had junior officers for the various functions.
"Recently along the border regions,
officials have not been selected for their ability,
but purely by rank.
Some encounter corrupt individuals,
who greatly expand their patrols,
set up numerous commanders,
employ relatives or in-laws,
or accept bribes for appointments,
none with any mind for defense,
only for amassing wealth.
The strong and brave soldiers,
are driven to raid,
if they meet a powerful foe,
they become enslaved,
capturing, enrich themselves.
The weak, old, and young,
have little skill in metalwork,
a little knowledge of agriculture,
search the encampments for means to survive.
They suffer harsh labor in countless ways.
Others, cut timber from deep forests,
or till the flatlands,
trade back and forth,
forming a constant stream along the roads.
These receive few rewards,
their resources are limited,
gather cloth for themselves,
receive inadequate grain,
exhaust their strength,
wear thin clothes,
for their labor,
have meager food,
endure from winter to summer,
compounded by sickness and hardship,

From ancient times to now,
border troops have all suffered from this.
'Mào,'
pronounced 'Mào.'
It is the disturbance of our borderlands,

I believe that henceforth,
for the northern and southern border provinces and the counties under their jurisdiction,

The Empress Dowager could not implement this.
By the end of Zhèngguāng,
bandits on the northern frontier emerged secretly,

invading the tombs,
just as Chéng had feared.
In the fourth year of Zhèngguāng,
the rebels of Liù Hánbālǐng and Wèi Kěgū were defeated,
at the beginning of Xiàochāng,
Yúnzhōng was lost.
In winter,
in the 11th month,
the Inspector of Jiāozhōu, Lǐ Chì, beheaded the rebel in Jiāozhōu, Ruǎn Zōngxiào,

17. Initially,
Emperor Shìzōng of Wei built the Yáoguāng Temple,

virtuous teaching can illuminate the four seas,
frugality and love for the people,
both law and custom will rely on this. "
Soon an edict was issued to discuss the shìdiàn rites externally,
and from then on, the sovereign met with the various officials in the palace once each month,
all due to Pǔhuì's words.
Pǔhuì further submitted a memorial discussing the successes and failures of current governance.
The Empress Dowager and the Emperor summoned Pǔhuì to the Xuānguāng Hall,
questioning and challenging him on each matter.
11 The younger brother of a concubine of Línchuān King Hóng, Wú Fǎshòu, killed someone and hid in Hóng's residence.
The Emperor ordered Hóng to hand him over,
and that day he was executed.
The Southern Department petitioned to dismiss Hóng from office.
The Censorate was called the Southern Terrace,
also the Southern Department.
"To love Hóng is the private affection of brothers;
to dismiss Hóng is the correct law of the sovereign;
the petition is approved."
In the fifth month,
on the Wùyín day,
the Grand Tutor, General of Agile Cavalry, and Governor of Yángzhōu, Línchuān King Hóng, was dismissed.
Since the defeat at Luòkǒu,
see scroll one hundred forty-six, fifth year.
whenever there were secret uprisings in the capital,
they were often carried out in Hóng's name,
and he was frequently impeached by the authorities,
but the Emperor pardoned him each time.
The Emperor visited the Guāngzhái Temple,
the Emperor used his old residence at Sānqiáo as the Guāngzhái Temple,
Sānqiáo was in Tóngxià Village, Mòlíng County.
Hóng's residence faced the Qínhuái River,
and a pontoon bridge was built in front of the residence;
it was called the Agile Cavalry Pontoon,
named after Hóng's official title.
The Emperor was about to depart,
but felt uneasy,
and thus crossed at the Zhūquè Pontoon instead.
When the incident occurred,
it was claimed to have been ordered by Hóng,
and the Emperor tearfully said to Hóng:
"My talent surpasses yours a hundredfold,
yet even I fear I cannot handle this position,
what are you doing?
It is not that I cannot be like Emperor Wén of Hàn,
referring to executing Huáinán King Liè Wáng Cháng.
Hóng kowtowed, claiming he had not done it,
thus because of hiding Fǎshòu, Hóng was dismissed from office.
Hóng was excessively extravagant and overstepped his bounds,
accumulating goods without satiety.
His storerooms numbered nearly a hundred,
nearly,
meaning almost.
The locks were extremely secure,
locks,
same as keys,
meaning door bolts.
This was secretly reported.
The Emperor was very affectionate towards his brothers,
and was greatly displeased.
One day,
he sent a lavish feast to Hóng's beloved concubine, Jiāng shì, saying:
"I shall come to your place for a joyful banquet."
He went alone with his old friend, the Commandant of Archers and Crossbowmen, Qiū Tuóqīng,
and drank heavily with Hóng and Jiāng.
After half-drunk,
he said:
"I now wish to tour your inner chambers."
He immediately called for a sedan chair and went straight to the rear hall.
Hóng feared the Emperor would see his wealth and bribes,
his countenance filled with terror.
The Emperor grew even more suspicious,
and so inspected each room.
Every million coins were piled together,
marked with a yellow placard,
ten million made one treasury,
hung with a purple marker.
There were over thirty such rooms.
The Emperor and Tuóqīng counted on their fingers,
seeing over three hundred million in cash.
The remaining rooms stored miscellaneous goods like cloth, silk, floss, lacquer, honey, ramie cloth, wax, etc.,
filling the storerooms to the brim,
too much to count.
The Emperor then realized it was not weaponry,
and was greatly pleased,
saying:
"Ā Liù,
your livelihood is truly grand!"
Hóng was the sixth among his brothers.
Ā,
pronounced with the entering tone from ān.
They then returned by torchlight.
The brothers' relationship thus became more harmonious.
Hóng had several dozen estates in the capital,
where he issued loans with pledged deeds.
Often using fields, houses, estates, and shops as collateral on the deeds,
once the term ended,
he would drive out the deed holders and seize their properties.
In the capital,
the people of the eastern regions,
many lost their livelihoods.
The Emperor later learned of this,
and decreed that pledged deeds could no longer be used to seize properties,
starting from then.
The Palace Attendant,
General of the Central Army, Marquis Wúpíng Bǐng,
was upright and influential,
highly regarded by the Emperor.
He was consulted on all major military and state affairs,
and was appointed General Who Pacifies the Right,
overseeing Yángzhōu.
General Who Pacifies the Right,
one of the hundred titles of generals established by the Emperor.
Bǐng,
pronounced bǐng.
Oversee,
pronounced jiān.
Bǐng,
was the Emperor's paternal cousin,
and Yángzhōu was the capital region.
Bǐng felt that occupying this post exceeded the bounds of kinship,
so he earnestly declined.
The Emperor did not permit it.
In the province, he was especially known for clear judgments,
and his orders were strict and orderly.
On Xīnsì,
Hóng was appointed General of the Central Army and Supervisor of the Secretariat.
In the sixth month,
on Yǐyǒu,
he was additionally made Acting Minister of Education under his original title.
Original title,
referring to the title of General of the Central Army.
Your servant Guāng remarks: Hóng as a general caused the defeat of three armies,
as a minister he committed great treason.
Gāozǔ sparing his death penalty was acceptable.
But within a few dozen days,
he was restored as one of the Three Dukes.
While his affection for his brother was indeed deep,
where then was the law of the sovereign?
12. Earlier,
in Luòyáng, there was a Three-Script Stone Classic erected during the Hàn.
The Stone Classic matter is recorded in the 47th year of Emperor Hàn Língdì's Xīpíng era, fourth year.
Lì Dàoyuán said: Cài Yōng corrected and finalized the text of the Five Classics,
and had it engraved on stone erected outside the gate of the Imperial Academy.
During the Wèi Zhèngshǐ era, a Three-Script Stone Classic in ancient, seal, and clerical scripts was also erected.
By the time of the Wèi,
Féng Xī and Cháng Bófū successively served as Governors of Luòzhōu.
The Wèi capital was Píngchéng,
and Luòyáng was made Luòzhōu.
After moving the capital to Luò,
it was renamed Sīzhōu.
The stone classics largely collapsed and deteriorated,
with the remains left among brambles,
taken freely by Daoists, Buddhists, and others.
Palace Attendant and Director of the Imperial Academy Cuī Guāng requested officials be sent to guard and oversee them,
and ordered Erudites of the Imperial Academy like Lǐ Yù to repair the damages and missing parts.
Empress Dowager Hú permitted it.
But then Yuán Chā and Liú Téng started a rebellion,
and the matter was shelved.
Chā and Téng's rebellion,
is recorded in the next year, second year of Pǔtōng.
13. In autumn,
seventh month,
the Qiāng leader Què Tiěhū in Wèi's Hézhōu
rebelled,
proclaiming himself King of Shuǐchí;
Hézhōu administered Fúhǎn,
overseeing Jīnchéng, Wǔshǐ, Hónghé, and Líntáo commanderies.
Shuǐchí County,
established as a commandery by Wèi in the fourth year of Zhēnjūn,
later changed to a county,
belonging to Hónghé commandery.
Suí merged Hónghé commandery into Dāngyí County,
its location within the boundaries of Táng's Táozhōu Líntán County.
Cáo Wèi established the Gentleman of the Masters of Guests in the Department of State Affairs.
Strictly ordered the provinces, commanderies, and various armies,
not to harm even a single item of the people,
nor to lightly engage the rebels in battle,
then demonstrated both authority and kindness,
making them realize regret and fear.
In the eighth month,
Tiěhū and others led each other to surrender to Zǐgōng,
the whole affair taking less than twenty days.
Meaning from Zǐgōng's arrival in Hézhōu until the rebels' surrender,
the whole affair took less than twenty days.
Led,
read as shuài.
Surrender,
pronounced xiáng.
He was the son of Huái.
Yuán Huái,
son of Yuán Hè,
served under Emperors Wénchéng, Xiànwén, Xiàowén, and Xuānwǔ.

was full of cunning schemes,

The method of pitches states: Yang takes the circle as its form,

Cutting pipes to make pitch-pipes,
blowing to test the sounds,
arranging according to the breath of things,
is the foundation of the Way.
Specialists, because their sounds are subtle and their substance difficult to know,
and their fractional divisions unclear,
therefore made the standard to replace them.
The sound of the standard is clear and easy to reach,
and its divisions are also coarse;
however, the strings rely on tension and relaxation, clarity and turbidity,
and without pipes there is no way to correct them.
Tune its middle string,
so that it matches Huángzhōng,
press and mark to seek the various pitch-pipes,
and there is none that does not correspond to the numbers.
The sounds are subtle and refined,
and those who synthesize them understand.
Jìn Shū Yuè Zhì: Gōng,
is center,
the way of central harmony, wherever it goes, there is order.
Shāng,
is strength,
meaning the nature of metal is firm and strong.
Jué,
is contact,
symbolizing all yang things contacting objects and generating.
Zhǐ,
is cessation,
meaning when things are abundant, they cease.
Yǔ,
is expansion,
when yang energy is about to return,
all things breed and expand to grow.
Sòng Bó said: Harmonizing gōng and connecting sounds is called gōng,
its sound is majestic and vast.
Opening the mouth and emitting sound is called shāng,
its sound is clanging and clattering.
Baring teeth and protruding lips is called jué,
its sound is crowing and clucking.
Teeth closed and lips open is called zhǐ,
its sound is yǐyǐ xìxì.
Teeth open and lips gathered is called yǔ,
its sound is xǔ xù yú xū.
Having researched for a long time,
I have gained considerable understanding.
The standard is used to replace the pitch-pipes,
taking its fractional divisions,
to adjust and calibrate musical instruments.
I have privately sought the principles of tuning sounds,
gōng and shāng should be turbid,
zhǐ and yǔ should be clear.
If following Gōngsūn Chóng,
only using the twelve pitch-pipe sounds,
and saying they rotate as gōng,
clarity and turbidity are all sufficient.
Only the Huángzhōng pipe is the longest,
so taking Huángzhōng as gōng,
then often they follow smoothly.
If tuning the eight tones,
one must still interweave the various sounds,
to match and achieve their beauty.
If taking Yìngzhōng as gōng,
Ruíbīn as zhǐ,
then the zhǐ is turbid and the gōng is clear,
although there is its rhyme,
it does not form a musical melody.
If taking Zhōnglǚ as gōng,
then among the twelve pitch-pipes, there is nothing to take at all.
Now following Jīng Fáng's book,
taking Zhōnglǚ as gōng,
then using Qùmiè as shāng,
Zhíshǐ as zhǐ,
only then does it become rhythmic.
Yet Chóng takes Zhōnglǚ as gōng,
still using Línzhōng as zhǐ,
how can it be harmonious!
But the sounds are subtle and refined,
historical records are brief,
the old records say the standard has thirteen strings,
hidden interval nine chǐ,
not saying whether it requires bridges or not.
Also,
within one cùn there are nineteen thousand six hundred eighty-three divisions,
extremely fine and difficult to discern.
Zhòngrú has privately examined and tested,
The pillar should be properly placed,
but within the forward and backward positions of the pillar,
using the markings to divide the scale,
the harmonious tones that generate each other will naturally correspond.
The thickness of the middle string
must be similar to that of the qín's gōng string,
and tuning pegs should be applied to adjust the pitch,
making it harmonize with Huángzhōng.
Below the middle string, mark the intervals of the sixty pitches according to their clear and turbid qualities,
while the remaining twelve strings should have pillars placed like a zhēng,
then, by pressing along the entire range of the middle string,
measure and transfer the pitches onto the twelve strings.
Afterward, follow the method of mutual generation,
proceeding in sequence,
to derive the shāng and zhǐ of the twelve pitches.
Once shāng and zhǐ are determined,
then apply the tuning method of the qín's five modes to adjust the instrument,
and finally blend various sounds to embellish it.
If anything deviates from this,
the sounds will not harmonize.

Yánshòu,

This means he had no teacher to inherit from but transformed the twelve pitches into sixty.
Confucius said: "For anyone who brings even a small bundle of dried meat,
I have never refused to teach."
Zhū Yuánhuì notes: "Xiū
means dried meat,
and ten strips are bound together as a bundle.
In ancient times, when meeting, one must present gifts as a courtesy,
and a bundle of dried meat is the humblest of such gifts.
Those with enlightened minds understand through experience without a teacher;
if they gain even the slightest insight,
it all comes from their own heart and mind.
Why must one receive instruction from a teacher to be considered remarkable!"
The Shàngshū Xiāo Bǎoyín memorialized that Zhòngrú’s learning was not acquired from a teacher,
and he lightly sought to create,
so he dared not
grant approval;

The Empress Dowager casually said to the concurrent Zhōngshū Shèrén Yáng Yù:
"Relatives and in-laws outside the court do not meet expectations;
if you hear anything,
be careful not to conceal it out of hesitation!"
Yù reported that Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Chóng transported goods with five carts,
and Xiàngzhōu
Cìshǐ Yáng Jūn made silver utensils
as gifts for the Lǐngjūn Yuán Chā.
Xiàng,
read as xī liàng fān.
She wept and reprimanded him.
Weeping while reprimanding him shows her loving and admonishing intent.
Yù’s uncle Shū’s wife
was the sister of Wǔchāng Wáng Hé.
Hé was a cousin of Chā’s grandfather.
After Shū died,
Yuánshì repeatedly requested to live separately.
Yù’s father Chūn tearfully admonished her,
but she did not listen,
and Yuánshì resented him for it.
When the people of Yíngzhōu, Liú Xuānmíng, plotted rebellion,
the matter was discovered,
and he fled.
Chā had Hé and Yuánshì falsely accuse Yù of hiding Xuānmíng,
and further claimed:
"Yù’s father, Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ Chūn,
and uncle, Huázhōu Cìshǐ Jīn,
together sent three hundred sets of armor and weapons,
plotting treason."
Chā further fabricated the case.
He dispatched five hundred imperial guards to surround Yù’s residence at night,
and arrested him,
but found nothing.
The Empress Dowager inquired about the situation,
and Yù fully explained that it was due to Yuánshì’s resentment.
The Empress Dowager released Yù from his bonds,
sentenced Hé and Yuánshì to death,
but later Chā intervened to save them.
Hé was only dismissed from office,
and Yuánshì ultimately was not punished.
The historian notes that Empress Líng excessively favored and protected Yuán Chā, sowing the seeds of future trouble.

where he enshrined Tàizǔ Wén Huángdì and above as the six ancestral temples.
They were all in the same hall,
sharing a courtyard but with separate chambers.
There was also a small temple,
which was the temple of Tàizǔ's Tài Fūrén.
As she was not the principal wife,
a separate temple was established.
Each time the emperor finished offering sacrifices at the Grand Temple,
he would proceed to the small temple,
also using one tàiláo (a sacrificial ox),
following the same rituals as at the Grand Temple.
There were two temple officials,
who managed temple affairs.
The relevant officials reported this.
The emperor asked the Zhōngshū Shèrén Zhū [AS-82FA]:
"Auspicious and inauspicious events occurring on the same day—
can we proceed now?"
He replied:
"In the past, when Duke Xiàn of Wèi heard of Liǔ Zhuāng's death,
he went without removing his sacrificial robes.
The Lǐjì·Tángōng records: When the Grand Historian of Wèi, Liǔ Zhuāng, was critically ill,
the duke said:
'If his condition worsens,
even if I am in the midst of a sacrifice, you must inform me.'
The duke bowed twice and touched his head to the ground,
then requested before the ancestral representative:
'There is a minister named Liǔ Zhuāng,
who is not merely my minister,
but a minister of the state.
Upon hearing of his death,
I request to go.'
He went without removing his robes,
and subsequently presented burial garments.
This also shows his service to the royal house,
and attending to him
is in accordance with ritual."
The emperor then went to his residence,
and wept for him with great sorrow.
5 The crown prince Ān of Gāogōulí sent an envoy to present tribute.
In the second month,
on Guǐchǒu day,
Ān was appointed as Níngdōng Jiāngjūn and King of Gāogōulí.
The envoy Jiāng Fǎshèng was sent to confer upon Ān the official robes, crown, sword, and ornaments.
Troops from Wèi's Guāng Prefecture captured him at sea,
and sent him to Luòyáng.
In the fourth year of the Huángxīng era of Wèi,
Guāng Prefecture was established by dividing Qīng Prefecture.
It administered Dōnglái, Chángguǎng, and Dōngmóu Commanderies,
with its seat at Yè.
6 Wèi's Grand Tutor, Shìzhōng, and Qīnghé Wénxiàn Wáng, Yuán Yì,
was handsome and dignified in appearance.
Empress Dowager Hú forced herself upon him and had an affair with him.
However, he was inherently capable,
and in assisting with governance, he provided much correction and benefit.
He was fond of literature,
respected and treated scholars with courtesy,
and was highly regarded by his contemporaries.
The Shìzhōng and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn, Yuán Chā, served in the Ménxià agency,
and concurrently commanded the imperial guard troops.
Relying on favor, he was arrogant and unrestrained,
with ambitions knowing no bounds.
Yì often restrained him according to the law,
which caused Chā to resent him.
The Wèi Jiāngjūn and Yítóng Sānsī, Liú Téng,
wielded power that overshadowed both the court and the inner palace.
The Ministry of Personnel,迎合 Téng's wishes,
recommended appointing Téng's younger brother as a commandery administrator.
The person's qualifications were inappropriate and exceeded his rank.
A person not matching the required talent is termed 'guāi' (inappropriate),
and qualifications not matching the position are termed 'yuè' (exceeding).
Téng also resented him for this.
The Lóngxiāng Prefecture Chief Clerk, Sòng Wéi,
was the son of Biàn.
Sòng Biàn was employed during the reign of Wèi Xiàowéndì.
Xiāng,
is pronounced with the thought of 'general'.
Zhǎng,
is pronounced with the two-part reading.
Tōngzhíláng,
refers to Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng,
and after the Suí dynasty, it became an honorary salary post.
Chā promised Wéi wealth and honor,
and had him accuse the Sīrǎn Dūwèi Hán Wénshū and his son of plotting a rebellion to enthrone Yì.
The Zhōu official system had the 'rǎn rén' (dyeing officer),
the Hàn had the Píngzhǔn Lìng,
who oversaw dyeing and coloring.
Later, Wèi established the Sīrǎn Dūwèi,
and later, the Qí Tàifǔ Sì's subordinate officials included the Sīrǎn Shǔ Lìng and Chéng.
Lù Déming: Rǎn,
is pronounced as 'rǎn yàn';
Liú pronounces it as 'rǎn xiǎn'.
Upon investigation,
no evidence of rebellion was found,
and they were released.
Wéi should have been punished for false accusation;
'fǎn zuò' means
the false accuser is punished with the crime they accused others of.
"If we execute Wéi now,
later, if there is a real rebel,
no one will dare to report it."
Therefore, Wéi was demoted to Administrator of Chāngpíng Commandery.
Chāngpíng County,
belonged to Shànggǔ Commandery during the Hàn,
Later Wèi established Chāngpíng Commandery,
under Yān Prefecture.
The Suí dynasty again abolished the commandery and restored it as a county,
belonging to Yōu Prefecture.
Chā feared that Yì would ultimately become a threat to him,
so he conspired secretly with Liú Téng.
They had the Zhǔshí Zhōnghuángmén Hú Dìng confess
Zhǔshí means
the one in charge of the emperor's meals.
Liè means
to state.
"Yì bribed Dìng to poison the Wèi emperor,
promising Dìng wealth and honor
if he himself became emperor."
The emperor was eleven years old at the time,
and believed it.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Bǐngzǐ day,
the Empress Dowager was at Jiāfú Hall,
and had not yet proceeded to the front hall.
Chā escorted the emperor to Xiǎnyáng Hall,
while Téng closed the gates of the Yǒngxiàng corridor,
preventing the Empress Dowager from leaving.
When Yì entered,
he encountered Chā behind Hánzhāng Hall.
Chā sternly refused to let Yì enter.
Yì said:
"Do you intend to rebel?"
Chā said:
"Chā is not rebelling,
I am just about to arrest the rebel!"
He ordered the Zōngshì and Zhízhāi to seize Yì by the sleeves,
and took him into the eastern section of Hánzhāng Hall.
Wèi established the Zōngshī,
and Zōngshì were their subordinates.
Zhízhāi were
those on duty in the palace halls and chambers,
belonging to the Zhígé.
Jiāng means
to lead,
to escort.
Téng, claiming an imperial edict, assembled the ministers for deliberation,
accusing Yì of high treason.
Everyone feared Chā,
and none dared to dissent,
except the Púyè and Xīntài Wénzhēn Gōng, Yóu Zhào, who argued firmly that it was not permissible.
Wǔdài Zhì: Xīntài County belonged to Lángyá Commandery.
He did not put brush to paper to sign his name.
Chā and Téng brought the ministers' deliberation in,
and shortly after, obtained approval,
meaning the Wèi emperor approved their memorial.
Then they forged an edict from the Empress Dowager,
stating that she was ill,
and was returning governance to the emperor.
They imprisoned the Empress Dowager in the Xuānguāng Hall of the Northern Palace,
keeping the palace gates closed day and night,
cutting off all contact inside and out.
Téng personally held the keys,
and even the emperor could not visit her.
Shěng,
is pronounced xǐ jǐng.
Jiàn,
is pronounced xián biàn.
The Empress Dowager's clothing and meals were cut off,
and she suffered hunger and cold.
She then sighed:
"To raise a tiger and be bitten by it—
that describes me."
They also had the Zhōngchángshì
Jiǎ Càn attend the emperor during study,
secretly ordering him to monitor the emperor's every move.
Chā then, together with the Grand Preceptor Gāoyáng Wáng Yuán Yōng and others, jointly assisted in governance.
The emperor called Chā 'yífù' (uncle).
Chā and Téng collaborated inside and out to monopolize power,
with Chā handling external defense,
and Téng handling internal security.
They often served directly in the imperial agencies,
jointly deciding punishments and rewards.
No matter how major or minor the government affairs were,
they were decided by these two,
their authority shaking both inside and outside the court,
and all officials tread carefully.
Both court and commoners, upon hearing of Yì's death,
were disheartened without exception.
Several hundred Hú and Yí people slashed their faces in mourning for him.
Yóu Zhào died of indignation and sorrow.
7 On Jǐmǎo day,
the Jiāng, Huái, and sea all overflowed.
On the Xīnmǎo day (the 8th),
the Emperor of Wèi (Northern Wèi) held his capping ceremony (coming-of-age),
issued a general amnesty,
and changed the era name to Zhèngguāng.
9. Wèi's Governor of Xiàngzhōu, Zhōngshān Wénzhuāng Wáng Yuán Xī,
was the son of Yuán Yīng.
Yuán Yīng served Emperors Xiàowén and Xuānwǔ of Wèi,
leading troops on several occasions with merit.
Xiàng,
pronunciation Xīliàng.
Since the Cáo-Wèi period,
the ducal establishments have had Eastern and Western Pavilion Libationers.
Upon hearing of Yuán Yì's death,
(Yuán Xī) raised troops in Yè,
submitting a memorial desiring to execute Yuán Chā and Liú Téng.
(Yuán) Zuǎn fled,
and ran to Yè.
Ten days later,
Chief Clerk Liǔ Yuánzhāng and others led the city's people, clamoring as they entered,
killed his (Yuán Xī's) attendants,
seized Xī, Zuǎn, and their sons and placed them in a tall tower.
In the eighth month,
on the Jiǎyǐn day,
Yuán Chā sent the Left Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat Lú Tóng to go and behead Xī in the streets of Yè,
along with his sons and younger brothers.
Xī was fond of literature,
and had a righteous character,
many famous scholars associated with him.
About to die,
he wrote a letter to an old friend saying:
"My younger brother and I both received the Empress Dowager's recognition and favor.
I, the elder brother, governed a large province,
while my younger brother entered to serve in attendance.
Her earnest words and demeanor
showed kindness like a compassionate mother.
Now the Empress Dowager has been deposed to the Northern Palace,
the Grand Tutor, Prince of Qīnghé (Yuán Yì), has unjustly suffered brutal slaughter,
the Sovereign is young,
alone in the front hall.
With ruler and kin treated thus,
I could not find peace within myself,
therefore I led soldiers and people wishing to establish great righteousness in the realm.
But my wisdom and strength were shallow and short,
and I was swiftly captured and imprisoned.
Swiftly,
means 'in return'.
I am ashamed below to those who knew me.
Originally, it was because duty and righteousness stirred my heart,
that I could not but act thus.
Whether my entrails are spilled or my skull shattered,
what more is there to say!
All you gentlemen,
each revere your own conduct,
for the state and for yourselves,
diligently strive to uphold reputation and integrity!"
Those who heard pitied him.
Xī's head arrived in Luòyáng,
none of his relatives or old friends dared to look,
only the former General of the Rapid as Tigers Cavalry Diāo Zhěng gathered his corpse and concealed it.
Zhěng
was the grandson of Diāo Yōng.
Diāo Yōng left Jìn and entered Wèi,
establishing merit in the region between the Huái and Rǔ Rivers.
(The authorities) thoroughly investigated Xī's associates.
They shackled Jìyīn Administrator Yáng Yù and sent him to Yè.
Jìyīn Commandery,
during Hàn and Jìn belonged to Yǎnzhōu,
under Wèi it belonged to Xīyǎnzhōu.
Jì,
pronunciation Zǐlǐ.
Only then was he able to return to his post.
Chā appointed Tóng as Vice Director of the Chancellery.
Yuán Lüè fled and reached an old friend, Simǎ Shǐbīn of Hénèi.
Shǐbīn and Lüè bound a reed raft and crossed the Mèng Ford at night,
going to the home of Lì Fǎguāng in Túnliú.
Túnliú County since Hàn and Jìn times belonged to Shàngdǎng Commandery.
The Genealogy of Surnames: The surname Lì
descends from the Lìlù clan.
Among the wealthy families of Cháng'ān in Hàn times were the Lì clan.
Master Yán's note: Tún,
pronunciation chún.
They hid him for a full year.
At the time, the search for Lüè was very urgent,
Lüè became fearful,
and requested to be sent beyond the border.
(Fǎguāng) said:
"A man meets death but once,
what is difficult to encounter is dying for a true friend.
I hope you will not be concerned."
Lüè firmly requested to flee south,
(Fǎguāng) then had his nephew Chāng escort Lüè across the river,
and so (Lüè) came fleeing (to Liáng).
The Emperor (of Liáng) enfeoffed Lüè as Prince of Zhōngshān.
This sets the stage for Lüè's later return to Wèi.
(Fǎguāng) was a clansman's grandson of (Diāo) Yōng.
Chā falsely accused Diāo Zhěng of aiding Lüè's escape,
and arrested and imprisoned him along with his sons and younger brothers.
The Censor Wáng Jī and others strenuously argued for his vindication,
and only then was he spared.
10. On the Jiǎzǐ day,
the Palace Attendant, General of Chariots and Cavalry, Marquis Yǒngchāng Yán, Wěi Ruì died.
The Records of the Five Dynasties: Línglíng County in Línglíng Commandery was formerly divided to establish Yǒngchāng County.
The principles of posthumous names: Subduing the enemy and being just is called Yán;
being awe-inspiring but not fierce is called Yán.
Cavalry,
pronunciation qíjì.
Officials and commoners all followed the prevailing wind and bent with it,
only Ruì, considering himself positioned as a high minister,
did not wish to bend with the vulgar customs,
his conduct remained largely as usual.
The historian states that Wěi Ruì, in a court devoted to Buddhism,
corrected it with uprightness,
nearly one who serves his ruler with the Way.
11. In the ninth month,
on the Wùxū day,
Wèi appointed Gāoyáng Wáng Yuán Yōng as Chancellor,
to oversee all affairs internal and external,
and decide on governmental matters together with Yuán Chā.
12. Earlier,
the Rúrǎn Tuòhán Kèhán married Hòulǚlíng Shì, the wife of Fúmíngdūn,
and they bore the Fúbá Kèhán and Ānàhuái and five other sons.
Kè,
follows the entering tone of kān.
Hán,
pronunciation hán.
Huái,
pronunciation gǔhuí.
Suddenly, his youngest son Zǔhuì was lost,
and seeking with rewards could not find him.
There was a shamaness named Dìwàn who said Zǔhuì was now in heaven,
and she could summon him.
Then, in a great marsh, she set up a tent,
and sacrificed to the heavenly spirits.
Zǔhuì suddenly appeared in the tent,
saying himself he was constantly in heaven.
Fúbá was greatly pleased,
called Dìwàn a holy maiden,
and took her as his Kèhédūn.
The ruler of the Rúrǎn is called Kèhán,
his principal wife is called Kèhédūn.
She further had a wanton appearance,
Fúbá respected and loved her,
trusted and employed her words,
and she interfered and disordered state affairs.
Thus it continued for years.
Zǔhuì gradually grew older,
and told his mother:
"I was always at Dìwàn's home,
I never went to heaven;
going to heaven was something Dìwàn taught me."
His mother fully reported the situation to Fúbá.
Fúbá said:
"Dìwàn can foreknow what has not yet happened,
do not slander her."
Afterwards, Dìwàn became afraid,
and slandered Zǔhuì before Fúbá, who then killed him.
Hòulǚlíng Shì sent her great minister Jùliè and others to strangle Dìwàn to death;
Fúbá was enraged,
and wanted to execute Jùliè and the others.
It happened that the Āzhìluó invaded,
Āzhìluó,
are a separate tribe of the northerners,
dwelling east of the Northern River,
for generations attached to Wèi.
One version: Āzhìluó
are of the Gāochē tribe.
(Fúbá) was defeated in battle and returned.
Hòulǚlíng Shì and the great ministers together killed Fúbá,
and established his younger brother Ānàhuái as Kèhán.
Ānàhuái had been established for ten days,
when his clansman elder brother Shìfā led a host of several tens of thousands to attack him.
Ānàhuái was defeated in battle,
and with his younger brother Yǐjūfá fled on light cavalry to Wèi.
Shìfā killed Hòulǚlíng Shì and Ānàhuái's two younger brothers.
The historian states that the Rúrǎn were in disorder.
13. When Wèi's Prince of Qīnghé, Yuán Yì, died,
Prince of Rǔnán, Yuán Yuè, showed not the slightest resentment toward Yuán Chā.
He waited upon him with mulberry-fall wine.
The *Commentary on the Waterways Classic* states: In Hédōng Commandery, many people were relocated.
Among the people was one surnamed Liú, named Duò,
who was long skilled in brewing.
He drew water from the river's flow,
and fermented it into fragrant, rich wine.
The time for hanging up the meat was the same year as the withered branches,
and the wine was racked during the mulberry-falling season,
hence the wine got its name.
The color of the aromatic brew
was clear and white, like thin rice water.
Its distinct aroma,
unlike any other,
surpassed orchid's fragrance and musk's scent,
naturally forming an exquisite and elegant bouquet.
As a tribute from the region,
it was considered the finest vintage.
From princes and dukes to common friends, they would urge and invite each other,
often saying, "Let's seek the gentleman,"
where "seek the gentleman" (suǒ láng) is a reversed phrase for "mulberry-fall" (sāng luò).
It became even more a refined phrase in registers and a
brilliant topic of conversation among the Secretariat.
Yuán Chā was greatly pleased.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the yǐmǎo day,
he appointed Yuè as Palace Attendant and Grand Commandant.
Yuè then went to Yì's son, Yuán Dǎn, to request Yì's clothing and playthings.
They were not delivered in a timely manner to his satisfaction.
Not only was there delay in presenting them on time,
but what was presented also did not please Yuè.
Chēng,
read with the chǐzhèng pronunciation.
He nearly died.
14. The Rúrǎn kèhán Ānàguī was about to arrive in Wèi.
The Wèi sovereign sent the Minister of Works, Prince Jì of Jīngzhào, Palace Attendant Cuī Guāng, and others to welcome him in succession,
bestowing generous rewards and comforts.
The Wèi sovereign received Ānàguī in audience at the Xiǎnyáng Hall,
and accordingly held a banquet,
placing Ānàguī's seat below that of the imperial princes.
As the banquet was about to end,
Ānàguī, holding a memorial, stood behind his seat.
An edict summoned him before the imperial throne.
Ānàguī bowed twice and said:
"Your subject, due to familial calamity,
came lightly to Your Majesty's court.
The officials and people of my own state
have all fled and scattered.
Your Majesty's grace is as vast as heaven and earth.
I beg for troops to escort me back to my state,
to execute and eradicate the rebels,
and to gather the dispersed.
I shall then lead the remaining people
in serving Your Majesty.
Words cannot fully express it;
there is a separate memorial detailing my request."
He then handed the memorial to the Secretariat Drafter Cháng Jǐng to present it.
Jǐng
was the grandson of Cháng Shuǎng.
(Cháng Shuǎng appears in the 123rd scroll, in the sixth year of Yuánjiā of Sòng Emperor Wén.)
In the eleventh month,
on the jǐhài day,
Wèi established Ānàguī as Duke of Shuòfāng and King of Rúrǎn,
bestowing upon him clothing and a light carriage,
with stipends, comforts, ceremonial guards,
all identical to those of an imperial prince.
At that time, Wèi was powerful and prosperous.
East of the imperial way, south of the Luòshuǐ bridge, they established four hostels,
and west of the way, they established four wards: Those who surrendered from south of the Yangtze were settled in the Jīnlíng Hostel,
and after three years were granted residences in the Guīzhèng Ward;
those who surrendered from the northern barbarians were settled in the Yānrán Hostel,
granted residences in the Guīdé Ward;
those who surrendered from the eastern barbarians were settled in the Fúsāng Hostel,
granted residences in the Mùhuà Ward;
those who surrendered from the western barbarians were settled in the Yānzī Hostel,
granted residences in the Mùyì Ward.
The four hostels were all named after places in the four directions: Jīnlíng is south of the Yangtze,
Yānrán is north of the desert,
Fúsāng is in the east,
where the sun rises,
Yānzī is in the west,
where the sun sets.
The *Classic of Mountains and Seas* says: In the midst of the great wilderness,
above the Yáng Valley is the Fúsāng tree,
where the sun rises.
On the Huīyě Mountain there is a tree,
with green leaves and red flowers,
named the Ruòmù tree,
where the sun sets;
it grows west of Kūnlún,
southwest of the Niǎoshǔ Mountains,
called Yānzī.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says: Passing Xìliǔ, in the western lands,
is Yānzī, where the sun sets.
The *Record of the Ten Continents* says: Fúsāng is in the azure sea,
several thousand zhàng tall,
over a thousand arm-spans in girth,
with two trunks from the same root,
leaning on each other,
hence the name Fúsāng (Supporting Mulberry).
Jiàng (surrender),
read with the hùjiāng pronunciation.
Chǔ (settle),
read with the chānglǚ pronunciation;
same below.
Yān (Yānrán),
read with the yīnjiān pronunciation.
Yān (Yānzī),
read with the yīlián pronunciation,
also read yījiǎn.
Zī,
pronounced zī.
Guī
was settled in the Yānrán Hostel.
Ānàguī repeatedly requested to return to his state.
Court discussions were divided and no decision was reached.
Ānàguī bribed Yuán Chā with one hundred catties of gold,
and thus was permitted to return north.
In the twelfth month,
on the rénzǐ day,
Wèi ordered the Governor of Huáishuò to select two thousand elite cavalry to escort Ānàguī to the border head.
Border head
means the beginning of the border.
Qí (cavalry),
read with the qíjì pronunciation.
If they come to welcome and receive him,
bestow silks, carriages, horses, and send him off with ceremony before returning;
if they do not accept him,
allow him to return to the court.
The provisions and supplies for his journey
are to be provided by the Department of State Affairs according to measure.
15. On the xīnyǒu day,
Wèi appointed Prince Jì of Jīngzhào as Minister over the Masses.
16. Wèi sent the envoy Liú Shànmíng to pay a courtesy visit,
resuming friendly relations.
Since Lú Chǎng returned north in the second year of Jiànyuán of Qí Emperor Míng,
Wèi had not again sent envoys on courtesy visits south,
and at this time relations were resumed.
Fù (resume),
read with the fúyòu pronunciation.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the xīnsì day,
the Emperor performed the suburban sacrifice south of the capital.
2. He established the Garden of Solitude in Jiànkāng,
to receive and care for the impoverished people.
In ancient times, there was provision for widowers, widows, orphans, the childless, the disabled, and the ill.
The Emperor was not able to emulate antiquity;
he was merely following the example of the Buddhist layman Sudatta.
3. On the wùzǐ day,
a general amnesty was declared.
4. The Dí people of Wèi's Nánqín Province rebelled.
5 The Wei state dispatched fifteen thousand soldiers from the nearby commanderies,
(nearby commanderies,
meaning the commanderies near the capital region) to escort the Rouran Khan Ānàguī back to his country.
The Left Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Zhāng Pǔhuì, submitted a memorial,
believing:
"The Rouran have long been a border trouble.
Now Heaven has sent down calamity and chaos upon them,
tormenting their hearts,
likely wishing to make them understand the joy of following the Way,
so that they might reform themselves, bow their heads, and serve the great Wei.
Your Majesty should pacify the people and cultivate yourself with reverence to win over their hearts.
Ānàguī has come alone, submitting his fate;
it is sufficient to pacify him.
Yet instead, we first trouble and disturb ourselves,
raising troops within the suburban regions,
casting them into the distant wilderness,
rescuing a formidable enemy of many generations,
aiding a vile foe that Heaven intends to destroy.
In my foolish opinion, I do not see how this is acceptable.
This is merely border generals greedily seeking momentary achievement,
not considering that armies are instruments of ill omen,
which a true king uses only as a last resort.
(Using the meaning of Lǎozǐ's words.)
The sagely and compassionate [emperor] has reduced his meals,
yet he sends fifteen thousand men with Yáng Jūn as their general,
hoping to pacify the Rouran.
To act contrary to the times,
can it succeed?
If there should be a disastrous reversal,
would Yáng Jūn's flesh
be enough to eat?
(Using the meaning of the words with which Chǔ's Sūnshū'áo rebuked Wǔ Shēn in the Zuǒzhuàn.)
Not planning for the great scheme of safety and danger,
this is why your humble servant is filled with dread.
Moreover, if Ānàguī does not return,
what trust or righteousness would he be violating?
Your servant's rank is too low to participate in deliberations.
(In the Hàn dynasty, all officials from the rank of Yìláng upwards could participate in major court deliberations.
The two Assistant Directors of the Imperial Secretariat,
in that period, held positions that were not considered lowly.
Yet he considered his rank too low to participate in deliberations.
This is likely because, since the Cáo Wèi period onwards,
major court deliberations only involved officials of the Eight Ministers rank and above.
All documents passed through the hands of the two Assistant Directors of the Imperial Secretariat.)
Ānàguī took his leave in the Western Hall,
and an imperial edict bestowed upon him weapons, clothing and bedding, assorted silks, grain, and livestock,
treating him generously in every matter.
(Cǎi is the same as cǎi [silk fabric].
Chù [livestock] is pronounced xù.)
When Ānàguī fled south,
his paternal cousin (from his father's elder brother) Póluómén led tens of thousands of troops to attack Shìfā,
