20 On the *guǐwèi* day,
Wei proclaimed a general amnesty,
changing the era name to Xiàochāng.
21 Pòliùhán Bálíng besieged Yuán Shēn, Prince of Guǎngyáng of Wei, at Wǔyuán.
Army Commander Hèbá Shèng recruited two hundred men to open the east gate and engage in battle,
beheading over a hundred enemies,
causing the rebels to retreat slightly.
Shēn led his army toward Shuòzhōu,
with Shèng often serving as the rear guard.
Fèi Mù, Governor of Yúnzhōu,
rallied the scattered and dispersed,
resisting the enemy on all sides.
At that time, all the northern border commanderies and garrisons had fallen,
leaving only the city of Yúnzhōng standing alone.
The previous year,
Lǐ Chóng had ordered Fèi Mù to defend Yúnzhōng.
With roads blocked and cut off,
and reinforcements not arriving,
both provisions and weapons were exhausted.
Mù abandoned the city and fled south to Èrzhū Róng at Xiùróng.
Later, he went to the court to plead for punishment,
and an edict pardoned him.
Permanent Exile Army Advisor Yú Jǐn
Permanent Exile Army Advisor
was in charge of prohibitions and defenses.
The offices of dukes and above established Permanent Exile Army Advisors;
minor offices without Permanent Exile Advisors
established Prohibition and Defense Army Advisors.
"Now that bandits and rebels have arisen,
it is not easy to rely solely on military force to achieve victory.
I, Jǐn, request to carry Your Highness's majestic orders,
to explain to them the consequences of fortune and misfortune,
hoping they may be somewhat persuaded to disperse."
Shēn agreed.
Jǐn, being fluent in several foreign languages,
rode alone to the rebel Hú camp,
met their chieftains,
and demonstrated kindness and good faith.
Thereupon, Western Tiělè chieftain Miēlièhé and others led over thirty thousand households south to surrender to Shēn.
Shēn wanted to lead troops to Zhéfū Ridge to meet them.
The *Tōngdiǎn* records
"Zhé Dūn Ridge."
"Pòliùhán Bálíng's military strength is very formidable.
Hearing that Miēlièhé and others are coming to surrender,
he will certainly lead troops to intercept them.
If we first occupy the strategic points,
it will not be easy to oppose him.
It would be better to use Miēlièhé as bait,
and set an ambush to await him.
We will surely defeat him."
Shēn followed this advice.
Bálíng indeed led troops to intercept Miēlièhé,
capturing all his followers.
The ambush was sprung,
and Bálíng was heavily defeated.
They recovered Miēlièhé's followers and returned.
Róurán's Tóubīng Kèhán heavily defeated Pòliùhán Bálíng.
Kè,
pronounced as cóng kān rù shēng.
Hán,
pronounced as hán.
Bálíng, avoiding the Róurán,
moved south and crossed the river.
This river refers to the Northern River.
He sought aid from Yuán Shēn, Prince of Guǎngyáng.
Shēn led his troops to assist him.
Over two hundred thousand rebels surrendered and submitted in succession.
Shēn and Mobile Secretariat Yuán Zuǎn memorialized:
"We beg to establish separate commanderies and counties north of Héngzhōu,
to settle the surrendered households,
providing relief according to circumstances,
to pacify their rebellious hearts."
The Wei court did not comply.
An edict ordered Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat Yáng Yù to distribute them among Jì, Dìng, and Yíng Provinces for sustenance.
Shēn said to Zuǎn:
"These people will become 'beggars for life' again."
The matter of "beggars for life" is recorded in the first year of the Guāngxī era of Emperor Huì of Jìn, in the eighty-sixth volume.
According to the *Chronological Charts*, this year the Rúrú killed Pòliùhán Bálíng.
The *Comprehensive Mirror* records next year that Bálíng sent Fèi Lǜ to lure and behead Hú Chēn.
22 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the *rénxū* day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
23 In the eighth month,
Dù Luòzhōu, a resident of Wei's Róuxuán Garrison, gathered a crowd and rebelled at Shànggǔ,
changing the era name to Zhēnwáng.
He attacked and captured commanderies and counties.
Gāo Huān, Cài Jùn, Wèi Jǐng, Duàn Róng, and Āndìng Péng Lè all joined him.
Luòzhōu besieged Cuī Bǐng, Governor of Yānzhōu of Wei, from Bólíng.
In the ninth month,
on the *bǐngchén* day,
Wei appointed Cháng Jǐng, Governor of Yōuzhōu, concurrently as Minister and Mobile Secretariat,
to join Yōuzhōu Commander-in-Chief Yuán Tán in suppressing him.
Jǐng
was the grandson of Cháng Shuǎng.
Wei's Confucian ethos was promoted by Cháng Shuǎng.
They all stationed troops to guard strategic points.
Tán garrisoned Jūyōng Pass.
Lúlóng Pass was in Féirú County of Liáoxī.
The Táng changed Féirú to Lúlóng County.
Dù Yòu said: Lúlóng Fortress is two hundred *li* northwest of Lúlóng County town in Píngzhōu.
Jūndū Pass was in Jūndū County of Yān Commandery.
The *Táng Annals* state: North of Chāngpíng County in Yōuzhōu, fifteen *li* away, is Jūndū Defile;
thirty-five *li* northwest is Nàkuǎn Pass,
which is the old Jūyōng Pass,
also called Jūndū Pass.
Examining the *Hàn Annals*,
Shànggǔ Commandery had both Jūndū and Jūyōng counties,
each likely having its own pass.
All these garrisons and defenses
were to guard against Dù Luòzhōu.
The *Commentary on the Waterways Classic* states:
Jūyōng Pass is sixty *li* southeast of Jǔyáng city in Shànggǔ Commandery.
Jūndū Pass is south of Jūyōng Mountain.
24 In winter,
the tenth month,
Tǔyùhún sent troops to attack Zhào Tiān'ān.
Tiān'ān surrendered,
and Liángzhōu was restored to Wei.
The previous year,
Zhào Tiān'ān had used Liángzhōu to respond to Mòzhé Niànshēng.
Restored,
pronounced as fú yòu fān.
Surrendered,
pronounced as hù jiāng fān.
Píngxī General Gāo Huī, having been sent on a mission to Yàndá,
returned
to Fúhǎn.
It happened that Yuán Zuò, Governor of Hézhōu, died.
Liáng Zhāo's son, Jǐngjìn, led Mòzhé Niànshēng's troops to besiege the city.
Senior Administrator Yuán Yǒng and others recommended Huī to act as Governor,
mobilizing troops to defend firmly.
Jǐngjìn also acted as Governor himself.
Huī requested troops from Tǔyùhún.
Tǔyùhún came to his aid.
Tǔ,
pronounced as cóng tūn rù shēng.
Yù,
pronounced as yù.
Huī
was the grandson of Gāo Hú.
The history traces Gāo Huī and Gāo Huān's common ancestry.
25. The state of Wèi was occupied with affairs in the northwest,
while the Mán tribes of Èr Jīng and Xī Yǐng all rebelled,
cutting off the Sān Yā route.
Xī Jīng was administered from Shàngluò,
Běi Jīng from Xiāngchéng,
and Xī Yǐng from Zhēnyáng County in Rǔnán.
Dù Yòu said: Běi Jīngzhōu is now Yīyáng County.
The Sān Yā garrison was located nineteen lǐ southwest of Lǔyáng County in modern Rǔzhōu,
named Gāopíng Fortress.
The ancient Ràojiǎo Fortress was southeast of the county.
It is also said: Bǎilǐ Mountain is north of Xiàngchéng County in Dèngzhōu,
which is the first of the Sān Yā;
further north, beyond the Fēnlíng Mountain,
is the second of the Sān Yā;
the third enters the boundaries of Lǔshān County in Rǔzhōu.
Cut off,
pronunciation: Dīng Guǎn's gloss.
Their raids and plunder reached as far north as Xiāngchéng.
In the Rǔ River region, there were the Rǎn, Xiàng, and Tián clans,
whose tribes were the most powerful.
These three surnames likely all resided near the source of the Rǔ River.
Tribe,
pronunciation: Zhāng Yǒng's gloss.
The smaller ones had a thousand households,
each claiming the titles of kings and marquises,
occupying and holding strategic points,
blocking the roads.
In the twelfth month,
on the Rénwǔ day,
the Wèi sovereign issued an edict, saying:
"I shall personally lead the six armies,
to sweep away the fugitive filth.
Now, I shall first campaign against the Jīng Mán,
to bring order to the southern regions."
At that time, the Mán tribes had led Liáng general Cáo Yìzōng and others to besiege Wèi's Jīngzhōu.
This Jīngzhōu was administered from Rǎngchéng.
General,
pronunciation: Jí Liàng's gloss.
They reached Lǔyáng,
but dared not advance.
Wèi then appointed Línhuái Prince Yù as Grand General Who Conquers the South,
to lead troops against the Lǔyáng Mán.
The Chief Clerk of the Minister of Works, Xīn Xióng, was made Left Assistant Director of the Mobile Secretariat,
heading east towards Yèchéng.
Yèchéng was then the seat of Xiāngzhōu administration,
this being the Yè County town of the Hàn dynasty's Nányáng Commandery.
Head towards,
pronunciation: Qī Yù's gloss.
Yè,
pronunciation: Shì Shè's gloss.
He led ten thousand troops,
exiting through Wǔguān to open the Sān Yā route,
in order to rescue Jīngzhōu.
Before Péi Yǎn and others arrived,
Yù's army had already encamped on the upper Rǔ River.
Upper Rǔ,
refers to the upper reaches of the Rǔ River.
Yù, considering they were on a different route of operation,
was unwilling to respond to them.
Xīn Xióng said:
"Now Péi Yǎn has not yet arrived,
but Your Highness's troops are already assembled.
The Mán tribes are running rampant.
Since the Sòng dynasty,
the various Mán tribes in the Yù region have generally been called 'Mán Zuǒ',
and the established Mán commanderies are called 'Zuǒ Commandery'.
Your Highness holds authority outside the capital,
seeing an opportunity, you should advance.
Why debate about different routes!"
Yù, fearing he might later be held accountable for success or failure,
requested Xióng to issue an official order.
Order,
refers to an order from the Mobile Secretariat of the Department of State Affairs.
Issue,
pronunciation: Xiá Jià's gloss.
Their morale will surely be shaken,
and we can take advantage of the situation to defeat them."
He then issued an order to Yù's army,
commanding them to advance quickly and attack.
When the Mán tribes heard this,
they indeed scattered and fled.
The Wèi sovereign wished to personally campaign against the rebels,
but the Director of the Central Secretariat, Yuán Fān, remonstrated and stopped him.
Xīn Xióng submitted a memorial from the army, stating:
"The reasons why men, when facing battle, forget themselves
and do not fear touching white blades are:
first, to seek glory and fame;
second, to covet substantial rewards;
third, to fear punishment and penalty;
fourth, to avoid calamity and hardship.
Without these several factors,
even a sage king could not command his ministers,
nor a kind father urge on his sons.
An enlightened ruler deeply understands this sentiment,
therefore rewards must be carried out,
punishments must be trustworthy,
so that whether close or distant, noble or base, brave or timid, worthy or foolish,
upon hearing the sound of bells and drums,
seeing the array of banners and flags,
none fail to be stirred and excited,
vying to rush onto the battlefield.
How could they be content with long life and delight in swift death?
Content,
same as 'yàn'.
Delight,
pronunciation: luò.
It is that they cannot stop themselves.
Since the revolt in Qín and Lǒng,
and the Mán Zuǒ disrupting order,
several years have already passed.
The armies on the three
fronts,
have suffered more defeats than victories.
Tracing the cause,
it is due to unclear rewards and punishments.
The armies on the three fronts,
refer to the western campaign against Qín and Lǒng,
the northern defense of the border garrisons,
and the southern attack on the Mán Zuǒ.
Rewards should be given without delay.
Yet the merits of officers and soldiers
remain undecided for years.
'Lì rěn',

One harvest of the five grains occurs in a year,

They stay peacefully at home.
This causes principled men to have nothing encouraging them to aspire,
and ordinary men to have nothing to fear or dread.
Advancing to attack the enemy,
they face death in battle while rewards are distant;
distant,
means far off.
Keeping oneself whole incurs no penalty.
This is why they look at the enemy and flee in defeat,
unwilling to exert their full effort.
If Your Majesty can truly ensure that orders are trustworthy,
and rewards and punishments are carried out,
then the army's prestige will surely be displayed,
and bandits and rebels will surely be quelled."
The memorial was submitted,
but went unheeded.
Cáo Yìzōng and others captured Shùnyáng's Mǎjuàn,
and fought with Péi Yǎn and others at Xīyáng.
The Hàn dynasty's Hóngnóng Commandery had Xī County.
The Jìn dynasty placed it under Shùnyáng Commandery.
The Yuán Wèi established Xīyáng Commandery,
because its location was north of the Xī River.
This is the area of the Suí and Táng dynasties' Nánxiāng and Nèixiāng counties.
Yǎn and others recaptured Shùnyáng,
and advanced to besiege Mǎjuàn.
The Governor of Luòzhōu, Dǒng Shào, considering Mǎjuàn's walls strong
and Yǎn and others having little grain,
submitted a memorial stating they would certainly be defeated.
Not long after,
Yìzōng attacked Yǎn and others,
defeated them,
and recaptured Shùnyáng.
Wèi appointed Wáng Pí as Governor of Jīngzhōu.
26. Shàolíng Prince Lún was overseeing the affairs of Nán Xúzhōu.
In the province, his moods were unpredictable,
and he flagrantly violated the law.
He roamed the markets and streets,
and once asked a vendor of eels:
"What is the governor like?"
The vendor replied:
"Irritable and cruel."
Lún became enraged,
and ordered the man to swallow an eel and die.
is the same as 鱓,

pronounced zhǐ ruǐ fān.

Huìyì could not endure this,

28. Earlier,
the Chìlè chieftain Húlǜ Jīn served Yáng Jūn, the commander of Huáishuò Garrison, as a military officer.

estimating the number of cavalry and infantry by observing the dust,

When Pòliùhán Bálíng rebelled,

Gāozǔ Wǔ Emperor, Part Seven
Seventh year of Pǔtōng (Bǐngwǔ, 526)
1. In spring,
first month,
on the Xīnchǒu day, the new moon,
a general amnesty was declared.
2. On the Rénzǐ day,
Wèi appointed Rǔnán Prince Yuè as Grand Commandant.
3. Soldiers from the three garrisons of Shílí, Xuécheng, and Húyán in Wèi's Ānzhōu rebelled,
responding to Dù Luòzhōu.
Their combined forces numbered twenty thousand,
and Luòzhōu came from Sōngqiān to join them.
(The Shuǐjīngzhù states: The Dàyú River originates from the northern passes of the Yùyí Garrison,

The water flows west past the south of Kǒng Mountain,

The Dàyú River flows southeast,
and the Báiyáng Spring water flows into it.
The water originates from the Báiyáng Stream in the north, looking toward Líshí.
The Dàyú River flows southeast out of the gorge,
passing south of Huáyán County in the old Yúyáng Commandery of Ānzhōu,
commonly called Húyán City,
two hundred lǐ northwest of Yùyí Garrison.
岍,
pronounced qīng yān fān,

and should be read as

Zhòngzhé died in battle,
and Yuán Tán's army fled at night.
(Yuán Tán's army was at Jūyōng Pass,
see the previous year in the previous volume.)
Zhòngzhé
was the son of Bǐng.

4. Earlier,
Wèi's Guǎngyáng Prince Shēn had a close relationship with Chéngyáng Prince Huī's wife.

When the people of Héngzhōu requested Shēn as governor,

When Dù Luòzhōu rebelled,
surrendered households from Wǔyuán in Héngzhōu plotted to support Shēn as their leader.

submitted a memorial requesting to return to Luòyáng.
(At that time, Shēn's army was in Shuòzhōu.
恆,
pronounced hù dēng fān.
降,
pronounced hù jiāng fān.
上,
pronounced shí zhǎng fān.)
An edict appointed Shēn as Minister of Personnel.
Huī
was the son of Chángshòu.
(Chángshòu
was the son of Jǐngmù.)
The surrendered households of Wǔyuán, led by Xiānyú Xiūlǐ and others, rebelled with northern garrison refugees in Zuǒchéng of Dìngzhōu.

Zuǒchéng should be within the boundaries of Bólíng.

there is a Zuǒrén City in Táng County of Zhōngshān.)
read as shuài.)
They led their troops toward the provincial capital,

Yáng Jīn arrived at Língqiū,
(Língqiū County,
belonged to Dài Commandery in Hàn,

led troops to rescue,
and entered to occupy the provincial capital.
When Xiūlǐ arrived,
Jīn wanted to attack,
but his Chief Clerk Xǔ Bèi disagreed.
Jīn struck him with his sword,
and Bèi escaped unharmed.
Jīn opened the gates and went out to fight,
beheading several hundred,
and the rebels retreated,

An edict soon appointed Jīn as Governor of Dìngzhōu and Northern Circuit Commissioner.
Wèi appointed the Governor of Yángzhōu, Zhǎngsūn Zhì, as Grand Commander of Northern Expedition Forces,
to jointly suppress Xiūlǐ with Héjiān Prince Chēn.
5. In the second month,
on the Jiǎxū day,
the northern expedition armies stood down from alert.
6. The western Chìlè Húlǜ Luòyáng rebelled west of Sānggān,
and allied with the Fèiyětóu herdsmen.
In the third month,
on the Jiǎyín day,
Guerrilla General Ěrzhū Róng defeated Luòyáng at Shēnjǐng,
and the herdsmen west of the river.
(West of the northern river.)
7 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the Yǐyǒu day,
Línchuān Jìnghuì Wáng Hóng passed away.
8 The Northern Wei declared a general amnesty.
9 On the Guǐsì day,
the Northern Wei appointed Shìzhōng and Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn Chéngyáng Wáng Huī as Yítóngsānsī.
Huī, together with Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng Xú Hè, jointly slandered Shìzhōng Yuán Shùn before the Empress Dowager,
causing him to be sent out as Hùjūn Jiāngjūn and Tàicháng Qīng.
Shùn offered his farewell at the Xīyóu Garden,
with Hè attending at her side.
Shùn pointed at him and said to the Empress Dowager:
"This is the Zǎi Pǐ of Wei.
Zǎi Pǐ,
was the Tàizǎi Pǐ of Wú,
fond of slander.
King Fūchāi of Wú trusted and employed him,
leading to the state's downfall.
Pǐ,
pǐ bǐ fān.
This one will not die in the end!"
Hè hunched his shoulders and withdrew.
Zhū Yuánhuì said: "Xiéjiān"
means to straighten the body,
the posture of a petty man currying favor.
"You possess only the petty talent of a clerk,
fit only for handling documents at a desk.
How could you be worthy of defiling the Ménxià,
corrupting our moral principles!"
Thereupon, he shook his robes and rose.
The Empress Dowager remained silent.
10 The townspeople of Shuòzhōu in Wei, led by Xiānyú Āhú and others, seized the city and rebelled.
Ā,
cóng ān rù shēng.
11 Dù Luòzhōu moved southward,
plundering Jìchéng.
Cháng Jǐng of Wei sent Tǒngjūn Liáng Zhònglǐ to attack and defeat him.
On the Dīngwèi day,
Dūdù Lǐ Jū engaged Luòzhōu in battle north of Jìchéng,

Cháng Jǐng led troops to resist him,

tú hé fān.

13 In the fifth month,
on the Dīngwèi day,
the Wei Emperor issued an edict announcing a northern campaign,
imposing martial law both inside and outside,
but it was not carried out in the end.
14 Héngzhōu Cìshǐ Yuán Lüè,
since arriving south of the Yangtze,
wept morning and night,
constantly as if in mourning.
When Yuán Chā of Wei died,
Chā's death is recorded in the previous year's scroll.
Sāng,
xī láng fān.
he learned that Lüè had been spared thanks to Diāo Shuāng,

The nine
other forts all collapsed.

claiming that Ěrzhū Zhào was going to assign the people of the Six Garrisons to the Qìhú as private troops,
causing everyone to worry and fear.
He also forged an order from Bìng Province,
conscripting troops to attack the Bùluòjī,
and Ěrzhū Zhào accordingly ordered the mobilization in Bìng and Fén.
This was also a false order from Zhào forged by Gāo Huān.
(Bùluòjī
refers to the Jīhú.)
They were about to be dispatched.
Sūn Téng and Dūdū Wèi Jǐng requested a five-day delay for them,
and this was done twice.
(Since Sūn Téng and Wèi Jǐng had requested a delay for the garrison troops,
they must have further incited the troops below by capitalizing on their desire to stay.
This should be understood from the context.)
read as yú wèi fān.)
They bid farewell with tears,
and the crowd wailed in grief,
their cries shaking the plains and fields.
Huān then addressed them,
(first moving their hearts,
and then instructing them.)
read as hù dāo fān.)
"You and I are all exiles from our hometowns,
bound by righteousness as one family.
(Gāo Huān was also a garrison household,
hence he said this.)
Now, heading directly west,
we are already facing death;
(traveling from Xìndū to Bìng and Fén is heading west.)
facing death again,
being assigned to the 'guórén',
and facing death once more.
(Ěrzhū
were of the Qìhú ethnicity,
hence referring to the Qìhú as 'guórén'.)
The crowd said:
"There is only rebellion left!"
Huān said:
"Rebellion is an urgent plan,
but we must elect one person as leader.
Who is suitable?"
The crowd unanimously recommended Huān.
Huān said:
"Your fellow villagers are difficult to control.
Have you not seen Gě Róng? Although he had a million troops,
there were no laws or discipline,
and he ultimately brought about his own defeat and destruction.
Now, with me as your leader,
it must be different from before.
Do not oppress the Hàn people,
violate military orders,
and leave life and death to me—then it can be done.
Otherwise,
I cannot become a laughingstock for the world."
(Gāo Huān first established laws and discipline to unify his troops,
thus he was able to achieve great things.
History says even bandits have their principles.)
"We will follow your orders in life and death!"
Huān then slaughtered an ox to feast the soldiers.
On Gēngshēn,
he raised troops in Xìndū.
(Textual analysis: The Wèi Shū imperial annals record the uprising on Gēngshēn,
while the Běi Qí Shū imperial annals record it on Gēngzǐ,
and the Běi Shǐ, Wèi annals, and Qí annals also agree.
Here, we follow the Wèi Shū annals.)
At this time, Lǐ Yuánzhōng raised troops and pressured Yīn Province.
Huān ordered Gāo Qián to lead troops to rescue it.
(Gāo Qián was involved in Huān's secret plans,
yet he was sent to rescue Yīn Province.
This was merely to have him lure out and capture Ěrzhū Yǔshēng.)
Ěrzhū Yǔshēng
discussed military plans with him.
Yǔshēng went out together with Qián,
who then captured and beheaded him,
and brought Yǔshēng's head to pay respects to Huān.
Huān patted his chest and said:
"Today, the decision to rebel is final!"
(Gāo Huān's rebellious plot was not formed in a single day.
Only after Ěrzhū Yǔshēng was beheaded

This was likely because he initially still had doubts about Lǐ Yuánzhōng and Gāo Qiányōng.
Yuánzhōng had already raised troops to pressure Yīn Province,
and Qiányōng had beheaded Yǔshēng.
Huān then fully understood the intentions of these two men,
and the forces of Jì and Yīn had already united.
Thus, he decided to rebel.)
He garrisoned Guǎng'ē.
Huān then submitted a memorial denouncing the crimes of the Ěrzhū clan.
Ěrzhū Shìlóng concealed it and did not forward it.
(Shìlóng was the Shàngshū Lìng,
hence he was able to conceal Huān's memorial.)
20. Yáng Bō of Wei and his younger brothers Yáng Chūn and Yáng Jīn were all renowned for their virtue.
Bō was resolute and firm,
while Chūn and Jīn were humble and respectful.
Their family had a tradition of filial piety and fraternal love.
They wore mourning garments of the same grade and shared a common kitchen.
(For all three degrees of mourning, they wore sīmá garments.)
No one had any criticism of them.
Chūn and Jīn both reached the rank of Sāngōng,
and their family produced seven commandery governors
and thirty-two provincial governors.
(History records the prominence and prosperity of the Yáng clan.)
Bō's son, Yáng Kǎn, was involved in the plot;
(the event is recorded in the previous year's scroll.)
all were his relatives by marriage.
When Ěrzhū Zhào entered Luòyáng,
Kǎn fled back to Huàyīn.
Ěrzhū Tiānguāng sent Kǎn's father-in-law, Wéi Yìyuǎn, to recruit him,
making an oath with him
and promising to pardon his crime.
Kǎn said:
"Even if he breaks his promise,
the one who dies will be only me,
and I still hope to save the hundred members of my family."
He then went out to respond,
and Tiānguāng killed him.
At that time, Chūn had retired from office

Chūn's younger brother, Jì Province Governor Yáng Shùn; Sikōng Yáng Jīn; Shùn's son, Dōngyōng Province Governor Yáng Biàn; and Zhèngpíng Commandery Governor Yáng Zhòngxuān were all in Luòyáng.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Ěrzhū Shìlōng falsely accused the Yáng clan of plotting rebellion,
requesting their arrest and punishment.
The Wei emperor did not permit it.
Shìlōng insisted on his request,
and the emperor, having no alternative,
ordered the relevant officials to investigate and report.
On the night of Rénshēn,
Shìlōng sent troops to surround Jīn's residence.
Tiānguāng also sent troops to raid Chūn's home in Huàyīn.
Members of the eastern and western branches of the clan, young and old, were all killed.
(Shìlōng and Tiānguāng had already agreed to exterminate the Yáng clan together,
hence the eastern and western branches were attacked simultaneously.)
(Those residing in Huàyīn were the western branch,
and those in Luòyáng were the eastern branch.)

read as zhī liǎng fān.)
Shìlōng reported:
"The Yáng clan indeed rebelled,

The emperor sighed with regret for a long time,
saying nothing further.
When the court and the common people heard of it,
none were not pained and indignant.
Jīn's son, Yáng Yì, was the Governor of Guāng Province.
Ěrzhū Zhòngyuǎn sent an envoy to kill him.

He fled and hid,
thus escaping death.
He went to Xìndū to see Gāo Huān,

He then proposed a strategy to attack the Ěrzhū clan.
Huān held him in high regard

(Yáng Yīn's family background was eminent,
and he also had practical ability.

This is why he promoted and employed him.)
Whether scholars were worthy or not,
upon entering the court, they faced jealousy.

21. On Yǐhài,
the Emperor held court to confer the title of Crown Prince upon the heir,
and issued a general pardon.
22. On Bǐngxū,
Ěrzhū Yànbó of Wei resigned from his position as Sītú due to drought.
On Wùzǐ,
Yànbó was appointed as Shìzhōng and Kāifǔ Yìtóng Sānsī.
(Yànbó was relatively less guilty among his brothers.)
Ěrzhū Shìlōng firmly declined the position of Tàibǎo.

ranking below the Shànggōng.

On Gēngyín,
Shìlōng was appointed to this position.
Húsī Chūn slandered Zhū Ruì to Shìlōng,

On the 23rd day (Gēngyín),
an edict was issued:
"All imperial relatives within mourning degrees,
that is,
those within the fifth degree of mourning (sīmá) or closer,
shall be enfeoffed as village or township marquises;
women shall be granted bath manors,
while men shall receive the titles of village marquis or township marquis.
The ranks shall be differentiated according to the closeness of the mourning relationship."
On the 24th day (Rénchén),
Hé Jìngróng, the Minister of Personnel, was appointed as the Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs.
Hé Jìngróng
was the son of Hé Chāngyǔ.
Hé Chāngyǔ
was the younger cousin of Hé Shàngzhī.
25. When Èrzhū Zhòngyuǎn and Èrzhū Dùlǜ of Wei heard that Gāo Huān had raised an army,
they relied on their strength
and did not consider it a concern.

Èrzhū Zhào led 20,000 infantry and cavalry out of Jǐngxíng,
heading toward Yīnzhōu.
Lǐ Yuánzhōng abandoned the city and fled to Xìndū.
In the eighth month,
on the Bǐngwǔ day,
Èrzhū Zhòngyuǎn and Èrzhū Dùlǜ led troops to attack Gāo Huān.
In the ninth month,
on the Jǐmǎo day,
Wei appointed Zhòngyuǎn as Grand Tutor.
On the Gēngchén day,
Èrzhū Tiānguāng was appointed as Grand Marshal.
26. On the Guǐsì day,
the Wei emperor posthumously honored his father, Prince Huì of Guǎnglíng, as the Late Emperor.
When a collateral son succeeds to the main line,
honoring his biological father as "imperial"

honoring him as "emperor"
began with Sūn Hào of Wú.
He enfeoffed his younger brother Yǒngyè as Prince of Gāomì,

27. In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Jǐyǒu day,
the Emperor visited Tóngtài Temple,
ascended the Dharma seat,

28. Marquis Lèshān Zhèngzé,
who had previously been exiled to Yùlín for a crime,

was an ancient Hàn commandery,

intended to attack Pānyú,

should be

History records that all sons of Prince Línchuān Hóng were violent and rebellious.
29. Sūn Téng advised Gāo Huān:
"Now the court is isolated,

Lǎng
was the son of Róng.

On the Rényín day,
Lǎng ascended the throne west of Xìndū City,

The deposed emperor, named Lǎng,
style Zhòngzhé,
was the third son of Prince Zhāngwǔ Róng.
Gāo Qián was appointed as Palace Attendant and Minister of Works;
Gāo Áocáo was appointed as General of Agile Cavalry, Pillar of State, and Governor of Jìzhōu.

a position he held for life.)
(Piào
is pronounced piào.
Qí

Wèi Lángēn was appointed as Vice Director of the Right.

On the Jǐyǒu day,

Èrzhū Zhòngyuǎn and Èrzhū Dùlǜ, along with General of Agile Cavalry Húsī Chūn, General of Chariots and Cavalry and Pillar of State Hèbá Shèng, and General of Chariots and Cavalry Jiǎ Xiǎnzhì, encamped at Yángpíng.

the area of Yángpíng.)
(He went by his style name;
he was the younger brother of Xiǎndù.)
Èrzhū Zhào emerged from Jǐngxíng
and encamped at Guǎng'ē,
with a force reportedly numbering 100,000.
Gāo Huān spread disinformation,
saying
"Shìlóng and his brothers plotted to kill Zhào,"
and also saying
"Zhào conspired with Huān to kill Zhòngyuǎn and others,"
causing them to suspect each other,
and they hesitated to advance.
Zhòngyuǎn and others repeatedly sent Húsī Chūn and Hèbá Shèng to persuade Zhào.
Zhào led 300 light cavalry to meet Zhòngyuǎn,
sat together under a tent,
with an uneasy expression,
waving his horsewhip,
gazing into the distance with a long sigh.
(Zhèng Xuán said: A sigh
is made by pursing the lips to produce sound.)
He then hurried out
and galloped back.
Zhòngyuǎn sent Chūn and Shèng to pursue him,
to persuade him at dawn.
Zhào seized Chūn and Shèng and took them back to camp.
Zhòngyuǎn and Dùlǜ were greatly frightened
and led their troops south in retreat.
Zhào enumerated Shèng's crimes,
intending to execute him,
saying:
"You killed Wèi Kěgū,
that is the first crime.
(The event is recorded in the 150th scroll, fifth year of Pǔtōng.)
You did not come with Shìlóng and others,
but went east to attack Zhòngyuǎn,
that is the second crime.
(The event is recorded in the previous scroll, last year.)
What more do you have to say now?"
Shèng replied:
"Kěgū was a great threat to the state;
Shèng and his father killed him,
which was no small achievement.
How can that be considered a crime?
When the Pillar of State was executed,
it was a case of the ruler punishing a subject.
Shèng would rather betray the Prince
than betray the court.
In today's matter,
life or death lies with the Prince.
But with enemies close by,
and kin creating rifts,
from ancient times to the present,
there has never been a case like this that did not end in ruin.
Shèng does not fear death,
but fears the Prince's misjudgment."
Zhào then spared him.
Gāo Huān planned to battle Zhào,
but feared his enemy's superior numbers.
He inquired of his trusted General Duān Sháo,
a trusted commander.
At the end of the Wèi, all generals began to wield military power.
Thus, this position was established
to lead loyal troops.
The so-called strength of numbers,
lies in gaining the people's willingness to fight to the death;
it refers to the strength of the people's willingness to sacrifice.
Winning the hearts of the world.
Ěrzhū Shì overthrew the emperor,
slaughtered ministers and lords,
oppressed the common people.
The king, fighting against rebellion for justice,
like boiling water melting snow,
what strength of numbers is there to fear?"
Huān said:
"Even so, by using a small force against a large one,
I fear that without heavenly mandate, it cannot be accomplished."
Sháo replied:
"Sháo has heard that 'the small can overcome the large,
as integrity triumphs over corruption.'
'Heaven shows no favoritism,
only assisting the virtuous.'
'The small can overcome the large,
as integrity triumphs over corruption.'"
This is a quote from the Zuǒ Zhuàn, concerning the words of Sui Minister Jì Liáng.
'Heaven shows no favoritism,
only assisting the virtuous.'
This is a phrase from the Book of Shàng, concerning the command of Cài Zhòng.
Duān Sháo and his father rose to prominence on the northern frontier,
excelling in mounted archery,
and could not write formal speeches.
Wèi Shōu wrote for them due to their honored standing in Northern Qí,
and their clan's strength and prosperity,
hence he composed these words for them.
Mèngzǐ said:
"To fully believe in a book,
is not as good as having no books at all."
Indeed!
Internally, losing the hearts of heroes,
the wise do not scheme,
the brave do not fight,
the people's will is gone,
how can Heaven not follow them?"
Sháo,
was the son of Róng.
Duān Róng was on friendly terms with Gāo Huān.
In the year Xīnhài,
Huān decisively defeated Zhào at Guǎng'ā,
capturing over five thousand armored soldiers.
On the 30th of November,
Yǐwèi day,
the emperor visited Tóng Tài Temple,
expounding the Prajñā Sūtra,
ceasing after seven days.
On the 31st of Gēngchén,
Wèi Gāo Huān led troops to attack Yè,
where Liú Dàn, Prefect of Xiāng Province, guarded the city resolutely.
That year,
the citizens of the city of Nán Yǎn of Wèi's Southern Prefecture under Wáng Qǐdé seized Prefect Liú Shìmíng,
and surrendered the entire province.
During Zhèngguāng in Wèi, Nán Yǎn Prefecture was established,
governing Qiáo City,
comprising Chénliú, Liáng, Qiáo, Pèi, Xiàcài, Běiliáng, and Mǎtóu counties.
Surrender,
dynamism reversed.
He belonged to the same clan as Fāng.
Liú Fāng employed Confucian studies under Xiàowén and Xuānwǔ Emperors,
guarding Qiáo City.
Shìmíng was made Great General Conqueror of the West and Prefect of Yǐng Province,
concurrently with the title of Same Rank as the Three Dukes.
Shìmíng declined,
repeatedly requesting to return north,
which the emperor granted.
When Shìmíng reached Luòyáng,
he presented his seals,
returned to his hometown,
and died without further service.
"To exert effort and assume one's position,
those unable should desist,"
this is true of Liú Shìmíng.
The Liú family resided in Péngchéng for generations.
In spring,
the first month,
Bǐngyín day,
Sounan Píng Wáng Wěi was made Grand Marshal,
Yuán Fǎsēng was made Grand Commandant,
Yuán Áng was made Minister of Works.
In the second month,
Xī Fēng Hóu Zhèngdé was made Línhè Wáng.
Zhèngdé had personal ties with Zhū [AS-82FA],
having already conferred titles upon Zhāomíng's sons,
[AS-82FA] critiqued Zhèngdé's demotion,
noting the emperor raised Zhèngdé as a son,
yet reverted his status,
preventing him from ranking equally with other sons.
[AS-82FA],
pronounced yáng zhì with a reversal tone.
In the third month,
Táizǐ Yòuwèi Shuaì Xuéfǎ Hù was made the governor of Sīzhōu,
escorting Wèi Wáng Yuè into Luòyáng.
On the Gēngwǔ day,
Táizǐ Gāng's eldest son Dàqì was made Xuānchéng Wáng.
Wèi Gāo Huān attacked Yè,
creating tunnels beneath,
setting pillars and burning them,
causing the city to collapse into the ground.
As the tunnels were yet uncompleted,
fearing the earth might collapse and ruin the effort,
pillars were placed.
Once the tunnels were completed,
the pillars were burned,
causing the city to fall into the ground.
Rénwǔ,
Yè was taken,
Liú Dàn was captured,
and Yáng Yīn was appointed acting right chancellor.
During this time, the state was engaged with numerous affairs,
official documents and decrees,
were all issued by Yīn and advisor to the establishment, Cù Wěng.
Wěng,
fifth-generation descendant of Chěng.
In the second month,
Táiwèi Yuán Fǎsēng was made Eastern Wèi Wáng,
also appointing Yuán Yuè as Wèi Wáng,
entered through the western passage;
Yuán Fǎsēng was sent through the eastern passage,
hence named Eastern Wèi Wáng.
Yǎnzhōu Prefect Yáng Kǎn as Army Major,
traveled with Fǎsēng.
Yángzhōu Prefect Shàolíng Wáng Lún sent people to the market to borrow and buy hundreds of brocades and silks,
all the merchants closed their shops in refusal;
Chief Secretary Hé Zhìtōng reported the matter.
Lún was reprimanded and returned to his brother,
then sent watchdog Dài Zīgāo and others with lances to assassinate Zhìtōng in the capital street,
known before as the capital lane.
Lance,
color horn reversed.
Assassinate,
seven also reversed.
Zhìtōng identified Zīgāo,
used blood to mark the carriage wall with the words
"Shàolíng,"
then died,
revealing the affair.
On the Gēngxū day,
Lún was dismissed and made a commoner,
imprisoned in his brother's home,
kept for twenty days,
before being released,
soon resuming his title and rank.
On the Xīnhài day,
Wèi Āndìng Wáng was conferred the posthumous title of Jìngzōng as Wǔhuái Huángdì,
having abdicated to Lǎng,
Xiàowǔ Dì conferred him as Āndìng Wáng.
On the Jiǎzǐ day
Gāo Huān was appointed Prime Minister, Pillar of the State, and Grand Tutor;
in the third month,
Bǐngyín day,
Gāo Chéng was made Great General of the Cavalry.
Dīngchǒu day,
Āndìng Wáng led all officials to reside in Yè.
Ěrzhū Zhào and Ěrzhū Shìlóng had mutual mistrust,
Shìlóng, using humble words and respectful rites, persuaded Zhào,
wishing him to go to Luò,
fulfilling his desires,
also requesting the emperor accept Zhào's daughter as empress;
Zhào thus was pleased,
and together with Tiānguāng and Dùlǜ pledged solemn oaths,
reconciling their bonds.
Húsī Chūn secretly said to Hèbá Shèng,
"The whole world resents the Ěrzhū clan,
yet we serve them.
Our downfall is near;
better to plan against them."
Shèng replied,
"Tian Guang and Zhào each hold a region;
it is difficult to eliminate them completely.
If we do not remove them entirely,
they will become future troubles.
What can be done?"
Chūn said,
"This is easy to achieve."
He then persuaded Shìlóng to summon Tian Guang to Luòyáng
to jointly attack Gāo Huān.
Shìlóng repeatedly summoned Tian Guang,
but Tian Guang did not come.
Therefore, Chūn personally went to invite him, saying,
"Gāo Huān is causing chaos,
and only the king can settle it.
How can we sit by and watch the extermination of our family?"
Tian Guang had no choice
but to set out eastward.
He sought advice from the Inspector of Yōng Prefecture, Hèbá Yuè,
who had recently been transferred from Qí Prefecture to Yōng Prefecture.
Yōng
is pronounced like the word "use."
Yuè said,
"The royal family occupies three sides;
Zhào holds the north with Bing and Fén;
Tian Guang holds the west with the passes and Long;
Zhòngyuǎn holds Xú and Yǎn,
thus occupying three sides.
Gāo Huān's forces are a motley crowd;
how can they be an enemy?
If we unite our hearts and efforts,
we will surely triumph.
If we doubt each other like family,
there will not be enough time to ensure our existence,
so how can we control others?
As I see it,
it is best to first stabilize our base at Guānzhōng,
and send sharp troops to join the main army,
advancing to defeat the enemy,
retreating to ensure safety."
Tian Guang did not agree.
In the intercalary month,
on the day Rén Yín,
Tian Guang set out from Cháng'ān,
Zhào from Jìnyáng,
Dù Lǜ from Luòyáng,
and Zhòngyuǎn from Dōngjùn, and they all assembled at Yè,
declaring a force of 200,000,
camping along the Huán River.
According to the Water Classic Notes, the Huán River flows south of Yè city.
Huán,
is pronounced like Yuán.
The total command was arranged.
Gāo Huān ordered the Minister of Personnel, Fēng Lóngzhī, to guard Yè.
On the day Guǐchǒu,
he camped at Zǐmò.
According to the Water Classic Notes, the Zhāng River flows east from the mountains past Yè,
then north past the west of Jìmò.
In the Warring States period,
local shamans married women to the River Earl,
sacrificing at this mò.
Tián Róng called it Zǐmò.
In the eleventh year of Zhào Jiànwǔ,
the Zǐmò bridge was built on the water.
Huān said, "All that the High Governor leads are Han soldiers;
I fear they cannot complete the task.
I wish to mix in over a thousand Xianbei soldiers for use,
what say you?"
Áo Cáo replied,
"The troops under my command,
have been trained for a long time.
In previous battles,
they are no less than the Xianbei.
If mixed now,
their affections will not align.
If we win, they will fight for credit;
if we retreat, they will shift blame.
There is no need to reassign them."
On the day Gēngshēn,
Ěrzhū Zhào led 3,000 light cavalry in a night raid on Yè city,
attacking the west gate,
but retreated without success.
On the day Rénxū,
Huān's cavalry numbered less than 2,000,
and infantry less than 30,000.
Being outnumbered,

The Wèi sovereign took the daughter of Chancellor Gāo Huān as his empress,
and ordered the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices Lǐ Yuánzhōng to deliver the betrothal gifts to Jìnyáng.
Huān feasted with him,
and when discussing past events,
Yuánzhōng said:
"In the past, when we raised the righteous banner,
it was exhilarating and greatly joyful.
Lately, it has been silent with no one asking about it."
Huān clapped his hands and laughed, saying:
"This man forced me to raise troops."
Yuánzhōng said jokingly:
"If you do not give me the post of Palace Attendant,
I should seek another place to raise the righteous banner."
Huān said:
"Raising the righteous banner is not something to worry about lacking,
I only fear that such an old man as you cannot be encountered."
Yuánzhōng said:
"It is precisely because this old man is hard to encounter,
that I do not leave."
Thereupon, he stroked Huān's beard and laughed heartily.
Huān fully understood his sincere intent,
and deeply esteemed him.
(悉 means to be thoroughly familiar with, to investigate thoroughly,
to know.
雅 means inherent,
usual.)
After Ěrzhū Zhào reached Xiùróng,
he divided his forces to guard the strategic passes and narrows,
and went out to raid and plunder.
The Wèi Chancellor Gāo Huān loudly proclaimed he would attack him,
but his army set out and then halted four times,
and Zhào's vigilance slackened.
Huān surmised that at the beginning of the year he would be holding a banquet,
and sent the Commander Dòu Tài with elite cavalry to speed towards him,
covering 300 lǐ in one day and one night,
while Huān followed with the main army.
(This sets the stage for Dòu Tài's defeat of Ěrzhū Zhào the following year.)
(騎 is pronounced qí, with the meaning of cavalry.)

and also warned them to submit to him.
Chancellor Huān wrote to the nobles in Yè:
"Cuī Xiān is in charge of the Censorate;
the Prince of Xiányáng and Minister Sīmǎ are both my old friends from humble times,
honored, esteemed, close, and intimate—
none surpass these two,
yet they both committed offenses,
and I could not save them;
you all should be careful!"
Sòng Yóudào submitted memorials refuting several hundred instances of errors and violations by the Imperial Secretariat,
and had the powerful clerks in the department, such as Wáng Rú, whipped and reprimanded,
so that everyone from the President and Vice President down looked askance at him.
Gāo Lóngzhī falsely accused Yóudào of uttering disloyal words,
a crime punishable by death.
the Gentleman Cavalier Attendant Huángmén Shìláng Yáng Yīn said:
"We keep dogs to have them bark;
now if we kill them for barking too much,
I fear in the future there will be no more barking dogs."
Yóudào was ultimately removed from the register.
Chéng said to Yóudà:
"If you had followed me to Bìngzhōu earlier,
otherwise,
they would have schemed to kill you."
Yóudào followed Chéng to Jìnyáng,
and was appointed as the Director of the Bureau of Personnel in the Executive Bureau.
After "Bureau"
there should be
"Gentleman"
character.
15 On the Jǐchǒu day,
a general amnesty was declared.
16 Because after the turmoil of war, Eastern Wei
had inaccurate household registration,
leading to uneven corvée and taxes,
in winter,
the tenth month,
on the Dīngsì day,
the Grand Guardian Sūn Téng and the Grand Minister Over the Masses Gāo Lóngzhī
In the Wei and Qi official systems,
the Minister Over the Masses never had
"Grand"
added; the character "Grand"
is redundant.
were sent to tour the various provinces,

and those living away from their native places were all ordered to return to their original registration.
In the eleventh month,
on the Jiǎshēn day,
Gāo Lóngzhī was appointed to oversee the Imperial Secretariat,
and the former Grand Marshal Lóu Zhāo was made Minister Over the Masses.
17 On the Gēngzǐ day,
the ruler of Eastern Wei performed the suburban sacrifice at the Circular Mound.
18 The Chancellor of Eastern Wei, Gāo Huān, launched a surprise attack on the Shānhú,
defeating them.
The Shānhú
were the Jīhú in the mountains of Fénzhōu.
They were distributed among the various provinces.
19 This year,
Eastern Wei appointed the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Wèi Shōu to concurrently serve as Vice Director of the Central Secretariat,
to compile the national history.
Since Liang and Wei established friendly relations,
Wei's letters often said:
"We hope that within your borders there is tranquility,
and here under our rule there is peace and harmony."
The Emperor, in his reply,
simply removed
the word "your"
and that was all.
Shōu began to fix the wording of the letters to say:
"We hope that within the borders there is clear peace,

The Emperor also imitated this.

8 The Emperor dispatched Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ Yáng Piǎo to suppress Lǐ Bēn,
appointing Chén Bàxiān as Sīmǎ;
he ordered Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ Xiāo Bó to rendezvous with Piǎo at Xījiāng.
(Wǔdài Zhì: Yùlín Commandery,
Liáng established Dìngzhōu there.)
Bó deceitfully persuaded Piǎo to stay.
Piǎo assembled his generals to seek counsel,
and Bàxiān said:
"Jiāozhǐ's rebellion and defiance,
the fault lies with the imperial clan,
(meaning Lǐ Bēn's rebellion
was due to Wǔlín Hóu Zī.
The matter is recorded in the seventh year of the previous scroll.)
For years they have evaded punishment.
Dìngzhōu (Xiāo Bó) seeks only temporary ease,
disregarding the grand strategy;
Your Excellency, bearing the imperial mandate to punish the guilty,
should be prepared to risk life and death for it.
How can you hesitate and not advance,
thereby emboldening the enemy and disheartening our troops!"
He then led his troops to set out first.
Piǎo appointed Bàxiān as the vanguard.
Upon reaching Jiāozhōu,
(Cāoyì notes: Diǎn Lüè records
"arrived at Jiāozhōu on the guǐchǒu day of the twelfth month,"

they were defeated at Zhūyuān.

is pronounced yuán.)
Bēn fled to Jiāníng City.

Xīnxīng Commandery was established by dividing Jiāozhǐ,
and Jiāníng County was also established;
in the third year of Tàikāng under Jìn Wǔdì,

formerly established Xīngzhōu and Xīnchāng Commandery;

Bó
was the son of Bǐng.
(Wú Pínghóu Bǐng
was the Emperor's paternal cousin.
Bǐng
is pronounced bǐng.)
9 Wèi plotted with Róurán's Tóubīng Kèhán to join forces and attack Dōng Wèi.

Huān hesitated, unable to decide.
Lóu said:

Huān then sent Zhènnán Jiāngjūn Mùróng Yǎn to betroth her,

titled Rúrú Princess,

is pronounced ruǎn.)
In the eighth month,

should be north of Mùjǐng.

with Shàngguǎn and Xiàguǎn.)
Lóu vacated the main chamber for her;
Huān knelt and bowed in thanks.

was Huān's wife from his humble days,
the principal wife.
Chǔ
is pronounced chǔ.)
"She will notice,

and also to reciprocate the betrothal mission;
some versions say
"to betroth."

"I will wait to see my grandson before returning."
The princess had a stern and resolute nature,

Once, when Huān was ill

14 Wèi constructed a circular mound altar south of the city.
(South of Cháng'ān city.)
The Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Hè Chēn submitted a memorial presenting four matters: The first,
was that
"Now that the northern border has submitted and is pacified,
it is precisely the time to build up the population and provide training,
using Wǔ Zǐxū's
saying, 'The Yuè spent ten years building up their population,
and ten years in training.'
The situation beyond the passes is even more severe.
This refers to the newly recovered prefectures and commanderies in the Huái, Rǔ, Tóng, and Sì river regions, which lie outside the frontier passes.
The counties cannot bear the exactions and reductions imposed by the commanderies,
and they harass each other in turn,
focusing only on levying taxes,
levy,
lì shàn fān.
Each strives to flee and scatter,
is this not the fault of the governors and administrators!
The population in the eastern regions is depleted and empty,
the eastern regions,
refer to the lands of Sān Wú.
Even the remotest and most secluded places,
are all reached without exception,
whenever an envoy arrives,
the areas under his jurisdiction are harassed;
if the local officials are incompetent and weak,
they simply fold their hands and allow him to plunder at will,
while cunning and crafty senior clerks,
take advantage of this to further their greed and cruelty,
even if there are honest and fair ones,
the commandery still holds them back.
Under such circumstances,
even if edicts are issued yearly urging a return to one's occupation,
and favors of tax exemptions are repeatedly granted,
the people still cannot return to their homes."
The second,
was that
"The reason why
greed and cruelty prevail in the world today,
is truly due to the extravagant and wasteful customs that have brought this about.
Nowadays, at feasts and celebrations,
The Shī, Lǔ Sòng says: The Marquis of Lǔ feasts and rejoices.
Zhèng's commentary states: Yàn,
means to drink.
fruits are piled up like hills and mounds,
dishes are arrayed like brocade and embroidery,
the cost of the Lù Tái,
would not suffice for a single feast's expenses,
the cost of the Lù Tái,
refers to one hundred catties of gold.
The matter of the Lù Tái is seen in scroll fifteen, the seventh year of Emperor Wén of Hàn's later reign.
One takes only enough to fill the belly,
but before leaving the hall,
it has already become like foul rot.
Moreover,
those who keep singing girls,
have no distinctions of rank,
those who serve as officials and shepherd the people,
amass assets amounting to hundreds of millions,
hundreds of millions means,
a hundred million times a hundred million.
Yet within a few years,
they are all exhausted on feasting and drinking, and the tools for song and entertainment.
The expenses incurred are equal to hills and mountains,
but the joy lasts only a moment,
and then they regret not having taken more before;
as if they were given wings again,
increasing their ability to seize and devour,
how perverse is this!
As for other forms of wanton extravagance,
they manifest in a hundred ways,
meaning that everything people do nowadays,
involves wanton extravagance.
They grow more severe day by day,
if one wishes to make people uphold integrity and purity,
how can it be achieved!
It is truly appropriate to strictly impose prohibitions and regulations,
guide them with frugality,
impeach and report on superficial extravagance,
and change what they see and hear.
As for the sigh over lack of restraint,
it is also something the people themselves worry about,
they are ashamed precisely because they cannot keep up with the extravagant,
so they force themselves to do it;
The Yì says: If there is no restraint,
then there will be sighing,
but no blame.
The Xiàng says: The sigh over lack of restraint,
who is to blame for it!
Chēn quotes this to express his own meaning,
this argument truly hits the mark of human sentiment.
Force,
qí liǎng fān.
It is sufficient to correct the flaws of decadence and dissipation."
The third,
was that
"Your Majesty worries about and cares for all within the Four Seas,
not shunning toil and labor,
down to the various offices,
none fails to present memorials on affairs.
But petty-minded individuals,
once they gain the opportunity to present memorials before the curtained throne,
then wish to scheme and compete for advancement,
not considering the greater principles of the state,
nor holding in mind clarity and forbearance;
they only focus on nitpicking and fault-finding,
splitting hairs and dissecting minutiae,
blowing on hair to seek out blemishes and flaws,
splitting muscles to separate the grain of the flesh;
meaning they are苛刻 and meticulous.
They make it their task to pursue and expel.
Pursuing and expelling means,
investigating and impeaching others for their faults and then expelling them.
Matters thus enhance their authority and power,
those who commit offenses are many,
clever evasion becomes more rampant,
long-standing abuses increase and villainy grows,
truly this arises from such practices.
I sincerely hope to hold them accountable for achieving fairness,
and dismiss their slanderous and malicious hearts,
then those below will be at peace and those above tranquil,
without the troubles of those seeking undue advantage."
The fourth,
was that
"Now the world is at peace,
yet there is still not enough time in the day,
it is appropriate to reduce affairs and curtail expenses,
when affairs are reduced the people are nurtured,
when expenses are curtailed wealth is accumulated.

Each should internally examine their duties and responsibilities and inspect their respective departments: all offices, bureaus, residences, markets in the capital, as well as state ceremonies and military preparations,
offices,
are places for handling affairs.
Bureaus,
are places for lodging and stopping.
Residences,
are the mansions of various princes and nobles and the quarters for officials from various commanderies when attending court.
Markets,
are market rows.
State ceremonies,
refer to rites and music, carriages and robes, banners and insignia.
Military preparations,
are the weapons and equipment for using troops.
Military colonies,
are military agricultural colonies.
Relay stations,
are postal relay stations.
Relay,
zhāng liàn fān.
Abolish them,
where there should be reductions,
reduce them;
construction projects that are not urgent,
demands and requisitions that can be delayed,
all should be stopped and reduced,
to curtail expenses and give rest to the people.
Therefore, accumulating wealth,
is for using it greatly later;
nurturing the people,
is for employing them greatly later.
If it is said that small matters are not enough to harm wealth,
then they will never cease throughout the year;
if small labors are said not enough to trouble the people,
then they will never stop throughout the year.
This is also a sound argument.
Then it would be difficult to speak of achieving wealth and strength and planning for far-reaching greatness."
The memorial was presented,
and the Emperor was greatly enraged.
He summoned the Chief Secretary before him,
and orally dictated an edict to reprimand Chén.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn said: Since the Jiànwǔ era of the Qí dynasty,
imperial decrees and orders no longer passed through the Secretariat,
but were issued exclusively from the Bureau of Palace Attendants.
The four bureaus
were called the Four Gates.
Below them were Chief Secretaries and Clerks,
who were traditionally military officers,
but later changed to civilian officials.
Their numbers were not fixed,
and all were close and trusted confidants.
"I have ruled the empire for over forty years.
Honest remonstrations from the public carriage,
I listen to and review daily.
The matters presented
are no different from what you have said,
yet I am often troubled by haste,
and it only adds to my confusion.
You should not liken yourself to the mediocre,
merely seeking fame,
and proclaiming on the roads,
saying, 'I can present matters to the court,
but regret that the court does not employ them.'
Why not clearly specify: which Regional Inspector is tyrannical,
which Grand Administrator is corrupt and cruel,
which Minister or Lántái official is treacherous and cunning,
which envoy is plundering,
and what are their names?
Who are the givers and takers?
State the matters clearly,
so that they can be punished or dismissed,
and better talents can be selected.
Moreover,
if the food and drink of the officials and people are excessive,
and strict prohibitions are imposed,
how can one know
what happens in secret rooms and hidden chambers?
If every household is searched,
I fear it will only increase harsh disturbances.
If you refer to the court,
I have not done such things.
In the past, sacrificial animals
were not slaughtered for a long time.
The Zhōu Lǐ states: The king's meals use six sacrificial animals,
namely horses, cattle, sheep, pigs, dogs, and chickens.
It also says: The king offers one sacrifice daily,
with twelve tripods.
The commentary says: Slaughtering animals and preparing lavish feasts is called a sacrifice;
twelve tripods,
nine for the main sacrifice and three for supplementary offerings.
The Emperor served the Buddha,
and thus did not slaughter animals.
Only vegetables were used;
if even this is reduced,
there will surely be criticism like that in 'The Cricket.'
The poem 'The Cricket' from Táng
satirizes Duke Xī of Jìn for being frugal to the point of violating ritual.
Cháo,
pronounced as yáo.
Fù,
pronounced as fú yòu.
The Emperor considered serving the Buddha and monks,
and holding unrestricted and unobstructed assemblies as meritorious deeds.
Transforming one melon into dozens of varieties,
preparing one vegetable into dozens of flavors;
because of such transformations,
how does it harm matters!
Unless it is an official banquet,
I do not eat food provided by the state,
and this has been the case for many years;
even the palace ladies
do not eat food provided by the state.
The Emperor possesses the southeast,
and all the food he consumes,
from himself to the six palaces,
does not come from Buddhist provisions,
nor is it created by deities,
nor does it come from the Western land of India.
Is there any that does not come from the labor of the people of the southeast?
Just because it does not come from public taxes,
he considers it as not eating state-provided food.
If this is truly the case,
then whose state is it indeed!
It has nothing to do with the Craftsmen Office or the State Artisans,
this is merely glossing over the faults of constructing pagodas and temples.
The Craftsmen General
belongs to the Chamberlain for the Palace Revenues.
State Artisans
are those whose salaries and provisions are provided by the state for state use.
The Grand Artisan Minister
oversees construction and engineering.
The brave and timid are different,
the greedy and honest are each employed,
and it is not the court that gives them wings.
You say the court is perverse,
yet you willingly accept it.
You should think about why it has become perverse!
You say, 'It should be guided with frugality.'
I have abstained from the bedchamber for over thirty years.
As for my dwelling, it is no more than the space of a single bed.
Carved and decorated objects do not enter the palace.
Since birth, I do not drink alcohol,
nor do I enjoy music.
Therefore, in court banquets,
music has never been played.
This is what all the worthy officials have witnessed.
I rise at the third watch to handle affairs,
depending on how many matters there are.
If there are few matters, they are finished before noon.
If there are many, I eat only when the sun begins to set.
I usually eat one meal a day,
whether it is day or night.
In the past, my waist was over ten spans around,
but now I am emaciated, barely over two feet.
My old belt still exists,
and this is no false claim.
For whom did I do this?
For the sake of saving the people.
You also say, 'All officials present memorials,
deceitfully competing for advancement.'
If outsiders are not allowed to present matters now,
who will take responsibility for them?
Shī,
means to preside.
How can this be achieved?
The ancients said: 'Exclusive listening breeds treachery,
sole authority leads to chaos.'
These are the words of Zōu Yáng of Hàn.
The Empress Dowager Yuán's entrustment to Wáng Mǎng,
Zhào Gāo's affairs are recorded in the Annals of Qín,
Wáng Mǎng's affairs are recorded in the Annals of Hàn.
Are these to be emulated?
You speak of 'blowing apart hairs to find faults,'
but who is doing this?
'Splitting muscles to analyze principles,'
but what matters are these?
Offices, bureaus, lodges, markets, and so on,
which should be abolished?
Which should be reduced?
Which construction projects are not urgent?
Which demands can be delayed?
Present each matter separately,
and report them in detail!
Methods to enrich the state and strengthen the military,
and measures to give the people rest and reduce corvée labor,
should all be listed in detail!
If they are not listed in detail,
then it is deceiving the court.
I await
your detailed memorial.
Yǐ,
means to lean.
To lean
implies the meaning of attentive waiting,
such as leaning the ear, leaning the body, or leaning on the mat.
Chóng,
pronounced as zhí lóng.
Submit it to the Secretariat,
and promulgate it throughout the land,
so that the beauty of renewal
may be seen again today."
Chén could only apologize for his faults,
and dared not speak further.
The Emperor was filial, compassionate, respectful, and frugal by nature,
widely learned and capable in literary arts,

and there was nothing in which he did not excel, such as yin-yang divination, turtle-shell and milfoil divination, horsemanship and archery, musical temperament, cursive and clerical script calligraphy, and the game of Go.
He was diligent in governmental affairs.
In winter, he would finish by the fourth watch,
and at night, he divided his time into five watches,
each watch lasting until five points before finishing.
Holding the brush and enduring the cold,
his hands would become chapped and cracked.
Since the Tiānjiàn era, he adopted Buddhist practices,
observing a long-term vegetarian diet and abstaining from fish and meat,
eating only once a day,
consisting solely of vegetable soup and coarse rice.
If affairs became too numerous,
he would pass the day by rinsing his mouth when the sun passed its zenith.
"Rì yí zhōng" means the sun passing its zenith.
"Sòu"
should be read as
"shù,"
meaning to rinse the mouth,
pronounced xiān zòu fān.
"Guò"
means to pass the day.
He used a cotton black canopy.
Cotton was abundant in Jiāngnán,
and its seeds were sown at the end of the second or third month of spring.
After sprouting,
it required weeding around it three times a month.
If weeding was not done in time,
it would be overrun by weeds,
causing it to wither and die.
By summer, it gradually grew lush,
and by autumn, it produced yellow flowers and bore fruit.
When ripe,
its skin split open in four parts,
and cotton-like fibers emerged from within.
The locals used iron rods to roll away the seeds,
took the cotton-like fibers,
and used bamboo to make small bows,
about one chi four or five cùn in length,
strung with a cord to fluff the cotton,
making it even and fine.
It was then rolled into small tubes,
placed on a spinning wheel to spin,
naturally drawing out threads,
similar to reeling silk.
Without the labor of sewing or stitching,
it was woven into cloth.
Cotton from Mǐn and Guǎng was particularly beautiful and dense.
Fāng Shuò said: Mǐn and Guǎng grew much cotton,
with trees reaching seven or eight chǐ in height,
leaves like oak,
and fruits resembling large water chestnuts but green in color.
In late autumn, they would split open,
revealing white cotton fibers.
The locals picked them,
removed the shells,
used iron rods to press out all the black seeds,
and then slowly fluffed them with small bows,
after which they were spun into thread and woven into cloth,
called jíbèi.
The cotton sold today is particularly fine and tightly woven.
The quality is judged by the number of flowers,
with one hundred and twenty flowers counted horizontally considered the highest grade.
The barbarians of Hǎinán wove it into towels,
embroidered with fine characters and mixed floral patterns,
exceptionally skillful and delicate,
which were the so-called white叠 towels of ancient times.
"Shēn yī" means clothing.
One quilt lasted two years,
and from the noble ladies of the rear palace downward,
their garments did not drag on the ground.
By nature, he did not drink alcohol,
and unless it was for ancestral temple sacrifices, grand feasts, or various Buddhist ceremonies,
he never had music performed.
"Fǎ shì" refers to Buddhist ceremonies such as chanting sūtras.
He always sat properly with his clothes and cap on,
and even in the intense heat of summer, he never bared his arms or chest.
"Xiǎo zuò" means informal seating in the palace.
"Héng" is pronounced hù dēng fān.
"Zuò" is pronounced cú wò fān.
It was as if he were receiving an important guest.
However, he was overly lenient and indulgent toward scholars,
with many regional governors exploiting the common people,
and envoys interfering in commanderies and counties.
He also favored appointing petty men to close positions,
which led to excessive harshness and scrutiny.
He built many pagodas and temples,
causing financial losses to both the state and private individuals.
Jiāngnán had long been at peace,
and its customs had become extravagant and wasteful.
This is why Hè Chēn's memorial touched upon these matters.
The Emperor disliked his blunt exposure of the truth,
hence his anger.
Your subject Guāng remarks: Liáng Gāozǔ's failure to maintain his rule to the end was fitting indeed!
The fault in a ruler's acceptance of advice lies in being trivial and fragmented.
Kǒng Ānguó said: "Cóng cuǒ" means trivial and fragmented, lacking a grand strategy.
Mǎ Róng said: "Cóng" means to gather together.
"Cuǒ" means small.
Lù Démíng said: "Cuǒ" is pronounced cāng guǒ fān;
Xú gives the pronunciation as suǒ.
It lies in being overly detailed and trivial.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler holds to the essential way to govern the myriad affairs at their root,
while loyal ministers present the broad principles to correct the ruler's faults of mind.
Thus, the ruler expends little effort yet achieves far-reaching success,
and their words are extremely concise yet bring great benefit.
Observe how Hè Chēn's remonstrance had not yet
reached the point of blunt directness,
yet Gāozǔ was already enraged and furious,
defending his own shortcomings
and boasting of his own strengths.
He demanded the names of greedy and oppressive officials,
inquired about the specific items of labor and expense,
cornered him with difficult-to-answer scenarios,
and pressed him with questions that were impossible to fully address.
He considered his own frugality in eating vegetables as a great virtue,
and his diligence until sunset as the pinnacle of governance.
Believing that the way of a ruler was already complete
and could not be improved further,
he regarded the admonitions and guidance of his ministers
as entirely unworthy of listening to.
In this way, who would dare to offer any remonstrance more blunt and direct than Chēn's?
As a result, treacherous and flattering men stood before him, yet he did not see them,
referring to figures like Zhū Yì and Zhōu Shízhēn.
This refers to accepting Hóu Jǐng
and again making peace with Eastern Wèi.
He brought about the collapse of the state and the severing of its ancestral sacrifices,
becoming an object of pity and ridicule for millennia.
How lamentable indeed!
Emperor Wu of Liang esteemed and advocated refined culture,
neglected and simplified penal laws,
and from the highest ministers and senior officials downward,
none paid attention to judicial trials.
Corrupt officials seized power and manipulated the law,
bribery became rampant as if forming a market,
and many were wrongfully convicted or excessively punished.
Generally, those sentenced to two years or more of penal servitude numbered up to five thousand annually;
those sentenced to forced labor were assigned tasks according to their five skills,
"skill"
refers to the crafts or physical abilities a person possesses.
The five skills are:
those skilled in woodworking were assigned to carpentry,
those skilled in metalworking were assigned to metalwork,
those skilled in leatherworking were assigned to leatherwork,
those skilled in coloring/painting were assigned to coloring/painting,
those skilled in pottery-making were assigned to pottery-making.
"Skill"
is pronounced as "rén".
Emperor Wu of Wei established the Jiǎzǐ Code,
stipulating that for offenders whose feet were shackled with iron fetters,
these should be replaced with wooden cangues;
at that time, iron was scarce,
hence they were replaced with wood.
"Shackle",
is pronounced as "zhuó luè fān".
They were temporarily removed,
after which some prisoners received lenient or harsh treatment.
This means that prisoners who had the means to bribe officials,
the jailers would falsely claim they were ill,
temporarily remove their shackles and grant them leniency.
Those without the means to bribe officials,
even if they were genuinely ill,
would not have their shackles removed,
and would suffer even greater hardship.
Many became arrogant, licentious, and lawless.
The Emperor, being elderly,
grew weary of the myriad affairs of state.
Moreover, he devoted himself entirely to Buddhist precepts,
and whenever he passed a severe sentence,
he would remain unhappy all day;
Emperor Wu of Liang being unhappy all day after passing a severe sentence
reflects his reverence for life and aversion to killing.
However, examining the Emperor's entire life,
from raising troops in Xiāngyáng to capturing Jiànkāng,
he still claimed it concerned the state and family,
punishing the guilty and saving the people.
But after the defeat at Luòkǒu,
how many people died?
In the battle of Fúshān,
how many people died?
In the defeat at Hánshān,
how many more people died?
In the struggles for cities,
the slain filled the cities;
in the struggles for territory,
the slain filled the fields;
people from both north and south dying for each other,
the number cannot be counted.
As for the rebellion of Hóu Jǐng,
reaching east to Wú and Kuàijī,
west to Jiānglíng and Yǐngzhōu,
those who died by war or famine,
since the Jin court crossed south,
had never been seen before.
Driving innocent people to their deaths,
is not only unacceptable to Confucian and Daoist principles,
but also makes one a sinner in Buddhism;
yet passing one severe sentence makes him unhappy all day?
Whom is he deceiving,
is he deceiving Heaven?
"Pass sentence",
is pronounced as "dīng luàn fān".
When such matters were discovered,
he would also weep and pardon them.
Such as with Prince Línhè Zhèngdé and his son.
Some committed murder in broad daylight on the capital's streets,
others openly robbed and plundered at night;
fugitives with crimes
hid in royal residences,
and officials dared not search or arrest them.
The Emperor was well aware of these abuses,
but being immersed in misplaced compassion,
he could not prohibit them.

"Yù",

supporting his plan to remain in Dūnhuáng.

"Dūn",

"Lìng",

Intimidated by the claim that a large army was coming,

First year of Zhōng Dàtóng (Bǐngyín, 546)
This year, in the summer fourth month,
the era name was changed to Zhōng Dàtóng.
1 Spring,
first month,
Guǐchǒu day,
Yáng Biāo and others captured Jiāníng City,

and the various armies halted at the river mouth.
The river mouth,
is where the Sūlì River enters the sea.
"Lǎo",

2 Second month,
Wei appointed Shǐ Níng as Governor of Yì Prefecture.
Previously, Eastern and Western Wei contended for Yì Prefecture,

so Western Wei appointed him as Governor.
The former Governor Yǔwén Zhònghé held the prefecture,
refusing to hand over authority,
while the people of Guā Prefecture, Zhāng Bǎo, killed Governor Chéng Qìng to respond to him,
and the people of Jìnchāng, Lǚ Xīng, killed Grand Administrator Guō Sì,
offering the commandery to Bǎo.
Liú Xù's *Tángshū* records: Jìnchāng County in Guā Prefecture,
was the Qián'ān County of Hàn's Dūnhuáng Commandery.
Formerly, Jìnchāng Commandery and Qián'ān County were established there,
then Jìnchāng was renamed Yǒngxīng;
Sui changed it to Guā Prefecture,
and Qián'ān to Chánglè;
in the seventh year of Wǔdé,
it was restored as Jìnchāng.
Táng also had Chánglè County,
which was the area of Hàn's Guǎngzhì County.
Also, according to *Wǔdài Zhì*,
Chánglè County in Guā Prefecture,
was established by Later Wei as Chánglè Commandery.
Later Zhōu merged Liángxīng, Guǎngzhì, Qián'ān, and Rùnquán to form Liángxīng County;
Sui abolished the commandery,
and renamed the county Chánglè.
Comparing and examining these,
then Jìnchāng Commandery was likely established within the boundaries of Sui's Chánglè County.
3 Third month,
Yǐsì day,
a general amnesty was declared.
On the Gēngxū day (the 47th),
the Emperor visited Tóngtài Temple.
He then halted at the temple's administrative office,
as Tóngtài Temple had a convenient administrative office.
A note on discrepancies: The Diǎnlüè states: On the Guǐmǎo day (the 40th),

"On the eighth day of this month, an unrestricted great assembly shall be held at Tóngtài Temple.

In the fourth month,

the dukes and ministers redeemed him with two hundred million in cash.
According to Hán Yù's "Memorial on the Buddha's Bone,"
"He three times relinquished his body to become a temple slave."
If this instance is included, it would make four.
We now follow the Liáng Shū.
In the fourth month,
on the Bǐngxū day (the 23rd),
the lecture series concluded,
a great amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed.

the pagoda at Tóngtài Temple caught fire.

'Xíng'

[We shall] redouble [our efforts] compared to before."

5. Wèi's Shǐ Níng persuaded the officials and people of Liángzhōu with clear instructions,

Only Yǔwén Zhònghé held the city and refused to surrender.
In the fifth month,

Jū,
Qiānyú fān.

Suǒjiǎo fān.
Zhì,
Zhílì fān.

The "Liù Jiǎ Gū Xū" method:
In the decade of Jiǎzǐ, there are no Xū or Hài,
thus Xū and Hài are "Gū" (isolated),
while Chén and Sì are "Xū" (void).
In the decade of Jiǎxū, there are no Shēn or Yǒu,
thus Shēn and Yǒu are "Gū,"
while Yín and Mǎo are "Xū."
In the decade of Jiǎshēn, there are no Wǔ or Wèi,
thus Wǔ and Wèi are "Gū,"
while Zǐ and Chǒu are "Xū."
In the decade of Jiǎwǔ, there are no Chén or Sì,
thus Chén and Sì are "Gū,"
while Xū and Hài are "Xū."
In the decade of Jiǎchén, there are no Yín or Mǎo,
thus Yín and Mǎo are "Gū,"
while Shēn and Yǒu are "Xū."
In the decade of Jiǎyín, there are no Zǐ or Chǒu,
thus Zǐ and Chǒu are "Gū,"
while Wǔ and Wèi are "Xū."
Xián's commentary states: Opposing "Gū" is "Xū."
Xuánnǚ said to the Yellow Emperor: The method of warfare,
is to avoid the isolated and strike the void.
North,
is a natural barrier.
A natural barrier,
is a barrier formed by nature;
created by heaven and shaped by earth,
not relying on human effort.
The Yìjīng says: A natural barrier cannot be ascended.
They intercepted the enemy's tunnels,

Wéi Xiàokuān is a man of Guānxī,

Zhū Yì sent a letter to Jǐng,

“Since recent years, Liáng

Jǐng’s letter reached this point—
what words could Yì and others use to respond?
I point out and denounce the powerful and treacherous,

The Odes of the States says: ‘Who says the river is wide?

means to cross.
The commentary says: ‘Who says the river water is wide?

This metaphor illustrates narrowness.

last month,

Jǐng intended to use humble words to welcome his family—

The Emperor angrily said:
“Accepting surrender is a common principle—

The Crown Prince summoned the ministers for a meeting,

The Crown Prince said:
“We will firmly defend the city and await external relief.
Once the relief troops arrive,
how could the rebels be difficult to pacify?
This is a perfectly safe strategy.
Now, if we open the gates to admit Táobàng,
Táobàng’s true intentions—
how easily can they be known?
If by any chance he turns against us,

Yì said:
“If Your Highness considers the urgency of state affairs,
you should admit Táobàng;

The Crown Prince ultimately could not decide.
Táobàng again sent Xīn to report, saying:

Tài realized his error,

first month,

Gān (dried),

directed and deployed,

Chén Yuánkāng wrote a farewell letter to his mother by hand,

Hóng,

Allocation and assignment,

Gāo Lóngzhī, Sīmǎ Zǐrú, and others hated the Minister of Revenue Cuī Xiān,
