(Hóu Jǐng established Wúzhōu; see the previous year in the previous scroll.)
13. On Yǐsì,
Shàngshū Púshè Wáng Kè was appointed as Zuǒ Púshè.
14. On Gēngyín,
Dōng Wèi appointed Shàngshū Lìng Gāo Lóngzhī as Tàibǎo.
15. Xuānchéng Nèishǐ Yáng Báihuá advanced and occupied Ānwú,
(Sūn Wú established Ānwú County,
belonging to Xuānchéng Commandery;
Suí abolished Ānwú and merged it into Jīng County.)
but was unsuccessful.
16. Dōng Wèi Xíngtái Xīn Shù led troops to invade,
besieged Yángpíng,
but was unsuccessful.
17. Hóu Jǐng married the emperor's daughter, Lìyáng Gōngzhǔ,
and loved her dearly.
In the third month,
on Jiǎshēn,
Jǐng requested the emperor to hold a purification feast at Lèyóu Yuàn,
(the purification feast,
a banquet held for the purification ritual.
Xì,
pronounced hú jì fān.)
(Lèyóu Yuàn
is south of Xuánwǔ Lake.)
After the emperor returned to the palace,
Jǐng and the princess together occupied the imperial couch,
sitting side by side facing south,
while the assembled civil and military officials sat in rows attending the feast.
18. On Gēngshēn,
Dōng Wèi promoted Chéngxiàng Gāo Yáng's noble rank to King of Qí.
19. Línchuān Nèishǐ Shǐxīng Wáng Yì and others attacked Zhuāng Tiě,
(Wáng Yì,
a native of Shǐxīng;
Yì is the
"yì"
character.
Later scribes, when transcribing,
changed the
"lì"
to
instead.)
Yì and others were defeated and died.
20. Póyáng Shìzǐ Sì fought Rèn Yuē at Sānzhāng,
and Yuē was defeated and fled;
Sì therefore moved his garrison to Sānzhāng,
calling it the Ānlè Stockade.
(Last year, Póyáng Wáng Fàn went west,
leaving Shìzǐ Sì to guard the Ānlè Stockade.
Now he moved the stockade to Sānzhāng,
also naming it Ānlè Stockade.
Lè,
pronounced luò.)
In the summer of the 21st year,
in the fourth month,
on the first day, Gēngchén,
Xiāngdōng Wáng Xiāo appointed Shàngjiǎ Hóu Sháo as Chángshā Wáng.
Shàngjiǎ Hóu Sháo had fled to Jiānglíng,
as seen in the previous volume, last year.
According to the Liáng Shū,
Chángshā Wáng Yì's son Yuānyè succeeded to the title;
upon his death,
his son Xiàoyǎn succeeded;
upon his death,
his son Shèn succeeded.
Shèn,
the great-grandson of Yì,
was in Jiànkāng at the time.
Xiāngdōng Wáng returned Sháo to him,
and thus made him Chángshā Wáng,
which was improper.
On the 22nd, Bǐngwǔ,
Hóu Jǐng requested the Emperor to visit Xīzhōu.
The Emperor rode in a plain carriage,
accompanied by over four hundred guards,
while Hóu Jǐng had several thousand armored soldiers,
flanking him on both sides.
"Armored soldiers"
refers to soldiers in iron armor so smooth and hard
it was as if washed with water.
The Emperor shed tears sorrowfully,
and ordered Hóu Jǐng to dance;
Hóu Jǐng also requested the Emperor to dance.
When the wine was finished and the gathering dispersed,
the Emperor embraced Hóu Jǐng by the bed and said:
"I miss you, Chancellor."
Hóu Jǐng replied:
"If Your Majesty did not miss me,
how could I have reached this position!"
The event lasted until nightfall.
At that time, the Jiangnán region suffered from consecutive years of drought and locusts,
with Jiāng and Yáng particularly severe.
The common people fled into exile,
gathering in mountain valleys, rivers, and lakes,
foraging for grass roots, tree leaves, water caltrops, and foxnuts to eat.
Water caltrops,
are also known as jì.
Foxnuts,
pronounced jùxiǎn fān;
according to Shuōwén, they are called "chicken heads."
The Fāngyán states: In Nánchǔ, they are called chicken heads,
in Běiyān, they are called yì,
and in the regions of Qīng, Xú, Huái, and Sì, they are called qiàn.
The dead covered the fields.
Wealthy families had no food,
their faces gaunt like crows and their bodies emaciated like swans.
Dressed in fine silks,
clutching pearls and jade,
they lay prostrate by their beds and curtains,
awaiting death.
For a thousand miles, no smoke rose,
human traces were rarely seen,
white bones piled up,
like mounds and ridges.
Hóu Jǐng was by nature cruel,
erecting a large mortar at Shítóu,
where lawbreakers were pounded to death.
He often warned his generals:
"When breaking through stockades and capturing cities,
you must kill everyone cleanly,
so the world knows my fearsome name."
Thus, whenever his generals won a battle,
they focused solely on burning and looting,
slaughtering people like grass,
treating it as a jest.
For this reason, even in death,
the people never submitted to him.
The historian notes that Hóu Jǐng was heading toward defeat.
Offenders were punished along with their external clans.
For men, the external clan refers to the mother's family;
for women, it refers to their parents' family.
External clans
are the clans of the external family.
All were called Xíngtái,
and those who surrendered and submitted
were all called Kāifǔ.
Those with close and honored positions were called Zuǒyòuxiāng Gōng,
and those with exceptional courage and strength were called Kùzhí Dūdū.
The Nánshǐ Hóu Jǐng zhuàn records it as
"Kùzhēn Bùdū."
This is an error.
On the 23rd, Wèi enfeoffed the imperial prince Rú as Yān Wáng,
and Gōng as Wú Wáng.
On the 24th, Hóu Jǐng recalled Sòng Zǐxiān to Jīngkǒu.
Last year, Sòng Zǐxiān captured Dōngyángzhōu,
and now he was recalled to Jīngkǒu.
On the 25th, Shàolíng Wáng Lún was in Yìngzhōu,
using the audience hall as the Zhèngyáng Diàn,
with all internal and external chambers and pavilions
bearing inscribed plaques.
His subordinates bullied the military headquarters,
and the officers of Yìngzhōu resented them deeply.
Advisory Counselor Jiāng Zhòngjǔ,
the chief strategist of Nánpíng Wáng Kè,
urged Kè to plot against Lún.
Kè was startled and said:
"If I kill Shàolíng,
bringing peace to this region,
the brothers in Jīng and Yì will surely rejoice inwardly.
Since the Emperor is in distress,
Lún, being next in line among the brothers, should succeed.
If I eliminate Lún,
public expectation will shift to Jīng and Yì,
and they will certainly rejoice inwardly.
At the time, Xiāngdōng Wáng Xiāo was in Jīngzhōu,
and Wǔlíng Wáng Jì was in Yìzhōu.
They would then hold me accountable on grounds of righteousness.
Moreover, the great rebel remains unpunished,
the great rebel
referring to Hóu Jǐng.
Punished,
means beheading him.
Punished,
pronounced jiān yáo fān.
This would be a path to self-destruction.
Please cease this plan."
Zhòngjǔ did not listen,
and proceeded to assign tasks to the generals,
setting a date for action.
The plot was leaked,
and Lún crushed him to death.
Kè hurriedly went to apologize,
and Lún said:
"This was the work of a petty man,
not due to you, elder brother.
The villainous clique is already dead,
do not worry deeply, elder brother!"
Nánpíng Wáng Kè,
the son of Wěi,
was elder to Lún.
On the 26th, Wáng Sēngbiàn urgently attacked Chángshā,
on Xīnsì,
and captured it.
He captured Hédōng Wáng Yù,
beheaded him,
and sent his head to Jiānglíng.
Xiāngdōng Wáng Xiāo returned the head and buried it.
He returned the head to Chángshā,
and buried it with the body.
The death of his heir, Fāngděng,
is recorded in the previous volume, last year.
Wú established Línzhēng County,
named for its proximity to the Zhēng River,
under Héngyáng Commandery,
and during Jìn, under Xiāngdōng Commandery.
Lì Dàoyuán said: Línzhēng was the former Líng County,
and the county was Xiāngdōng Commandery.
Liú Xù said: Suí changed Línzhēng to Héngyáng County,
which is the present Héngyáng County, the seat of Héngzhōu.
The Héngzhōu Zhì states: Wú divided Líng County to establish Línzhēng County,
overlooking the Zhēng River,
where the steam rose like vapor.
Yáo Sīlián's Chén Shū states: Zhōu Tiěhǔ,
of unknown origin,
crossed south during the Liáng dynasty,
served Hédōng Wáng Yù,
and was the magistrate of Línzhēng.
Thus,
the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn omits
the character "magistrate"
here.
Sēngbiàn captured Tiěhǔ,
ordered him boiled alive,
but Tiěhǔ cried out:
"Hóu Jǐng is not yet destroyed,
why kill a brave man!"
Sēngbiàn, struck by his words, released him,
and returned him to his command.
Xiāo appointed Sēngbiàn as Left Guard General,
and added the titles of Palace Attendant and West-Pacifying Chief Clerk.
Xiāo had learned of Gāozǔ's death last year,
but because Chángshā was not yet captured,
he concealed it.
On Rényín,
he finally announced the mourning,
carved a sandalwood statue of Gāozǔ,
placed it in the Bǎifú Hall,
attended to it with great reverence,
consulting it on every action.
Xiāo believed the Son of Heaven was controlled by rebel ministers,
and refused to adopt the era name Dàbǎo,
still using Tàiqīng 4th year.
On Bǐngwǔ,
Xiāo ordered a major campaign against Hóu Jǐng,
issuing proclamations far and wide.
27. King of Póyáng, Fàn, arrived at Pénchéng.
He made Jìnxī into Jìnzhōu.
Emperor Ān of Jìn divided Lújiāng Commandery to establish Jìnxī Commandery.
Wǔdài Zhì: Huáiníng County of Tóng'ān Commandery was formerly established as Jìnxī Commandery.
Táng made Tóng'ān Commandery into Shūzhōu.
The commanderies and counties of Jiāngzhōu were frequently changed and altered.
This refers to changing the commandery and county governors and magistrates.
The reach of government orders
did not extend beyond a single commandery.
It was only Xúnyáng Commandery alone.
Sì and Tiě had long been on good terms,
and requested troops to rescue him.
Fàn sent Hóu Zhèn to lead five thousand elite armored troops to assist Tiě.
From then on, the two garrisons became suspicious and jealous of each other,
and no longer had the will to campaign against the rebels.
Dàxīn sent Xú Sìhuī to lead two thousand troops,
to build fortifications at Jītíng to guard against Fàn.
According to the Qí Shū, biography of Prince Zǐmào of Jìn'ān: Zǐmào plotted to raise troops in Jiāngzhōu.
Prince of Xuānchéng sent Péi Shūyè to launch a surprise attack and capture Pénchéng.
Zǐmào had already prepared boats at Jītíngzhǔ beforehand.
Hearing that Shūyè had taken Pénchéng,
he then occupied the province to defend himself.
Thus, Jītíngzhǔ was east of Jiāngzhōu city.
Shuài
is read as shuài.
Fàn's tens of thousands of troops
obtained no food,
and many starved to death.
Fàn, enraged and resentful,
developed a carbuncle on his back.
In the fifth month,
on the day Yǐmǎo,
he died.
Fàn's followers kept his death secret and did not announce the funeral,
instead installing Fàn's younger brother, the Marquis of Ānnán, Tián, as their leader.
They had several thousand troops.
28. On the day Bǐngchén,
Hóu Jǐng appointed Yuán Sīqián as Grand Commissioner of the Eastern Circuit,
to garrison Qiántáng.
On the day Dīngsì,
he appointed Hóu Zǐjiàn as Governor of Nányǎnzhōu.
29. When the King of Qí of Eastern Wèi, Yáng, held the position of Kāifǔ,
Yáng was Kāifǔ,
see scroll 157, first year of Emperor Wǔ's Dàtóng era.
Guǎnjì
refers to the position of Jìshì Cānjūn.
He spoke exhaustively on all matters.
Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū of Dānyáng, Xú Zhīcái, and Tàishǒu of Běipíng, Sòng Jǐngyè of Guǎngzōng,
From Hàn and Jìn times onward, Zhōngshān had Běipíng County.
During the Xiàochāng era of Later Wèi,
Běipíng Commandery was separately established,
belonging to Dìngzhōu.
Guǎngzōng County,
belonged to Jùlù Commandery in Hàn times,
later belonged to Ānpíng Principality,
in the twenty-first year of the Tàihé era of Later Wèi,
Guǎngzōng Commandery was separately established;
at that time it belonged to Sīzhōu.
Believing that the Tàisuì was in the wǔ year,
there should be a dynastic change,
they used Dézhèng to inform Yáng,
urging him to accept the abdication.
Yáng told Lóu Tài.
Tài said:
"Your father was like a dragon,
your elder brother like a tiger.
Yet they still considered the imperial position could not be recklessly occupied,
and faced north as subjects their whole lives.
What kind of person are you alone,
that you wish to perform the deeds of Shùn and Yǔ!"
Yáng told Zhīcái.
Zhīcái said:
"It is precisely because you are not equal to your father and brother,
that you should ascend to the honored position early."
Yáng cast an image to divine and it succeeded.
He then sent Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Duàn Sháo to ask the Governor of Sìzhōu, Húlǜ Jīn.
Jīn came to see Yáng,
firmly stating it was not permissible,
and because Sòng Jǐngyè was the first to present the prophetic mandate,
requested to have him killed.
Yáng discussed with the various nobles before Tài.
Tài said:
"My son is timid and straightforward,
he certainly does not have this intention.
Gāo Dézhèng delights in calamity,
and taught him this."
Yáng, because people's hearts were not united,
sent Gāo Dézhèng to Yè to observe the intentions of the ministers.
He had not yet returned;
Yáng gathered troops and marched east,
arriving at Píngdūchéng.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Liáozhōu Liáoshān County had Píngchéng Town.
Sòng Bái said: Píngchéng County of Liáozhōu was originally the territory of Niè County in Hàn times.
Jìn established Wǔxiāng County,
and this territory belonged to it.
In the sixteenth year of the Suí Kāihuáng era,
Píngchéng County was established at the old city of Píngdū, which was built by Zhào Jiǎnzǐ.
None dared to respond.
Chief Clerk Dù Bì said:
"Guānxī
is a formidable enemy of the state."
This refers to the Yǔwén clan.
Qíng,
is pronounced qú jīng fān.
"I fear they might hold the Son of Heaven,
call themselves righteous troops and march east."
This Son of Heaven
refers to the ruler of Western Wèi.
Xú Zhīcái said:
"Now, those who contend for the world with you, King,
also wish to do what you, King, are doing.
Even if they stubbornly resist,
at most they will follow us in proclaiming themselves emperor."
Bì had nothing to reply.
Gāo Dézhèng arrived at Yè,
hinted to the ministers,
but none responded.
Sīmǎ Zǐrú welcomed Yáng at Liáoyáng.
Liáoyáng County had belonged to Lèpíng Commandery since the end of Hàn.
In the eleventh year of the Suí Kāihuáng era,
it was renamed Liáoshān County.
In our dynasty, it is the seat of Liáozhōu.
Yáng wished to turn back.
Granary Assistant Lǐ Jí said:
According to the system of Northern Qí,
the Grand Granary and granaries at water transport points all had Superintendents and Assistants.
The Northern Qí Jì records
"Shàngshí Assistant Lǐ Jí".
"For what purpose did you, King, come,
and now wish to turn back?"
Yáng falsely ordered him executed at the eastern gate,
but separately ordered ten bolts of thin silk bestowed upon him,
and then returned to Jìnyáng.
From then on, he was often unhappy in his daily life.
Xú Zhīcái, Sòng Jǐngyè, and others daily expounded on the theories of yīn-yáng and miscellaneous divinations,
saying it was appropriate to receive the mandate early.
Gāo Dézhèng also urged and encouraged incessantly.
Yáng had the diviner Lǐ Mì perform a divination for him.
He encountered the "Great Horizontal" hexagram.
He said:
"This is the hexagram of Emperor Wén of Hàn."
The Great Horizontal appears in scroll 13, eighth year of Empress Gāo of Hàn.
He encountered the change from Qián to Dǐng.
The first and fifth lines of the Qián hexagram
moved and changed to become Dǐng.
"Qián
is the ruler.
Dǐng
is the hexagram of the fifth month.
It is appropriate to receive the abdication in mid-summer."
Someone said:
"One must not assume office in the fifth month.
If one violates this,
one will die in that position."
According to the theory of the yīn-yáng school,
taking up an official post is taboo in the first, fifth, and ninth months.
"If you, King, become the Son of Heaven,
there will be no further demotion.
How could you not die in that position!"
Yáng was greatly pleased,
and then set out from Jìnyáng.
Initially, nine grades of households were established,
with households divided into upper, middle, and lower classes,
each further subdivided into upper, middle, and lower,
making nine grades in total.
The poor were required to contribute their labor.
54 In the ninth month,
on Dīngsì day,
the Wèi army set out from Cháng'ān.
They departed Cháng'ān to campaign eastward against Qí.
55 Wáng Sēngbiàn's army reached Yīngwǔ Zhōu,
Yīngwǔ Zhōu is in the middle of the river at Jiāngxià.
In the past, Huáng Zǔ had Mí Héng compose the "Parrot Rhapsody" on this islet,
hence it acquired its name.
Below the islet lies Huánghú Jī.
Shàolíng Prince Lún, upon hearing this,
dispatched his son, Wēizhèng Hóu Zhì, to lead troops to attack them.
Lónghǔ was defeated,
and fled to Sēngbiàn.
Lún sent a letter reproaching Sēngbiàn, saying:
"Last year, General, you killed my nephew,
referring to the killing of Hédōng Prince Yù.
Lún is the elder brother of Yì.
I fear the world will not permit this!"
Sēngbiàn sent the letter to Xiāngdōng Prince Yì,
and Yì ordered the advance of the army.
On Xīnyǒu day,
Lún gathered his subordinates at the Western Garden,
the garden is located on the western side of Yǐngchéng,
hence called the Western Garden.
There is also an Eastern Garden,
situated on Dōnghú east of the city.
"I originally had no other intentions,
my aim was to exterminate the rebels.
Xiāngdōng often claimed I was contending with him for the throne,
and thus I was attacked.
Today, if I wish to hold out, supplies and provisions are cut off;
if I wish to fight, I will be mocked for generations.
I cannot remain idle and be captured,
I should avoid this by going downstream."
Brave warriors among his subordinates vied to request to go out and fight,
but Lún did not consent.
Together with Zhì, he boarded a boat from the Cāngmén gate and headed north.
According to Yáo Sīlián's *Liáng Shū*,
Cāngmén,
is the northern gate of Yǐngchéng,
bordered by the river and strategically hazardous.
Yì appointed Nánpíng Prince Jué as Shàngshū Lìng and Kāifǔ Yìtóng Sānsī,
his heir Fāngzhū as Governor of Yǐngzhōu,
and Wáng Sēngbiàn as General of the Imperial Guard.
Lún encountered General Zhèndōng Péi Zhīgāo on the road,
Zhīgāo's son Jī plundered his military equipment.
Lún, with his attendants, took a light boat and fled to the Chàngsì Temple in Wǔchāngjiàn,
Wǔchāng,
is present-day Shòuchāngjūn.
Lún's Chief Clerk Wéi Zhì and Sima Jiāng Lǜ, upon hearing that Lún was still alive,
rushed to welcome him,
and persuaded the displaced people of the seven stockades to provide provisions and weapons.
At that time, displaced people in Běijiāngzhōu formed seven stockades for mutual protection.
Persuade,
read as shuì.
Eight to nine thousand displaced people attached themselves to him,
gradually gathering scattered troops,
and encamped at Qíchāng.
According to Wèi Shōu's records: Emperor Wǔ of Liáng established Běijiāngzhōu,
with its seat at Lùchéngguān,
administering Yìyáng, Qíchāng, Xīnchāng, Liáng'ān, Qíxīng, and Guāngchéng commanderies.
*Wǔdài Zhì*: Mùlán County of Huángzhōu,
was called Liáng'ān commandery during Liáng.
There was also Yìyáng commandery,
later Qí established Xiāngzhōu,
later renamed Běijiāngzhōu.
Thus, Qíchāng should also be within the boundaries of Mùlán County,
Táng abolished Mùlán into Huánggāng County.
Sòng Bái said: Wú established Qíchūn commandery,
Jìn Emperor Huì changed it to Xīyáng commandery,
Southern Qí and Northern Qí changed Xīyáng to Qíchāng commandery,
Táng made it Qízhōu.
As for Qí,
Qí appointed Lún as Prince of Liáng.
56 Xiāngdōng Prince Yì changed the enfeoffment of his son Dàkuǎn to Línchuān Prince,
Dàchéng to Guìyáng Prince,
and Dàfēng to Rǔnán Prince.
57 On Guǐhài day,
the Wèi army reached Tóngguān.
58 On Gēngwǔ day,
the Qí ruler went to Jìnyáng,
ordering Crown Prince Yīn to reside at Liángfēng Hall to oversee state affairs.
According to the *Běishǐ* biography of Qí Prince Bǎinián of Lèlíng: Liángfēng Hall is in the Xuándū Garden of the Yè palace.
Oversee,
read as jiān.
59 Zhāng Biāo, Military Consultant of the Southern Commandery Prince,
when Southern Commandery Prince Dàlián was stationed at Kuàijī,
appointed Zhāng Biāo as Military Consultant.
Ruòxié Mountain,
is located forty lǐ southeast of present-day Yuèzhōu.
He had a following of tens of thousands.
Lù Lìnggōng and others from Wú commandery persuaded Grand Administrator Nánhǎi Prince Dàlín to go and rely on him.
Dàlín said:
"If Biāo succeeds,
he will not rely on my strength;
if he fails,
he will use me to exonerate himself,
meaning he will shift blame onto Dàlín to exonerate himself before Hóu Jǐng.
60 Rèn Yuē advanced and invaded Xīyáng and Wǔchāng.
Initially,
Xú Wénshèng, Governor of Níngzhōu from Péngchéng, recruited tens of thousands of troops to campaign against Hóu Jǐng.
Xiāngdōng Prince Yì appointed him as Governor of Qínzhōu,
*Wǔdài Zhì*: Liùhé County of Jiāngdū commandery,
formerly established as Qín commandery,
later Qí established Qínzhōu.
Perhaps Liáng had already established it?
He encountered Yuē at Wǔchāng.
Yì appointed Lúlíng Prince Yìng as Governor of Jiāngzhōu,
and appointed Wénshèng as Chief Clerk to administer the prefectural affairs,
supervising the generals to resist him.
Yìng,
was the son of Xù.
Lúlíng Prince Xù,
died in the first year of Emperor Wǔ's Tàiqīng era.
They moved camp to Mǎzhà,
eighty lǐ from Xīyáng.
Xīyáng,
is present-day Huánggāng County of Huángzhōu,
the ancient Zhūchéng.
He dispatched Yìtóng Chìluó Zǐtōng and others leading two hundred armored cavalry to raid them,
Chìluó,
is a Xianbei compound surname.
Cavalry,
read as jì.
They whipped their horses and fled.
At that time, Xiāngdōng Prince Yì also formed an alliance with Qí,
so the Qí people watched and waited,
not aiding Lún.
Tián Zǔlóng, Governor of Dìngzhōu, welcomed Lún.
Lún, because Zǔlóng was favored by Yì,
feared being captured by him,
and returned to Qíchāng.
Traveling to Rǔnán,
Lǐ Sù, the Rǔnán city commander appointed by Wèi,
was a former subordinate of Lún,
opened the city and admitted him.
Wèi Shōu's records: Yǐngzhōu had Rǔnán commandery,
with its seat at Shàngcài County.
*Wǔdài Zhì*: Jìnglíng commandery formerly established Yǐngzhōu,
administering Hàndōng County,
formerly called Shàngcài.
Thus, Rǔnán city is the city of Hàndōng County.
Also, according to Yáo Sīlián's *Liáng Shū*: Rǔnán's seat was at the fortified city of Ānlù.
Sòng Bái said: People of Jìn's Rǔnán commandery took refuge in Xiàkǒu,
and thus established the Rǔnán commandery and Rǔnán County at Tóngkǒu.
*Jīngxiāng Jì* states: North of the Jīnshuǐ river is the old city of Rǔnán.

for whom do you wish to be loyal?
Would it not be better to turn calamity into fortune,
and let blessings flow to your descendants!"
Xún then requested to surrender.
Dàiwéi
was the son of Liǔ Qìng.
Liǔ Qìng appears in scroll 161, the second year of Emperor Wǔ's Tàiqīng era.
(Some) requested to attack the city,
but the Grand Commander Hèlián Dá said:
"To obtain a city without fighting
is the best strategy.
How can we covet their sons and daughters,
be greedy for their goods and wealth,
and not cherish the lives of the people!
Moreover, observe that their soldiers and horses are still strong,
and the city walls and moats are still solid.
If we attack and even if we overcome them,
then both sides will suffer casualties;
like a cornered beast still fights,
words of Wú Fūgài Wáng from the Zuǒ Zhuàn.
Wǔ said:
"Your words are correct."
He then accepted Xún's surrender,
capturing twenty thousand men and women and returning,
whereupon the area north of Jiàn all entered Wèi.
26. In the sixth month,
on Dīngwèi,
the Qí ruler returned to Yè;
on Yǐmǎo,
he again went to Jìnyáng.
27. On Gēngyín,
Ānnán Hóu Fāngjǔ was established as Crown Prince.
28. Qí sent the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Xiè Jìqīng to congratulate (Liáng) on pacifying Hóu Jǐng.
29. The Governor of Héng Province, Wáng Huáimíng, rebelled,
and the Governor of Guǎng Province, Xiāo Bó, attacked and pacified him.
30. Qí's governance was burdensome and taxes heavy,
the people north of the Jiāng were not happy to belong to Qí,
and their local leaders repeatedly requested troops from Wáng Sēngbiàn.
Sēngbiàn, because of the friendly relations with Qí,
did not grant any.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
the immigrant Zhū Shèng and others in Guǎnglíng
(Immigrants:
those who were originally not from Guǎnglíng but resided there.)
plotted to surprise and kill the Qí Governor Wēn Zhòngyōng,
and sent an envoy to seek aid from Chén Bàxiān,
saying they had already captured the outer city.
Bàxiān sent word to inform Sēngbiàn,
Sēngbiàn said:
"The truth or falsehood of men's words
is not easy to gauge.
If they have indeed captured the outer city,
urgent aid is required;
if it is not so,
there is no need to trouble the army to advance."
Before the envoy's reply arrived,
Bàxiān had already crossed the Jiāng,
so Sēngbiàn then ordered the Governor of Wǔ Province, Dù Zè, and others to assist him.
It happened that Shèng and others' plot was exposed,
and Bàxiān therefore advanced his army to besiege Guǎnglíng.
31. In the eighth month,
Huáng Zhòngbǎo of Ānkāng in Wèi rebelled,
attacked Wèixīng,
captured the Grand Administrator Liǔ Guì,
and advanced to besiege Dōngliáng Province.
(Liáng established Nánliáng Province in Xīchéng Commandery,
Western Wèi changed it to Dōngliáng Province;
Xīchéng,
was the old seat of Wèixīng Commandery.
According to Wèi Shōu's records: In the fifth year of Tàiyán of Later Wèi,
a separate Wèixīng Commandery was established within the boundaries of Shàngluò Commandery,
attached to Yángtíng County,
belonging to Luò Province;
Luò Province,
was later changed to Shāng Province.)
Guì did not submit and died.
Guì
was the younger brother of Liǔ Qiú.
Liǔ Qiú,
was the elder brother of Liǔ Qìng,
appears in scroll 251, the third year of Emperor Wǔ's Dàtóng era.
32. Prince Wǔlíng, Xiāo Jì, raised troops and proceeded eastward via the Outer River,
appointing the Marquis of Yǒngfēng, Xiāo Huī, as Governor of Yì Province,
to guard Chéngdū,
and had his son, the Prince of Yídū, Yuánsù, assist him.
33. In the ninth month,
on Jiǎxū,
the Minister of Works, the Prince of Nánpíng, Xiāo Kè, died.
On Jiǎshēn,
Wáng Sēngbiàn was appointed Governor of Yáng Province.
34. The Qí ruler sent a message to Wáng Sēngbiàn and Chén Bàxiān, saying:
"Please lift the siege of Guǎnglíng,
and we will certainly return the two cities of Guǎnglíng and Lìyáng."
Bàxiān led his troops back to Jīngkǒu,
and over ten thousand people from north of the Jiāng followed Bàxiān across the river.
The Prince of Xiāngdōng appointed Bàxiān as Grand General Who Conquers the North, Equaling in Status the Three Ministers, and Governor of Nánxú Province.
He summoned Bàxiān's eldest son, Chāng,
(Bàxiān was enfeoffed as Marquis of Chángchéng County,
Chāng was his heir.)
appointing Chāng as Cavalier
Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and Xū as Commander of the Guards.
(Liáng's palace guard officials included Commanders of the Four Wings,
likely commanding the guard soldiers,
hence the name of the office.)
This sets the stage for Chāng and Xū's later capture by Wèi.
35. When the Marquis of Yìfēng, Xiāo Xún, surrendered to Wèi,
the Chancellor Yǔwén Tài promised he could return south,
but after a long time had not sent him back.
Casually, (Tài) asked Liú Fán:
"To whom among the ancients can I be compared?"
He replied:
"Fán has always considered you comparable to Tāng and Wǔ,
but from what I see today,
you are not even equal to Huán and Wén!"
Tài said:
"How dare I compare myself to Tāng and Wǔ,
I only hope to approach Yī and Zhōu,
how could I be inferior to Huán and Wén!"
He replied:
"Duke Huán of Qí preserved three perished states,
(Zuǒ Zhuàn: Sīmǎ Zǐyú of Sòng said: Duke Huán of Qí preserved three perished states and attached them to the feudal lords.
Dù Yù's annotation says: The three perished states
were Lǔ, Wèi, and Xíng.)
Before he finished speaking,
Tài clapped his hands and said:
"I understand your meaning,
you wish to provoke me."
He then said to Xún:
"Does the Prince wish to go to Jīng,
or to Yì?"
(Prince Wǔlíng, Xiāo Jì, had enfeoffed Xún as Prince of Suí Commandery,
hence he addressed him as 'Prince'.)
Tài sent him off with generous gifts.
(Textual analysis note: Diǎn Lüè states:
"In the tenth month,
on the first day, Yǐwèi,
Tàizǔ said to Xún"
and so on.
According to Tàiqīng Jì,
Xún arrived at Jiānglíng in this month,
now we follow this.)
The Prince of Xiāngdōng was suspicious of him,
and sent envoys to spy and observe,
who passed each other on the road;
On the night of his arrival,
he ordered (someone) to rob and steal his property,
and by dawn,
Xún reported and handed over his horses and weapons,
whereupon the Prince felt at ease,
summoned him in,
they wept facing each other,
and appointed Xún as Palace Attendant, General of Agile Cavalry, and Equaling in Status the Three Ministers.
36. In winter,
the tenth month,
the Qí ruler went from Jìnyáng to Líshí,
and from Huánglú Ridge began building a long wall,
extending north to the Shèpíng Garrison,
over four hundred lǐ,
establishing thirty-six garrisons.
(This long wall likely started in the Táng-era Shí Province,
reaching north to the borders of Wǔ Province.
Lú,
pronounced lú.
"Shèpíng",
in the Qí Jì is written as
"Shèzǐ".
According to the biography of Hùlǜ Jīn: Huánglú Ridge is east of the Wūtū Garrison.)
37. On Wùshēn,
the Prince of Xiāngdōng arrested the Governor of Xiāng Province, Wáng Lín, in the palace hall,
and killed his deputy general, Yīn Yàn.
Lín was originally from a military family in Kuàijī,
and his sisters had all entered the royal palace,
so Lín grew up serving the Prince.
Lín was fond of valor,
and the Prince appointed him as a general.
Lín devoted himself to treating his subordinates with humility,
and whatever rewards he received,
he never brought them home.
Under his command were ten thousand men,
many of whom were bandits from the Jiāng and Huái regions.
He followed Wáng Sēngbiàn in suppressing Hóu Jǐng,
and his achievements were ranked first alongside Dù Kān.
While in Jiànkāng,
relying on favor, he acted violently and unrestrained,
and Sēngbiàn was unable to restrain him.
Sēngbiàn, because of the burning of the palace,
believed it was caused by soldiers accidentally setting fire to the Tàijí Hall and the Eastern and Western Halls.
Wanting to use Lín to shift the blame,
he secretly reported to the Prince,
requesting Lín’s execution.
The Prince appointed Lín to Xiāngzhōu,
but Lín suspected he was facing disaster,
so he sent his Chief Clerk Lù Nà to lead his troops to Xiāngzhōu,
while he himself went to Jiānglíng to explain and apologize.
He said to Nà and the others:
“If I do not return,
where will you go?”
“Zhī” means to go.
“We request to die for it.”
They wept together and parted.
Upon reaching Jiānglíng,
the Prince handed Lín over to the officials.
On Xīnyǒu,
the Prince appointed his son Fānglüè as the Governor of Xiāngzhōu,
and also appointed the Commandant of Justice Huáng Luóhàn as Chief Clerk,
sending him together with the Grand Minister of Boats Zhāng Zǎi to Bālíng,
to first take control of Lín’s army.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: The Grand Minister of Boats,
during the early Liáng, was the Commissioner of the Waterways Bureau,
renamed in the seventh year of Tiānjiǎn,
his rank equivalent to a Secretariat Gentleman,
the lowest among the Nine Ministers,
in charge of boats, navigation, dikes, and canals.
However, he governed his subordinates harshly and severely,
and the people of Jīngzhōu hated him like an enemy.
When Luóhàn and the others arrived at Lín’s army,
Lù Nà and the soldiers all wept,
unwilling to accept the orders,
and seized Luóhàn and Zǎi.
The Prince sent the eunuch Chén Mín to go and explain to them,
but Nà, in response to Mín, cut open Zǎi’s belly,
pulled out his intestines to tie around a horse’s legs,
making it run in circles
until the intestines were exhausted and he died.
They then dismembered him,
took out his heart,
and danced joyfully toward it.
“Biànwǔ” means to clap hands and dance.
They spared Huáng Luóhàn because he was honest and cautious.
Nà and the various generals led troops to attack Xiāngzhōu.
At that time, there was no ruler in the province,
so Nà occupied it.
38 The high officials and regional commanders repeatedly urged the Prince of Xiāngdōng to ascend the throne.
In the eleventh month,
on Bǐngzǐ,
Shìzǔ assumed the imperial throne at Jiānglíng,
changed the era name,
and issued a general amnesty.
He changed Tàiqīng to Chéngshèng.
The Emperor did not ascend the main hall;
the officials merely stood in attendance.
History records that the Emperor could not properly begin his reign.
39 On Dīngchǒu,
he appointed Yífēng Hóu Xún as the Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
40 On Jǐmǎo,
he established the Prince’s heir Fāngjǔ as Crown Prince,
changing his name to Yuánliáng.
The imperial son Fāngzhì was made Prince of Jìn’ān,
Fānglüè was made Prince of Shǐ’ān,
and Fāngděng’s son Zhuāng was made Prince of Yǒngjiā.
Fāngděng had campaigned against Xiāngzhōu,
was defeated in battle, and died.
Xiūróng,
established by Emperor Wén of Wèi,
since the Jìn dynasty,
held the rank among the Nine Concubines.
During the rebellion of Hóu Jǐng,
more than half of the provinces and commanderies fell to Wèi.
From Bālíng down to Jiànkāng,
the boundary was the Cháng Jiāng.
The northern boundary of Jīngzhōu extended to Wǔníng,
the western boundary reached Xiákǒu,
the northern boundary extended to Wǔníng,
forming the boundary with the Prince of Yuèyáng, Chá.
The western boundary reached Xiákǒu,
forming the boundary with the Prince of Wǔlíng, Jì.
“Xiá” should be written as “Xiá.”
The reach of imperial decrees
was only about a thousand lǐ,
and the registered households
numbered no more than thirty thousand.
41 Lù Nà attacked Héngzhōu Governor Dīng Dàoguì at Lùkǒu,
and defeated him.
Héngzhōu’s seat was at Héngyáng County.
Twenty lǐ east of the county was Líng Lake,
whose water was deep and green,
used for brewing wine,
which was sweet and delicious,
called Línglù.
Lùkǒu was the mouth of Líng Lake.
The Táng Zhì states: Tánzhōu had a garrison at Lùkǒu.
Dīng Dù said: East of Xiāng was the Lù River.
Zhāng Shùnmín’s Chēn Xíng Lù: From the mouth of Jiāyú County, traveling by boat over seventy lǐ,
one reaches Lùxīkǒu.
The Nánběi Duìjìng Tú: From Yuèzhōu, following the river northeast,
passing Hóujìng Harbor, Shénlín Harbor, Xiànghú Harbor, Xīndǎkǒu, Shítóukǒu,
one reaches Lùxīkǒu.
According to the Chēn Xíng Lù and Duìjìng Tú, Lùxīkǒu was not where Dīng Dàoguì was defeated;
only the Táng Zhì’s garrison at Lùkǒu in Tánzhōu is correct.
Lù is pronounced lǜ.
His troops all surrendered to Nà.
The Emperor, hearing of this,
sent envoys to summon Minister of Education Wáng Sēngbiàn, General of the Right Guard Dù Zé, General Who Pacifies the North Péi Zhīhéng, and Yífēng Hóu Xún to jointly campaign against Nà.
Xún stationed his army at Bālíng to await them.
During the rebellion of Hóu Jǐng,
Línglíng native Lǐ Hóngyǎ occupied his commandery,
and the Emperor appointed him as Governor of Yíngzhōu.
Yíngyáng Commandery was also part of the former Hàn Línglíng Commandery,
hence Yíngzhōu was established there.
Suí later made it Yǒngzhōu.
The Emperor approved it.
Dīng Dàoguì gathered his remaining troops and joined him.
Nà sent his general Wú Cáng to attack,
defeated them,
and Hóngyǎ and others retreated to defend Kōngyún City.
Yáo Sīlián’s Liáng Shū writes it as “Kōnglíng Tān.”
The Shuǐjīng Zhù: The old city of Chángshā Jiànníng County,
to the south had Kōnglěng Gorge,
through which the Xiāng River flowed,
with terrifying waves like thunder,
deep like the Three Gorges.
Zhāng Shùnmín’s Chēn Xíng Lù said: From the mouth of Lǐlíng River, traveling south over ten lǐ,
there is Kōnglíng Bank.
The Kǎoyì states: The Diǎn Lüè writes it as “Kōnglíng City,”
but now follows the Liáng Shū.
I believe
“Kōnglíng”
is likely
a mistake for
“Kōnglíng.”
Shortly after,
Nà requested to surrender,
asking to send his wife and children,
sending his wife and children as hostages to show sincerity.
Nà’s troops all wept,
saying:
“Because Wáng Láng was imprisoned,
we fled to Xiāngzhōu to escape punishment,
with no other intentions.”
Then they handed over his wife and children to Mín.
When Mín reached Bālíng,
Xún said:
“This is deceit;
they will surely attack us.”
So he secretly made preparations.
Nà indeed followed Mín at night with light troops,
planning to reach the city walls and raise a clamor.
In the twelfth month,
on the morning of Rénwǔ,
ten lǐ from Bālíng,
meaning Nà’s troops marched at night until morning,
ten lǐ away from Bālíng,
they raised a clamor,
and the army was all startled.
Xún sat on a folding chair,
watching from the fortress gate.
Nà attacked by water,
arrows falling like rain,
but Xún was eating sugarcane,
showing no fear at all.
Calmly, he directed his officers and soldiers to attack,
capturing one of their warships;
Nà retreated to defend Chángshā.
42 On Rénwǔ,
the Qí ruler returned to Yè;
on Wùwǔ,
he went again to Jìnyáng.
12. The Tǔyùhún kèhán Kuālǚ,
although he had exchanged envoys with Wei, continued his raids and plunder without cease.
Tǔ,
follows the entering tone of tūn.
Yù,
pronounced yù.
Shǐ,
Shūlì fān;
same below.
Chāo,
Chǔjiāo fān.
[The Wei forces] reached Gūzāng,
to attack him.
Kuālǚ became fearful,
and requested submission;
but soon after, he again exchanged envoys with Qí.
The Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Shǐ Níng spied on his return,
and ambushed him at Chìquán.
Táng Records: Gūzāng County in Liángzhōu had the Chìshuǐ Army,
originally the Chìwū Garrison,
with the Chìwū Spring,
hence the name.
Its area was five thousand one hundred eighty lǐ,
the largest of the armies.
Fù,
Fúyòu fān.
Chān,
Chǒuyán fān,
also Chǒuyàn fān.
13. Lù Nà built fortifications along both banks,
to resist Wáng Sēngbiàn.
Nà's soldiers were all veterans of a hundred battles,
and Sēngbiàn feared them,
not daring to advance lightly.
He gradually constructed connecting walls to press them.
Nà thought Sēngbiàn was timid,
and made no preparations;
in the fifth month,
on Jiǎzǐ,
Sēngbiàn ordered his armies to advance simultaneously by water and land,
launching a fierce attack.
Sēngbiàn personally held the flags and drums,
and Yífēng Hóu Xún personally endured arrows and stones,
capturing two of his fortifications;
Nà's forces were greatly defeated,
fleeing on foot,
and defended Chángshā.
On Yǐchǒu,
Sēngbiàn advanced and besieged it.
Sēngbiàn sat on a mound overseeing the construction of the siege works,
when Wú Zàng and Lǐ Xiánmíng led a thousand elite troops, opened the gates and charged out,
shielded by their shields, they advanced straight,
heading for Sēngbiàn.
At that time, Dù Cè and Dù Kān were both by his side,
with only a little over a hundred armored guards,
they fought fiercely to resist them.
Sēngbiàn remained seated on his folding chair, unmoving,
Péi Zhīhéng attacked Zàng and others from the side,
Zàng and others were defeated and retreated,
Xiánmíng died.
Lǐ Xiánmíng,
was originally a general of Hóu Jǐng,
after Jǐng's defeat,
he submitted to Wáng Lín.
14. Wǔlíng Wáng Jì reached Bājùn,
and hearing there were Wèi troops,
sent the former Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Bāxī Qiáo Yān to lead his army back to rescue Shǔ.
Earlier,
Yáng Qiányùn had requested to be Liángzhōu Cìshǐ,
but Jì made him Tóngzhōu Cìshǐ;
Yáng Fǎchēn requested to be Lízhōu Cìshǐ,
but was made Shāzhōu Cìshǐ:
it seems he used Píngxīng as Shāzhōu.
Tóng,
pronounced tóng.
Chēn,
Chǒulín fān.
Qiányùn's nephew Lüè advised Qiányùn, saying:
"Now that Hóu Jǐng has just been pacified,
we should unite our hearts and join our strength.
Shuì,
Shìruì fān.
Lù,
pronounced liú,
also pronounced liù,
meaning to combine strength.
Yet brothers take up arms against each other.
Zuǒzhuàn,
Zǐchǎn said:
"In ancient times, Gāoxīnshì had two sons,
the elder was Èbó,
the younger was Shíchén,
they could not get along,
daily they sought spears and shields,
to attack each other."
When wood is rotten, it cannot be carved.
Lúnyǔ,
Confucius said:
"Rotten wood cannot be carved."
It would be better to send word to Guānzhōng,
then both merit and fame can be preserved."
Qiányùn agreed with him,
and ordered Lüè to garrison Jiàngé with two thousand men,
and also sent his son-in-law Yuè Guǎng to garrison Ānzhōu.
Wǔdài Zhì: Pǔ'ān Jùn,
Liáng established Nán'ānzhōu,
later changed to Ānzhōu.
Pǔ'ān was formerly called Nán'ān,
Western Wèi changed it to Pǔ'ān.
Jiàng,
Jíliàng fān.
The Wèi Tàishī Yǔwén Tài secretly bestowed an iron pledge to Qiányùn,
appointing him Piàojí Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Liángzhōu Cìshǐ.
In Western Wèi's official hierarchy,
Piàojí Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
ranked below Zhùguó Dàjiāngjūn.
Piào,
Pìmiào fān.
Hóulǚlíng,
a three-character Xìng of the northern tribes.
Lüè retreated to join Yuè Guǎng,
turned the city over to respond to Yuán Shǐ,
and Shǐ entered and occupied Ānzhōu.
On Jiǎxū,
Yǔwén Jiǒng reached Fúshuǐ,
the Fúshuǐ flows from Lóngzhōu into Tóngzhōu's territory.
Tóngzhōu was administered from Fú,
its city walls faced west towards the Fúshuǐ.
Fú,
pronounced fú.
Jiǒng divided his army to guard it,
and advanced to attack Chéngdū.
At that time, Chéngdū had less than ten thousand troops,
its granaries and storehouses were empty,
Yǒngfēng Hóu Huī defended the city walls,
and Jiǒng besieged him.
Qiáo Yān sent Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Jǐng Xīn and Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ Zhào Báhù to aid Chéngdū.
Wǔdài Zhì: Lóngshān Jùn Lóngshān Xiàn,
formerly called Qiánwéi Xiàn,
where Jiāngzhōu was established.
Wǔlíng Wáng Jì reached Bādōng,
and hearing that Hóu Jǐng had already been pacified,
then regretted his actions,
summoned the Crown Prince Yuánzhào and reprimanded him.
[Yuánzhào] replied:
"Although Hóu Jǐng is pacified,
Jiānglíng is not yet subdued."
Jì also, having already assumed the imperial title,
Jì assumed the imperial title,
see the previous year in the previous scroll.
wished to continue advancing east.
His officers and soldiers day and night longed to return home,
his Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Kāiyè thought they should return to rescue the foundation,
and reconsider plans later;
all the generals agreed.
Yuánzhào and Liú Xiàoshèng firmly said it could not be done,
Jì followed them,
and declared to the multitude:
"Whoever dares to remonstrate shall die!"
On Jǐchǒu,
Jì reached Xīlíng,
his military might was very strong,
ships and vessels covered the river.
Hùjūn Lù Fǎhé built two fortifications on both banks of the gorge mouth,
transported stones to fill the river,
and blocked it with iron chains.
The Emperor released Rèn Yuē from prison,
making him Sīmǎ to the Prince of Jìn'ān,
the Emperor had enfeoffed his son Fāngzhì as Prince of Jìn'ān.
Rèn,
pronounced rén.
During the battle of Chìtíng,
Fǎhé saved Yuē,
thus there was old kindness,
so he sent him to assist.
"Your crime is unpardonable,
I did not kill you,
precisely for today!"
Thereupon he withdrew imperial guards to assign to him,
and also promised him the daughter of Lúlǐng Wáng Xù in marriage,
sending Xuānměng Jiāngjūn Liú Fēn to go with him.
15. On Gēngchén,
Bāzhōu Cìshǐ Yú Xiàoqǐng led ten thousand troops to join Wáng Sēngbiàn at Chángshā.
16. Yùzhāng Tàishǒu Guānníng Hóu Yǒng,
was indecisive and slow to judge,
his attendants Wǔ Mánnú wielded power,
the army commander Wén Zhòng despised this.
Yǒng led troops to attack Lù Nà,
reaching Gōngtíng Lake,
Zhòng killed Mánnú,
Yǒng's army collapsed,
and he fled to Jiānglíng.
Zhòng led his troops to flee to Kāijiàn Hóu Fān,
Fān killed him and took his troops.
Kāijiàn Hóu Fān was at that time garrisoning Póyáng.
Shěn Yuē said: Sòng Wéndì divided Fēngyáng Xiàn of Línhè Jùn to establish Kāijiàn Xiàn.
On the 17th day of the sixth month,
Rénchén,
Wǔlíng Wáng Jì constructed connecting fortifications,
attacked and severed the iron chains,
and Lù Fǎhé sent urgent pleas for help one after another.
The Emperor again released Xiè Dárén from prison;
last year, when Hóu Jǐng was defeated,
Xiè Dárén was captured,
but instead of being killed, he was imprisoned.
The Eastern Palace of Liáng had three commandants including the Infantry Commandant.
Commandant,
pronounced as hù jiào fān.
He also sent an envoy to escort Wáng Lín,
ordering him to persuade Lù Nà.
On Yǐwèi,
Lín arrived at Chángshā,
Sēngbiàn had him escorted and shown to Lù Nà,
Lù Nà's troops all bowed and wept,
and sent word to Sēngbiàn saying:

3 The Grand Preceptor of Wei, Yǔwén Tài, first established the system of nine ranks of appointment,
to order the official titles and ranks within and outside the court,
changing the out-of-stream grades to nine orders.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Tài ordered the Minister of Works Lú Biàn to extensively model it on the Zhou dynasty's establishment of offices,
setting up the Three Dukes and the Three Solitaries,
to serve as officials for discussing the Way;
next, he established the Six Ministers,
to divide and manage the various affairs.
The "inner appointments" refer to the ministers of the royal court: the Three Dukes are of the ninth rank of appointment,
the Three Solitaries are of the eighth rank of appointment,
the Six Ministers are of the seventh rank of appointment,
the Senior Grand Masters are of the sixth rank of appointment,
the Middle Grand Masters are of the fifth rank of appointment,
the Junior Grand Masters are of the fourth rank of appointment,
the Senior Servicemen are of the third rank of appointment,
the Middle Servicemen are of the second rank of appointment,
the Junior Servicemen are of the first rank of appointment.
The "outer appointments" refer to the feudal lords and their ministers: the various Dukes are of the ninth rank of appointment,
the various Marquises are of the eighth rank of appointment,
the various Earls are of the seventh rank of appointment,
the various Viscounts are of the sixth rank of appointment,
the various Barons are of the fifth rank of appointment,
the Solitaries and Ministers of the various Dukes are of the fourth rank of appointment,
the Solitaries and Ministers of the Marquises, and the Grand Masters of the Dukes are of the third rank of appointment,
the Solitaries and Ministers of the Viscounts and Barons, the Grand Masters of the Marquises and Earls, and the Senior Servicemen of the Dukes are of the second rank of appointment,
the Middle Servicemen of the Dukes, and the Senior Servicemen of the Marquises and Earls are of the first rank of appointment,
the Junior Servicemen of the Dukes, the Middle and Junior Servicemen of the Marquises and Earls, and the Servicemen of the Viscounts and Barons are not appointed.
The system of salary grades: Junior Servicemen receive 125 shi,
from Middle Servicemen up to Senior Grand Masters, each rank doubles the previous,
with Senior Grand Masters receiving 4,000 shi;
Ministers receive two parts,
Solitaries receive three parts,
Dukes receive four parts,
each increasing by one part,
thus the Dukes, reaching the full number, receive 10,000 shi.
The ninth order receives 120 shi,
from the eighth order down to the seventh order,
for every two orders, it is divided into six parts,
and going downward, each loses one part,
with the second order both being 40 shi.
In distributing salaries,
they look at the quality of the year:
a yield of up to four fu per mu is considered an upper year,
in an upper year, the full salary is distributed;
three fu is considered a middle year,
in a middle year, half the salary is distributed;
two fu is considered a lower year,
in a lower year, one-tenth of the salary is distributed;
a year with no yield is considered a famine year,
and no salary is distributed.

In the summer of the 12th year,
in the fourth month,
the Róurǎn invaded Qí's Sìzhōu.
The ruler of Qí personally led a punitive expedition against them from Jìnyáng,
reaching Héngzhōu,
where the Róurǎn scattered and fled.
The emperor, with over two thousand cavalry as his rearguard,
encamped at Huángguāduī.
A separate force of the Róurǎn, tens of thousands of cavalry strong, suddenly arrived.
The emperor slept peacefully,
rising only at dawn,
his demeanor calm and composed.
He pointed out the terrain and situation,
then unleashed his troops in a fierce attack;
the Róurǎn were routed,
and he broke through their encirclement.
The Róurǎn fled,
and he pursued and attacked them,
leaving corpses strewn for over twenty lǐ,
capturing Ānluóchén's wife and children,
and taking over thirty thousand prisoners.
He ordered the military governor of Shànwú, Gāo Ānàgōng, to lead several thousand cavalry to block their escape route.
At that time, the Róurǎn army was still strong,
and Ānàgōng, due to his small force,
requested reinforcements,
but the emperor instead reduced his troops by half.
Ānàgōng fought fiercely,
and utterly defeated them.
Ānluóchén fled over cliffs and valleys,
barely escaping with his life.
The same Gāo Ānàgōng,
when employed by Qí Wénxuān, fought to the death to defeat the enemy,
but when used by the later ruler, he betrayed his lord to save his own life.
It seems that stern authority can still make them know fear,
while excessive favor is insufficient to secure their utmost loyalty.
Sāi,
is pronounced xīzé fān.
On the bǐngyín day,
the emperor sent the cavalier attendant-in-ordinary Yǔ Xìn and others on a diplomatic mission to Wèi.
On the guǐyǒu day,
Chén Bàxiān was appointed as Minister of Works.
On the dīngwèi day,
the ruler of Qí again personally attacked the Róurǎn,
and utterly defeated them.
On the gēngxū day,
the Grand Preceptor of Wèi, Yùwén Tài, poisoned and killed the deposed emperor.
In the fifth month,
Yuè Chì from Zhízhōu and Huáng Guó from Yángzhōu in Wèi rebelled.
According to the Wǔdài Zhì: Ānkāng County in Xīchéng Commandery,
was established as Ānkāng Commandery during Qí,
and as Dōngliángzhōu during Wèi,
later renamed Zhízhōu by Western Wèi.
Xīxiāng County in Hànchuān Commandery,
formerly called Fēngníng,
had Yángzhōu and Yángchuān Commandery established there.
Examining the Hànchuān Zhì,
Shǔ divided Hàn's Chénggù County to establish Nánxiāng County,
which Jìn renamed Xīxiāng County.
Wèi abolished the county,
but still established Fēngníng County at the Fēngníng garrison.
They were unsuccessful.
Grand Preceptor Tài ordered the General of Chariots and Cavalry, Lǐ Qiānzhé, and Dūn to jointly suppress Chì and the others,
and pacified them.
Then, together with Dūn, they marched south,
conquering territory as far as Bāzhōu.
Later Hàn divided the northern boundary of Dàngqú to establish Hànchāng County,
which Shǔ's First Sovereign established as Bāxī Commandery;
Sòng Wǔdì established Guīhuà Commandery.
Wèi established Dàgǔ Commandery at the seat of Hànchāng County,
and also established Bāzhōu north of the commandery.
According to the Wǔdài Zhì: Huàchéng County in Qīnghuà Commandery,
was where Liáng established Guīhuà Commandery and Bāzhōu.
The Kǎoyì states:
"The Diǎn Lüè says: 'Beheaded Liáng's Bāzhōu Governor Móu Ānpíng.'"
Now we follow the Zhōushū and Běishǐ.
This was the state of the Bāzi during the Spring and Autumn period,
the territory of the Sānbā commanderies.
It was the land of the Bǎipǔ during the Spring and Autumn period,
located between Xīchéng and Shàngyōng.
Pǔ,
is pronounced bó mù fān.
Qiānzhé attacked them,
and the Wǔzǐwáng fled.
Qiānzhé pursued and attacked,
defeating them.
Tài appointed Qiānzhé as Governor of Xìnzhōu,
garrisoning Báidì.
Xìnzhōu initially had no stored provisions.
Qiānzhé and his soldiers together gathered kudzu roots for food.
Whenever there was unusual food,
he would share and taste it with them,
and the soldiers were moved and pleased.
He repeatedly attacked the rebellious Mán tribes,
defeating them,
until the various Mán tribes were awed into submission,
all sending provisions,
and sending their sons and younger brothers as hostages.
Thus, the region of the province was pacified,
and military supplies became ample.
The Róurǎn Yǐzhān Dáguān invaded Wèi's Guǎngwǔ.
According to Wèi Shōu's records: Piānchéng Commandery in Dōngxiàzhōu included Guǎngwǔ County.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Fēnglín County in Yán'ān Commandery,
was where Later Wèi established Guǎngwǔ County and Piānchéng Commandery.
In the 9th year of Xīníng of Sòng,
Fēnglín was abolished as a town,
and merged into Fūshī County.
They were defeated.
"Sent to attack,"
likely should be
"pursued and attacked."
[Chapter note: The 12-line edition correctly has
"pursued";
the 11-line edition is the same;
the Kǒng edition is the same.
The Marquis of Qǔjiāng, Bó, Governor of Guǎngzhōu,
considered himself not appointed by the emperor,
(Chén Bàxiān had supported Xiāo Bó as Governor of Guǎngzhōu,
see scroll 162, Emperor Wǔ's Tàiqīng 3rd year.)
and the emperor also suspected him.
Bó requested permission to come to court;
in the fifth month,
on the yǐsì day,
the emperor appointed Wáng Lín as Governor of Guǎngzhōu,
and Bó as Governor of Jìnzhōu.
According to the Wǔdài Zhì: Tóng'ān Commandery,
was where Liáng established Yùzhōu,
later renamed Jìnzhōu.
Also, because he had won the people's hearts,
the emperor wanted to send him far away.
Lín was on close terms with the Palace Secretary Lǐ Yīng of Guànghàn,
and privately said to Yīng:
"I, Lín,
am a man of lowly status,
yet have been promoted to this position by His Majesty.
Now the realm is not yet settled,
yet I am transferred to Lǐngnán.
Should any unforeseen event occur,
how could my strength be of use!
I suspect His Majesty's intention is merely to doubt me.
My own expectations are limited,
meaning I assess my own position and dare not harbor improper ambitions.
Fèn,
is pronounced fú wèn fān.
Why not appoint me as Governor of Yōngzhōu, garrisoning Wǔníng?
I would then release my troops to farm,
and defend the state."
Yīng agreed with his words but did not dare to report them.
The history records that Wáng Lín was loyal to his duty, but the emperor could not employ him.
Wèi guó,
is pronounced yú wèi fān.
The Cavalier Attendant, Yǔ Jìcái of Xīnyě, said to the emperor:
"Last year, on the bǐngshēn day of the eighth month,
the moon encroached upon the central star of the Heart constellation.
This month, on the bǐngxū day,
red qi violated the Northern Dipper.
The Heart represents the Heavenly King,
and bǐng governs the region of Chǔ.
I fear that in the jiànzǐ month, a great army will enter Jiānglíng.
Your Majesty should leave an important minister to guard Jiānglíng,
and return to the capital with the army's banners to avoid this calamity.
Even if the Wèi barbarians press upon us,
we would only lose Jīng and Xiāng,
and the altars of state
would still be secure."
The emperor was also knowledgeable in astronomy,
and knew that Chǔ would face disaster.
He sighed and said:
"Fortune and calamity lie with Heaven;
what good is avoiding it!"
Heaven warned the emperor,
not abandoning him;
but the emperor did not know to avoid it,
thus abandoning himself.
On the 21st day of the sixth month,
Rénwǔ,
Bùdàhán Sà of Qí led forty thousand troops towards Jīngzhōu.
Wáng Sēngbiàn sent Hóu Zhèn and Zhāng Biāo to lead troops from Shíliáng to assist Yán Chāodá in resisting them,
but Zhèn and Biāo delayed and did not advance.
General Yǐn Lìngsī led over ten thousand men intending to launch a surprise attack on Xūyí.
Duàn Sháo, the Governor of Jìzhōu in Qí, led troops to suppress Dōngfāng Bái'é at Sùyù.
Both Guǎnglíng and Jīngzhōu sent urgent reports,
causing concern among the generals.
Sháo said:
"The Liáng dynasty is in turmoil,
the state lacks a stable ruler,
the people are uncertain in their allegiances,
and the strong follow their own interests.
Chén Bàxiān and others outwardly profess unity,
but inwardly they are divided.
You gentlemen need not worry,
I have thoroughly assessed the situation!"
He then left Yítóng Sānsī Jìng Xiǎnxié and others to besiege Sùyù.
"Jìng Xiǎnxié"
should be
"Jìng Xiǎnjùn".
He then marched out via Xūyí.
Lìngsī did not expect the Qí army to arrive so suddenly,
and retreated upon seeing their approach.
Sháo advanced to attack Chāodá,
defeated him,
then turned towards Guǎnglíng,
causing Chén Bàxiān to lift the siege and flee.
Dù Sēngmíng returned to Dāntú,
while Hóu Zhèn and Zhāng Biāo returned to Qínjùn.
Wú Míngchè besieged Hǎixī.
Hǎixī County,
during the Western Hàn, belonged to Dōnghǎi Commandery,
during the Eastern Hàn, it belonged to Guǎnglíng Commandery,
during the reign of Emperor Míng of Qí, Dōnghǎi Commandery was established,
in the seventh year of Wǔdìng of Eastern Wèi,
it was renamed Hǎixī Commandery,
present-day Xīhǎi Prefecture is its location.
They carved wood into arrows,
cut paper for fletching,
besieged it for ten ten-day periods,
but ultimately could not capture it and withdrew.
On the 22nd, the Róurán led their remaining people eastward,
intending to raid southward.
The ruler of Qí led light cavalry to intercept them at Jīnchuān.
According to the Táng records: the Shànyú Prefecture administered Jīnhé County.
This is likely Jīnchuān.
Shuài,
read as lǜ.
They fled far away,
but the Governor of Yíngzhōu, Língqiū Wáng Jùn, set an ambush and attacked them,
capturing several dozen of their renowned chieftains.
On the 23rd, the Diānzhì Qiāng chieftain Dānhéng lost his state,
fled to Wèi,
and the Grand Preceptor Tài sent Yǔwén Dǎo, the Governor of Qínzhōu, to lead troops to install him.
On the 24th, Duàn Sháo of Qí returned to Sùyù,
sent a persuasive envoy to convince Dōngfāng Bái'é,
Bái'é opened the gates and requested an alliance,
whereupon he was seized and executed.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Gēngxū,
the ruler of Qí returned to Yè.
On the 26th, the Grand Preceptor Tài of Wèi toured westward,
reaching Yuánzhōu.
In the eighth month,
on Rénchén,
Qí appointed Yuè, the Prince of Qīnghé and Governor of Sīzhōu, as Grand Guardian,
the Minister of Works Wèi Càn as Minister over the Masses,
the Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent Hóumòchén Xiàng as Minister of Works,
the Prefect of the Imperial Secretariat Yān, Prince of Píngyáng, as Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
Yǎn, Prince of Chángshān, as Prefect of the Imperial Secretariat,
and Huàn, Prince of Shàngdǎng and Director of the Central Secretariat, as Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
On Yǐhài,
Yuán Xù, Yítóng Sānsī of Qí, was implicated in an affair and ordered to commit suicide.
On Dīngchǒu,
the ruler of Qí went to Jìnyáng.
Before the ruler of Qí became Chancellor of Wèi,
Gāo Lóngzhī, the Prince of Píngyuán, Grand Guardian, and Director of the Imperial Secretariat, often insulted him.
When he was about to receive the abdication,
Lóngzhī again considered it inappropriate.
The matter is recorded in the 163rd volume, the first year of the Jiǎnwén Emperor's Tàibǎo era.
Fù,
read as fú yòu.
Cuī Jìshū slandered him,
saying, "Lóngzhī often shows sympathy to those bringing lawsuits,
to indicate that he is not the one making the decisions."
The Emperor confined him in the Imperial Secretariat.
Cuī Jìshū was repaying a grudge from his exile to the frontier.
He said to Xù:
"In friendship with the Prince,
we should not betray each other in life or death."
Someone secretly reported this,
and the Emperor became enraged,
ordering strong men to strike him over a hundred blows with their fists before releasing him.
On Xīnsì,
he died on the road.
After some time,
the Emperor's resentment towards Lóngzhī resurfaced.
He seized his son Huìdēng and twenty others and brought them before him.
The Emperor struck the saddle with his whip,
and in an instant, their heads were severed,
and their corpses were thrown into the Zhāng River.
He also had Lóngzhī's tomb opened,
his corpse removed,
the bones chopped up and burned,
and the ashes discarded into the Zhāng River.

On the 29th, the ruler of Qí sent Yǎn, Prince of Chángshān, Huàn, Prince of Shàngdǎng, Yuè, Prince of Qīnghé, and Duàn Sháo, Prince of Píngyuán, to lead troops in constructing the cities of Fá'è, Xīnchéng, Yánchéng, and Hénánchéng southwest of Luòyáng.
In the ninth month,
the ruler of Qí inspected the four cities,
intending to provoke a response from the Wèi army.
The Wèi army did not emerge,
and the historian notes that Qí was strong,
and Yǔwén Tài feared them.
On the 30th, Yǔwén Tài of Wèi ordered the Palace Attendant Cuī Yóu to open the Huíchē Road to connect with Hànzhōng.
According to the biography of Cuī Yóu in the History of the Northern Dynasties,
Tài wanted to open the old Liáng-Hàn road,
so he ordered Yóu to open a road for carts,
cutting through mountains and filling valleys for over five hundred lǐ,
reaching Liángzhōu.
This was specifically to widen the old road
for cart traffic.
Previous historians likely mistakenly wrote the character for "connect" as
"huí" (meaning "return"),
and later copyists further omitted the radical, turning it into
"huí" (meaning "circle").
Tài is recorded by surname without his official title,
which also lacks any meaningful precedent.
The Emperor was fond of metaphysical discussions.
On Xīnmǎo,
he lectured on the Lǎozǐ at the Lóngguāng Hall.
On the 32nd, Bó, the Marquis of Qǔjiāng, moved to Shǐxīng,
and Wáng Lín sent his deputy general Sūn Yáng to first occupy Pānyú.
On Yǐsì,
Wèi sent the Pillar of State, Duke of Chángshān Yú Jǐn, the Duke of Zhōngshān Yǔwén Hù, and the Grand General Yáng Zhōng to lead fifty thousand troops on an invasion.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on Rénxū,
they departed from Cháng'ān.
Zhǎngsūn Jiǎn asked Jǐn:
"What strategy do you think Xiāo Yì will adopt?"
Jǐn replied:
"Displaying troops along the Hàn and Miǎn Rivers,
sweeping across and crossing the Yangtze,
directly occupying Dānyáng—this is the superior strategy.
This means returning east to Jiànkāng.
Juǎn,
read as juǎn.
Strengthening their walls and battlements,
awaiting reinforcements—this is the middle strategy.
If movement is difficult,
defending the outer city walls—this is the inferior strategy."
Jiǎn asked:
"What strategy do you predict Yì will choose?"
Jǐn said:
"The inferior strategy."
Jiǎn asked:
"Why?"
Jǐn replied:
"The Xiāo clan has protected and held Jiāngnán,
enduring for several jì.
Twelve years make one jì.
They have had no time for external expansion.
Moreover, with our troubles with the Qí clan,
they will certainly think we lack the strength to divide our forces.
Furthermore, Yì is timid and lacking in strategy,
suspicious and indecisive.
The common people are difficult to involve in new plans,
and they are all attached to their homes.
That is why I know he will adopt the inferior strategy!"
On the Guǐhài day,
Wǔníng Commandery Administrator Zōng Jūn reported that the Wei army was about to arrive.
The Emperor summoned his ministers to discuss the matter.
Commander-in-Chief Hú Sēngyòu and Minister of the Imperial Treasury Huáng Luóhàn said:
"Our two states maintain friendly relations;
there are no grievances between us.
This surely cannot be true."
Palace Attendant Wáng Chēn said:
"I have observed the demeanor of Yǔwén,
and it is certainly not plausible."
Last year, Wáng Chēn had been an envoy to Wei,
so he claimed to have gauged their demeanor,
insisting that such an event was impossible.
This can be said to be a poor assessment of the state's affairs.
On the Bǐngyín day,
Yú Jǐn arrived at Fán and Dèng,
and Prince Xiāo Chá of Liáng led his troops to join him.
On the Xīn
mǎo day,
the Emperor suspended his lectures,
specifically the lectures on the Laozi.
The character "shuài"
is read as "lǜ";
the same applies below.
Wáng Chēn reached Shílínjiǔ,
Dù Yòu said: Shílínjiǔ is located above Miǎnkǒu in Miǎn Prefecture.
According to the biography of Prince Xiù of Ānchéng in the Book of Liáng,
Shílínjiǔ at that time belonged to the territory of Jìnglíng.
He sent a swift message to Huáng Luóhàn, saying:
"I have reached Shílínjiǔ,
and the border is peaceful.
The earlier reports were nothing but child's play."
Upon hearing this, the Emperor grew suspicious.
On the Gēngwǔ day,
the lectures resumed,
with all officials dressed in military attire to listen.
On the Xīnwèi day,
the Emperor sent the Secretariat Director Lǐ Yīng to Jiànkāng,
summoning Wáng Sēngbiàn to serve as Grand Commander and Governor of Jīng Province,
and ordering Chén Bàxiān to relocate and garrison Yáng Province.
Wáng Sēngbiàn dispatched Yù Province Governor Hóu Zhèn, leading Chéng Língxǐ and others as the vanguard,
and Yǎn Province Governor Dù Sēngmíng, leading Wú Míngchè and others as the rear guard.
Upon receiving the summons, Wáng Sēngbiàn should have immediately rallied to support the emperor.
Yet, while outwardly deploying various armies,
there was no swift or urgent advance.
The fall of Jiānglíng
was Wáng Sēngbiàn's fault.
The character "shuài"
is read as "lǜ."
On the Jiǎxū day,
the Emperor ascended the Fenghuang Pavilion at night,
leaning against the railings and sighing:
"A guest star has entered the constellations of Yì and Zhěn."
Leaning against the railings and then shifting position is called "xǐyǐ."
Yì and Zhěn
correspond to the region of Chǔ and Jīng Province.
The imperial consorts and attendants all wept.
Lù Fǎhé, upon hearing that the Wei army had arrived from Yǐng Province,
entered Hànkǒu
and intended to march to Jiānglíng.
The Emperor sent someone to intercept him, saying:
"You are capable of defeating the enemy on your own.
Just guard Yǐng Province;
there is no need to move!"
Lù Fǎhé returned to his province,
whitewashed the city gates,
donned mourning garments,
and sat on a reed mat
for an entire day
before removing them.
In the eleventh month,
the Emperor held a grand military review outside the Jīnyáng Gate.
South of the Yangtze, the capital was Jiànkāng,
with twelve outer city gates,
all named after the gates of Luòyáng.
The Emperor's capital at Jiānglíng
also named its outer city gates after those of Jiànkāng.
The Jīnyáng Gate
was the second gate from the east on the southern wall of the city.
The Emperor returned to the palace in a light carriage.
On the Guǐwèi day,
the Wei army crossed the Hàn River.
Yú Jǐn ordered Yǔwén Hù and Yáng Zhōng to lead elite cavalry to first seize Jiāngjīn,
cutting off the eastern route.
On the Jiǎshēn day,
Yǔwén Hù captured Wǔníng
and captured Zōng Jūn.
On that day,
the Emperor rode out of the city to inspect the palisades.
The character "xíng"
is read as "xià mèng fān";

Zhái,

Húshù,

Shù,

In the 30th year, at the beginning,

Guīyàn

Guīyàn harbored resentment in his heart.

Yuè repeatedly led troops and achieved merit,

South of the city,

The Emperor took the courtesan Xuē Shì into the rear palace.

The Emperor was greatly angered,

Consort Xuē was favored by the Emperor,

Just as the toasts began,

Lǐ Yānnián's song from the Hàn dynasty says:

Zhì,
